#5528. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5526. Neoclouds face a shakeout as cloud-native software skills decide who survives

AI infrastructure clouds have multiplied as GPU capital pours into new data centers, but standing up capacity is proving easier than running it at scale. With Kubernetes now hardened into the operating layer for AI factories, the cloud-native community holds expertise that many of these new providers lack.

KubeCon has been shifting toward an AI infrastructure event, with container orchestration for AI and distributed inference now central to the conversation. The newer AI clouds run on the same computing fundamentals as the hyperscalers before them, yet many specialize narrowly and lack a bridge to the enterprise systems that will ultimately consume their capacity, according to Sarbjeet Johal (pictured), chief executive officer of Stackpane.

“I’m afraid that the neoclouds, if they don’t partner with the ones who are appreciating the brownfield, they will suffer,” Johal said. “They can’t survive on their own because, who is going to take that compute from them? It’s the hyperscalers. The neoclouds are the overflow.”

Johal spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the event’s first-day takeaways, from AI-written code and token economics to the maturing neocloud market and the skills needed to run it. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes spent more than a decade evolving in fits and starts, and the payoff is now showing up in AI. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track to this year’s KubeCon North America schedule, a sign of where practitioner attention has moved. Kubernetes now runs across about two-thirds of the enterprise, sits inside Nvidia Corp.’s reference architectures and underpins the neoclouds, Furrier noted. Skills honed through years of operating Kubernetes are now being applied directly to the commercial buildout of AI factories, where most of the capital is going.

“Now it’s hardened. So when you have hardened Kubernetes, we’re seeing inference being talked about,” Furrier said. “Who would have thought at this show inference would be discussed? Well, guess what? Distributed inference is the hottest area right now.”

That maturity matters because so much AI capital spending is flowing to new providers. SoftBank Group Corp. unveiled plans to enter the U.S. neocloud business this summer, joining a crowded field. Many existing operators started out building data centers for bitcoin mining or arbitraging spot pricing rather than running large-scale software, according to Furrier, who sees a reckoning ahead. The hard part is less about acquiring GPUs than operating them as a true cloud.

“Half the neoclouds will fail,” Furrier said. “To run a big neocloud, you’ve got to look like CoreWeave. Well, guess what CoreWeave is? The founders know data centers. … People who know large-scale software stacks at scale win.”

The rescue, in Furrier’s view, will come from the cloud-native community. He pointed to CoreWeave Inc., whose engineering is run by former Google Cloud LLC executive Chen Goldberg, as the model for pairing data center know-how with large-scale software skills. He also suggested private equity investors could buy smaller Kubernetes companies to fill the gap. Those companies could command billion-dollar valuations as data center owners with land, power and shell seek help with connectivity, multigeneration Nvidia hardware and workloads that span data centers, he explained. Johal, who watched a similar story play out at Rackspace Technology Inc., agreed that software will decide which providers last.

“We have seen this movie earlier. So if you want to be a good hyperscaler, if you don’t have the software chops, you’re dead,” Johal said of the new AI infrastructure clouds. “We knew how to run data centers at Rackspace, but we didn’t have software chops. … Without software chops, you’re dead in the water.”

#5525. EXCLUSIVE: Olympic Champion Tara Lipinski Shares Her ‘Controversial’ Christmas Decorating Rule—and Why She’s Starting Now

Olympic figure skating champion Tara Lipinski is picking sides in some of the most divisive holiday decor debates of all time as she hosts HGTV’s "Big Bargain Holiday Showdown."

The 44-year-old Lipinski, who earned gold in the 1998 Winter Games, reveals her holiday decor rules to Realtor.com® ahead of the Nov. 10 premiere of the new six-episode competition series.

She covers everything from when it's appropriate to start decorating to when decorations should be removed, and whether Christmas lights are better in multicolor or monotone.

On the show, two teams of family, friends, and neighbors go head-to-head in a holiday-themed design battle where they have just 48 hours and $500 to overhaul one room in their respective homes.

DIY experts Ashley Dixon and Clinton Tharp are on hand to help wrap things up before designers Stephen Brown and Pelar Fullilove judge the spaces and declare the winner of a $2,000 cash prize.

"I know it's very controversial, but I am starting to decorate this week. I am skipping Thanksgiving," Lipinski, who stays in her lane as a neutral host on the HGTV show, tells Realtor.com.

"The older I get, the wider the window has become. I really don't think it can be too early. It's just so fun to walk into your house when it's full of Christmas lights and so cozy and idyllic and warm. ... I like to stretch it as much as I can. That’s why in November, you have a ton of time, you can just relish in it."

Lipinski clarifies that, although she'll set her table to host Thanksgiving, it's jingle all the way until the start of the New Year.

"I always used to take it down right away. I do get a little tired of it when holidays are actually over, so I feel like you've got, like, one week after and then you've got to zip it up," she says.

In Lipinski’s house, which she shares with husband Todd Kapostasy and their 3-year-old daughter, Georgie, the holiday magic is spread in multiple spaces.

"We usually go [for] a more traditional Christmas, the classic, the red, the green," she shares. "Other rooms, we change it up. We do our bedroom a whole winter wonderland, white and gold and silver. And then Georgie, my daughter's room, we do a really fun pink Christmas so we can branch out.

"I feel like it's evolved throughout the years, and there's always adding and subtracting."

There is only one thing that never changes: the Christmas tree.

“We have a lot of artificial trees in the house, but for the one in the living room, our main one, we do a real one,” says Lipinski. “My husband loves that, so that's been his thing since we got married. We've always done a real tree. It's fun. That day we make it a tradition and get dressed up in our Christmas outfit and we go and pick out a tree and make it festive.”

The decision to go faux with trees everywhere except the living room has always been unanimous, but the couple have clashed in the past.

“My husband and I have gotten into a full-blown argument about the amount of Christmas lights that need to be on a tree. He fully understands now that it has to be every inch covered,” she says.

As for whether the Christmas tree lights should be a string of assorted colors or all white, Lipinski says for her house, it depends on the tree’s location.

“I like it to be the multicolored ones. That’s my go-to. Although the ones in my bedroom, since it's all the white theme, we do just the white,” she details.

Lipinski has been honing her holiday home design technique for decades. She credits her mother for inspiring a passion for all the pageantry.

“My mom was meant to be an interior designer, so I grew up with someone who was constantly making our house a home and making it so special, that loves decorating, and I have that same gene,” she shares.

“We are big holiday people. We have a storage unit of not just Christmas [decor]. We decorate every single holiday, so this show just feels like it was meant for both of us. After all the things I've done in my career, I feel like she's probably going to be most proud of this one because it's so spot-on.”

The annual task of decorating the home has become a festive event for the whole family.

“What's fun is my mom and dad still come over, and they decorate with me,” says Lipinski. “My dad's the handy one and my mom is so creative. I couldn't do it without them. We pull out the boxes, we put on Christmas music, we have some hot cocoa, and we decorate together. It's really become a tradition, and now [with] my daughter, it feels like the three generations all together doing it still.”

The family’s dedication to holiday decor already seems to be something Lipinski’s daughter is developing herself.

“The art of decorating, making it special, and doing it with family is what I'm passing down to my daughter—and that we do it together. She loves it,” shares Lipinski. “This year, she's finally really clocking what Christmas is. When I told her it's time to decorate, her eyes lit up, and I just thought, 'Oh, my goodness, I'm creating a little monster here.’”

This year, Lipinski and her team of holiday fanatics plan to spruce up their space with even more trimmings thanks to the seasonal inspiration the show’s creative contestants have gifted.

“Really opening your mind ... the way they utilize the space of the room, like using the chandelier, there [were] some really beautiful entries," she says.

"It felt super immersive and even more magical, so I'm going to try to up the ante this year on my own Christmas decorating from learning those things.”

'Big Bargain Holiday Showdown' premieres on Nov. 10 at 9 p.m. on HGTV and streams the next day on HBO Max.

Karli Mullane is a celebrity and entertainment journalist at Realtor.com. She previously worked at Celeb Map, POPSUGAR, and NBC, covering pop culture, lifestyle, travel, and news of all kinds. Karli earned a BA in History from UCLA and an MA in Broadcast Journalism from San Francisco State University. She is equally grateful to have reported from both Hollywood red carpets and the comfort of her Bay Area home.

#5524. Op-Ed: Open Real Estate Shouldn’t Need an Announcement

The announcement of Open Real Estate was welcome news. It also raised an uncomfortable question: How did we reach the point where keeping the housing market open required an announcement?

Buyers should be able to find available homes. Sellers should understand who can see their property and what they may sacrifice by limiting its exposure. Brokerages should compete on the quality of their advice, service and results.

These principles should be ordinary expectations of our profession. The fact that they now need a name, a coalition and a public defense is a troubling sign of how far the conversation has veered off course.

Brown Harris Stevens, where I serve as executive director, is an initial participating member of Open Real Estate. I support the initiative’s stated commitment to broader access, informed seller decisions and fair competition. But the larger issue extends beyond any platform or participating company. Openness should be how we conduct business every day.

The appeal of exclusive inventory to a brokerage is easy to understand. If buyers believe they need a relationship with a particular company to see certain homes, that company gains an advantage. Exclusive inventory can help attract buyers, recruit and retain agents and strengthen the firm’s position.

The benefit to the seller is less easy to understand and requires a separate explanation. A brokerage’s ability to use a listing to grow its business does not establish that limiting the property’s exposure is the best strategy for the homeowner. Those interests may align in a particular transaction, but that does not make them interchangeable.

Compass has made private exclusives and phased marketing central to its offering, promoting the opportunity to test pricing and generate interest before a broader public launch. Those claims deserve scrutiny because they concern decisions sellers are trusting their advisors to help them make.

What does the seller gain during that period? Which potential buyers cannot see the property? How representative is pricing feedback from a limited audience? What opportunities might the seller lose while broader exposure is delayed?

The recruiting appeal of the strategy is clear: Access to inventory agents and their buyers might otherwise miss. But sellers deserve to hear the other side of that pitch. The inventory attracting people into the network is their home, and restricting access may exclude buyers who could compete for it.

A large brokerage network can provide meaningful exposure, but it still represents only part of the market. The strength of that network does not, by itself, establish that a seller benefits from postponing access to everyone else.

For sellers seeking the strongest price within a practical time frame, I believe broad exposure should be the starting point. Making a home available to more potential buyers creates more opportunity for competing offers and gives the seller a fuller picture of demand. A recommendation to delay that exposure should explain what the seller stands to gain and what they may give up.

The pricing argument also deserves scrutiny. Sellers hire brokers in part for their ability to analyze comparable sales, assess competing inventory and recommend a pricing strategy. If an agent recommends testing a price privately, the seller should ask: Why is feedback from a limited audience more useful than feedback from the broader market? What uncertainty does this approach resolve, and why does resolving it require restricted exposure?

A broker should be prepared to answer those questions with evidence specific to the property and the seller’s circumstances. And the answer shouldn’t be just about obfuscating days on market. When we evaluate how quickly the strategy produces a sale, we should count any private marketing period. The absence of public days on the market does not mean the seller’s clock has stopped.

Some sellers have legitimate reasons to limit exposure. Security, personal circumstances, timing and discretion can all matter. A thoughtful advisor should understand those priorities and recommend a strategy that reflects them.

Those needs existed long before private exclusives became the manufactured proposition they are today. They deserve individual solutions. Their existence does not justify making restricted access the default starting point for sellers.

Seller choice matters. So does how an advisor presents that choice. Which option is introduced first? Which benefits are emphasized? Are the limitations explained with the same conviction? Did the conversation start by asking what the seller’s goals are in the selling process, or did the broker prescribe a strategy without first understanding the specific circumstances and goals?

A signed disclosure is needed, sure, but the quality of the conversation that leads to that signature matters even more.

An individual brokerage may argue that its private network is large enough to serve its sellers well. But imagine that argument becoming the operating model across the industry. Buyers would need to navigate multiple networks to understand what is available.

Their selection could depend on which brokerage they contacted. Sellers could reach substantial audiences while still missing qualified buyers connected to other firms. Each company might describe its own network as an advantage. Together, those networks could create a more fragmented and less useful marketplace.

Consider Southwest Airlines. For years, travelers searching online travel agencies would not see its fares. They had to search Southwest separately. In 2025, Southwest expanded distribution to Expedia, Priceline and the other aggregators, making its flights available where more travelers were already shopping.

The parallel has limits, but the visibility question matters: How many potential customers never consider an offering because it doesn’t appear where they are looking?

In real estate, that question carries an additional responsibility. An airline decides how to distribute its own inventory. A brokerage advises a homeowner on how to market theirs. If a brokerage recommends limiting exposure, it should explain why that serves the seller better than reaching the broader market.

Brokerage leaders have a responsibility to consider the marketplace our decisions create. Our clients, buyers and sellers alike, depend on it, and the practices we normalize shape its usefulness.

Open Real Estate’s promise deserves support. Its implementation will deserve scrutiny. Its governance, participation rules and distribution practices must deliver the openness it advocates. Every participating company, including my own, should be held to that standard. The initiative must demonstrate that it expands access in practice.

The underlying principle should already guide our decisions: a homeowner’s marketing strategy should serve the homeowner’s goals. Any benefit to the brokerage must be evaluated alongside that responsibility, and any conflict should be explained candidly.

Our advantage should come from understanding a property, interpreting the evidence, negotiating effectively and helping a client make a sound decision. Those are the capabilities clients hire us for. They should also be the basis on which we compete.

I welcome an initiative that helps protect those conditions. But its announcement should prompt industry-wide reflection. When keeping the housing market open becomes a position companies must organize to defend, we’ve let the conversation drift too far from the people we serve.

Open Real Estate should not be a novel idea. It should describe how we do business.

Jared Antin is the executive director of Brown Harris Stevens.

#5523. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5522. Rocket Alumni Solutions Puts Recognition at the Center of School Community Engagement

Interactive storytelling gives students, families and alumni a way to discover the people, achievements and traditions that shape their school.

BOSTON, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rocket Alumni Solutions helps schools turn their history and achievements into a shared community experience. Serving 1,500+ schools and organizations, the company provides interactive recognition software that brings alumni stories, student accomplishments, school records and yearbooks together on campus touchscreens and the web.

A school's story includes the students who set records, the teachers who shaped generations, the volunteers who supported a program and the graduates who carried its traditions forward. Rocket gives schools a place to tell those stories with the photographs, biographies and historical context behind each name.

The company's approach centers community engagement on something personal: giving people a way to find their connection to a school and explore the contributions of others. Its recognition engine makes room for both established traditions and the achievements being added to that history today.

Recognition that reflects the whole school

Rocket's History Showcase supports recognition across academics, athletics, the arts, alumni, staff, donors and community service. Schools can organize collections around their own priorities, from a hall of fame or scholarship program to an archive of student leadership and performing arts.

Searchable profiles let visitors explore the people behind an award. Team collections can bring together rosters, photographs and season stories. Donor recognition can explain the people behind a scholarship, building or program, while alumni profiles can show students where a graduate's path began.

This flexibility gives school leaders a practical way to broaden the stories they share. An athletic induction can sit alongside academic honors, an educator tribute or a volunteer's contribution, with each collection reflecting a different part of the same community.

Rocket makes recognition available where people gather and where they live. A compatible touchscreen gives visitors a place to explore during a campus visit, reunion or induction ceremony. The web-based showcase lets alumni and families revisit those stories without returning to the building.

Digital yearbooks and photo archives add another way to discover a school's past. A returning graduate can look for a class photograph, a student can explore an earlier generation's activities, and a family can browse the history of a team or tradition. Those possibilities give schools concrete ways to use their collections throughout the year.

The archive also gives an event a lasting home. Schools can prepare profiles for an induction or assemble historical material for an anniversary, then keep the collection available after the celebration ends.

A collection that grows with the community

Rocket lets staff maintain recognition content through a browser, adding new honorees, updating records and building out historical collections over time. Unlimited content gives schools room to keep expanding the archive as more material becomes available.

A project does not require every decade of school history to be organized before work begins. Schools can start with one meaningful collection, such as an upcoming induction class, a set of yearbooks or a group of alumni profiles, and establish a plan for what comes next.

Rocket offers complimentary data entry, content preparation and project support to help bring that first collection into use. Its team works with schools on source materials, responsibilities and display setup, with 24/7 support available as the recognition program continues.

Recognition is part of Rocket's wider School Engagement System. Alongside History Showcase, Rocket offers Media Management to organize source material, Digital Signage for timely campus messages and Social Media Graphics for branded visual communications. Hardware and Data Entry & Project Management support the work of bringing a project to campus.

These offerings address different parts of a school's storytelling effort: maintaining the archive, finding the right photograph, sharing a current achievement and giving visitors a place to explore. Schools can choose a starting point around the people they want to recognize and the material they already have.

Rocket Alumni Solutions partners with more than 1,500 schools and organizations, including the PGA Tour, New York University, Arizona State University and Virginia Tech. The company helps communities celebrate achievements, preserve their history and recognize the people who shaped them.

Rocket Alumni Solutions' touchscreen software maintains an 80 Net Promoter Score, reflecting exceptional ease of use and customer satisfaction. Its interactive touchscreen software helps schools create digital Halls of Fame, donor recognition walls, record boards and campus recognition displays that celebrate community achievements and preserve institutional history.

Rocket Alumni Solutions serves schools and organizations of all sizes. The platform offers pre-built templates and remote content management. Schools receive ongoing support as their recognition collections grow.

#5521. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

Skyline of Salt Lake City, Utah, USA in early spring as the sun sets.

AI-tech firm SERHANT. has announced the launch of SERHANT. Utah, bringing its proprietary AI platform, S.MPLE, and the largest media reach in real estate to Salt Lake City and Park City.

According to a release, SERHANT. Utah opens with more than 40 agents from firms including Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices, Engel & Völkers, Real, Sotheby’s International Realty, and Windermere Real Estate, who together have closed $700 million in sales over the past 12 months. #5518. Amazon’s open-source AWS Emulator lets developers validate their code locally, without the cloud

Amazon Web Services Inc. is turning its public cloud computing platform on its head with the launch of a new service called AWS Emulator.

It’s a free, locally hosted software suite built by autonomous artificial intelligence agents that can replicate hundreds of the company’s cloud services on developer’s workstations. In a blog post, AWS Senior Principal Engineer Matt Goldberg said that the entire service was designed and written exclusively by AI agents, with not even a single line of its code written or reviewed by a human engineer.

AWS Emulator is designed to help customers overcome a major bottleneck in the application development process that has arisen with the adoption of AI coding agents such as AWS Kiro and Claude Code. Those agents are generating line after line of code faster than human programmers can blink, and the sheer velocity of that production is causing real issues for the teams tasked with verifying it before it can ship in production.

All AI-generated code needs to be validated against real cloud infrastructure, but doing that in the real AWS cloud is becoming all but impossible given latency and cost considerations. Though there are some existing third-party AWS emulators that developers can use, those services cover only a small fraction of AWS’ sprawling catalog of cloud services and quickly drift out of sync as those services evolve. With AWS Emulator, developers now have access to a free-to-use, locally hosted emulator that developers can use to run multiple iterative test loops on their own machines, Goldberg said.

The new tool was the brainchild of Goldberg, but he was actually inspired by the creation of AWS’ foundational Paxos-based distributed locking service, called “Alf,” which still underpins core cloud services such as Amazon S3 and DynamoDB.

In a second blog post, Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS’ vice president of agentic AI and emerging technologies, explained that when he and his colleagues first built Alf more than 20 years ago, they could test it only by simulating its entire environment inside a Java virtual machine built manually over several months.

Sivasubramanian explained that his team would have to inject faults and isolate concurrency bugs manually before they could deploy new services in production. But as AWS’ cloud has scaled up, it’s no longer feasible to hand-craft a simulation of its entire platform.

This is the conundrum that inspired Goldberg to see if that task could instead be done by AI agents. After seeing research that showed how AI agents were able to build a C code compiler from scratch, he concluded that they should also be able to replicate any AWS service if given a formal specification and reference implementation.

So he set about doing so, using AWS’ public Smithy API models as the specification and the live AWS platform as the ground truth. He began by prompting AWS Kiro to rebuild the Amazon Simple Queue Service, and it generated a functional replica of that service within just 15 minutes.

Seeing the potential, Goldberg and his team then set about organizing dozens of autonomous agents running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore into three separate teams. The first is tasked with generating thousands of end-to-end fidelity test suites from API models and verifying them against the live AWS cloud. The second runs the tests against the emulator to try and find any bugs or discrepancies, and if any are identified, those agents will automatically file a GitHub issue.

The third team was tasked with creating and implementing the fixes for those bugs. As a final step before the code enters the GitHub repository, it goes through an automated merge gate that’s supervised by adversarial security agents to check for any vulnerabilities.

The AWS Emulator is available for anyone to download starting today. It’s built in the Rust programming language and runs as a local HTTP server that can be accessed via a command-line interface on Linux, Windows, macOS or as a Docker container. To get started, developers simply have to redirect their AWS CLI or SDK calls to the localhost to enable rapid, offline validation that’s free.

AWS Emulator has been open-sourced under a Creative Commons CC0 public-domain dedication license, together with its raw commit history and a public backlog of known discrepancies filed under “things-that-do-not-work.”

Sivasubramanian said AWS Emulator illustrates the dramatic evolution of the role of the software engineer. With AI agents now responsible for the grunt work of writing, testing and debugging the actual code, humans are now becoming “systems orchestrators,” tasked with defining the boundaries, architecting the test specifications and designing the guardrails that guide the work of those agents.

#5517. Higharc, ECI launch MarkSystems integration for big builders

Higharc and ECI Software Solutions launched a MarkSystems integration that syncs 3D home design, options and pricing with ERP workflows, aiming to cut manual data entry, errors and rework for production homebuilders.  AI Summary

Higharc and ECI Software Solutions have released a generally available integration that connects Higharc’s 3D home design and configuration platform with ECI’s MarkSystems ERP for production homebuilders, aiming to cut manual data entry and tighten the link between what is sold and what is built.

The companies announced the launch Nov. 10, saying the jointly developed connection is now available to MarkSystems builders and is already in use at New Home Inc., a Carolinas-based builder that has deployed the integration across its sales and construction operations, according to the announcement.

For many production builders, moving a home from sales to construction requires rekeying pricing, plan configurations and buyer selections across multiple systems and departments. That creates opportunities for discrepancies between sales contracts, purchase orders and what gets built in the field, which can show up as margin erosion, delays and rework.

MarkSystems functions as the system of record for housing production, scheduling and accounting for many small and mid-sized builders. Higharc positions itself as the source of truth for plans, options and the buyer-facing design experience. The integration is designed to let data flow between the two instead of relying on manual handoffs.

“The biggest difference we’re seeing is speed and confidence,” said Matt Riley, owner of New Home Inc., in the announcement. “Our sales team can now sit down with a buyer, configure their home with accurate, up-to-date pricing, and send those selections straight into MarkSystems to write the contract. We’re no longer relying on people to keep information updated in multiple places, where mistakes inevitably happen and we end up absorbing the cost.”

The Higharc–MarkSystems connection is built to close gaps between marketing, sales and operations in a typical production homebuilding workflow. Key capabilities, according to the companies, include:

For builders, this type of connection is aimed at tightening margins and shortening cycle times by eliminating redundant work between sales offices, options studios, purchasing teams and field superintendents. Aligning pricing and configurations across systems can also help reduce surprise variance purchase orders and options that are sold but not built—or built but not paid for.

Production builders have accelerated their adoption of connected ERP, sales and design tools over the past decade, but many still run option pricing, elevations and structural changes through spreadsheets or local databases that do not fully sync with ERP. As build costs and cycle times remain under pressure, misaligned data between sales contracts and job budgets can quickly erode gross margin on a per-lot basis.

By placing Higharc’s 3D, rules-based design engine upstream of MarkSystems and tying the two together, the new integration is trying to turn the plan and option configuration itself into structured data that can feed estimating, purchasing and scheduling. That is a shift from traditional workflows where sales and marketing produce static collateral and construction teams translate that material back into quantities and tasks.

For entry-level and move-up builders running high volumes of similar plans across multiple communities, even small reductions in change orders, option mistakes and rework can compound across hundreds or thousands of closings a year.

Homebuilders can learn more about the integration during ECI Connect, ECI’s customer conference that begins Nov. 16. Representatives from Higharc and ECI plan to be available at the event to discuss how the connection links home design, buyer selections, pricing and construction operations, according to the announcement.

Builders not attending the event can schedule personalized demonstrations with either company.

Higharc describes itself as an AI-driven homebuilding platform for design through construction. The company uses 3D spatial data to generate plans, estimates and construction documents, replacing static plan sets with “live” models that respond to design changes with updated drawings, lot-specific estimates and buyer-facing experiences.

ECI Software Solutions, based in Westlake, Texas, provides cloud-based business software for small and mid-sized businesses in manufacturing, building and construction, field service and distribution. Its portfolio includes ERP, CRM, business intelligence, e-commerce and payment tools, and it serves more than 30,000 customers in over 90 countries, according to the company.

#5516. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5515. Integris Composites Joins International Sea Power Conference Aboard HMS Prince of Wales

Silver Partner at the Royal Navy's flagship maritime conference highlights lightweight composite armor that protects ships and crews without the weight of steel

OSLO, Norway, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Integris Composites, a global engineering company specializing in composite armor and survivability systems, is attending the SEA POWER and the Atlantic Future Forum conferences hosted on HMS Prince of Wales in Oslo, Norway.

Integris armor solutions are protecting surface combatants, patrol craft and the crews who operate them â work that includes ballistic protection for Finland's new Pohjanmaa-class corvettes and support for the upkeep program for the Royal Navy's Type 45 destroyers.

Integris is a Silver Partner of the International Sea Power Conference (ISPC 2026), which took place yesterday aboard the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales. ISPC, the Royal Navy's annual flagship conference, brings together naval leaders, policymakers and industry to consider how maritime nations can deter aggression and protect the sea lanes.

Integris executives are attending the Atlantic Future Forum, which follows aboard the same ship Nov. 11-12.

"As navies add uncrewed, autonomous vessels in the drive for innovation, protection of the crewed ships that now carry more sensors and more weapons cannot be an afterthought," said Andrew Bonham, president and CEO of Integris Composites. "Integris' European naval teams have spent years engineering protection into ships, ensuring survivability does not cost a vessel its speed, range or payload.

"ISPC is where the people who will shape the next generation of fleets meet, and we are glad to be part of that conversation," Bonham said.

The threat to ships has widened. Attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea have shown how drones and missiles can put pressure on a global chokepoint, and Ukraine's campaign in the Black Sea has shown how quickly uncrewed systems can change the balance between fleets and coastal forces. In the High North and the Arctic, allied navies are operating more often, for longer and in harsher conditions.

"Each of those trends raises the same question: How can you protect vessels, aircraft, land vehicles and sensor technologies and reduce the signature on all of them without adding weight? The answer is an increasing adoption of lighter composite armor systems," Bonham said.

Integris systems integrate ceramics, ultra-high-strength polyethylene and aramid fibers, high-performance unidirectional (UD) laminates â and at times steel â to provide protection at a fraction of the weight of current armor systems. Lower weight supports speed and maneuverability, fuel economy, mission range and payload flexibility, Bonham said. Integris' naval protection solutions are deployed on a wide range of vessels worldwide, including patrol craft, corvettes, amphibious platforms and command vessels. The company is also experimenting with emerging materials such as graphene and new high-strength fibers.

Integris is supplying its naval ballistic protective systems for four next-generation vessels being built by Rauma Marine Constructions for Finland's major naval modernization project, Squadron 2020. The Pohjanmaa-class corvettes are intended to secure year-round maritime defense in the icy Baltic Sea.

"We worked together with the shipbuilder to fully integrate the protection into the ship design, meeting survivability requirements without compromising speed, range or payload," said David Cordova, chief commercial officer of Integris Composites USA.

For the Royal Navy's Type 45 destroyer upkeep program, Integris is supplying new and replacement ballistic protection systems in collaboration with BAE Systems.

"The lesson of the last few years is that not only does protection have to move at the speed of the threat, but we need to develop intelligent armor that can lower the platform signature," Cordova said. "Drones and uncrewed systems are changing what ships, vehicles and crews have to survive, and they are changing it in months, not decades.

"We are here, and at other major defense events to bring those of us who design protection closer to those who depend on it. This is key to how we'll shorten the path from a new threat to a fielded solution," Cordova said.

Integris has operations in North America, Europe and Asia, with manufacturing in Denmark, France and the United States and offices in the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The company took part in the Pacific Future Forum aboard HMS Prince of Wales in Tokyo in August 2025.

Integris Composites is a global engineering company specializing in composite armor for land vehicles, aircraft, naval vessels, protective housings for optronics and other sensitive technologies, and personal protection. With more than 30 years of experience, the company has earned Tier 1 supplier status with major aerospace original equipment manufacturers, including Bell, Boeing, Airbus and Embraer. Known as TenCate Advanced Armor until it was renamed Integris Composites in 2023, the business has built a reputation for innovative survivability solutions across military, law enforcement and security applications worldwide.

#5514. Reverse mortgage leaders on alleviating sales and referral pain points

Presenters at NRMLA’s Annual Convention discussed practical tactics for a rate-sensitive reverse mortgage market, from LESA reduction and insurance shopping to borrower communication. They also stressed using partner introductions, explaining line-of-credit growth and leveraging CRMP training.  AI Summary

The National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) kicked off its Annual Convention & Expo on Tuesday in San Antonio with some practical advice for originators who are looking to close more deals in a rate-sensitive environment.

Reverse mortgage production has shifted in 2026 as the majority of borrowers are now using proprietary products rather than federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs). But regardless of the product being used, experts stressed creative problem-solving, proactive communication, financial planner relationships and next-level education as ways for loan officers to distinguish themselves in a difficult market.

Dan Hultquist, co-founder of REVERSE plus and director of reverse mortgage communications at Movement Mortgage, focused his presentation on transactions that are short to close — when the proceeds don’t cover the required payoffs and closing costs.

Common reasons why a borrower needs to bring more money to the table include lower principal limit factors tied to higher mortgage rates, borrowers who have refinanced repeatedly and the required life expectancy set-aside (LESA) for HECMs. He advised loan officers to consider different solutions for the level of severity.

When borrowers are short to close by a small amount like a few thousand dollars, a potential solution is to schedule their closing within six months of the borrower’s next birthday, so they “age up” and qualify for additional proceeds and/or a smaller LESA.

For borrowers who are short to close by a larger amount, shifting from a HECM to a proprietary loan or a second-lien product can make more sense as it eliminates the need for an upfront mortgage insurance premium. Additionally, the LO might look to persuade the borrower to dip into their retirement savings or obtain gift funds from a relative, since the elimination of the monthly mortgage payment may help them recover that sum over time.

Hultquist said he’s seen deals that are short to close by more than $100,000 saved in this fashion.

When a borrower is short to close specifically because of the LESA, property tax exemptions may provide a way forward. With HECM transactions, Hultquist noted that the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) does not have a flat discount on taxable assets. While 15% is the default discount, the client’s actual tax rate can be used, potentially saving money.

Shopping for a new homeowners insurance policy with a lower premium should also be looked at. “Your insurance company, they know that seniors don’t shop. Guess what happens to their insurance premiums every year? They keep going up until they shop,” Hultquist remarked.

John Luddy, senior vice president at Supreme Lending, has spent 25-plus years exclusively originating reverse mortgages. Over the course of thousands of conversations, he’s identified some key questions to ask of borrowers, spouses and lead sources at the start of the transaction.

The first question Luddy asks every client is, “How did you get my name?” The answer can tell him whether paid advertising campaigns are working.

“Advertising is the empty well that will take as many buckets of your money as you want to put into it,” he said. “You might feel good seeing your name on the marquee somewhere, but if it’s not drawing results, you’re wasting money.”

The same question also helps him identify who to call if a borrower stalls. Many clients, Luddy said, hesitate before closing as they look for an alternative. But lead sources like attorneys, financial planners or accountants “can be a little bolder” in their interactions than an originator, so they may be able to nudge the client across the finish line.

With lead sources, Luddy’s key question is, “What can I do to earn your business?” Real estate agents, for example, want their phone calls to be returned and for the LO to demonstrate deep product knowledge, while financial planners want any loan to fit into their existing strategy with a client.

Banks that don’t offer reverse mortgages can be a rich source of leads due to customers who are denied for other types of credit. And Luddy said bank branch managers will send repeat referral business if there’s no surprises in the reverse mortgage process.

He also urged the audience to consider borrower disabilities, such as hearing loss, as a potential hurdle.

“If they were a veteran, if they worked in manufacturing, if they worked in construction, or if they’re over 62, they may be suffering from hearing loss,” he said. “They’re not going to feel comfortable moving forward if they only understand every third word.”

Ryan Ponsford of Equity Wealth Academy, who’s well known to the NRMLA audience, argued that psychology matters more than math in reverse mortgage sales, even when dealing with financial advisers to capture more business.

Originators should discuss voluntary payments and the lack of a prepayment penalty for reverse mortgages. This gives borrowers a better sense of control over their financial responsibilities.

When speaking with business partners, don’t ask for referrals, which Ponsford called “transactional.” Instead, ask for introductions.

“An introduction is different than a referral because an introduction done right is a transfer of trust. Somebody that is trusted is transferring their trust to you,” he explained.

Financial advisers, he said, should leave conversations with an understanding that reverse mortgages apply to more people than they realize and that homeowners should consider them earlier in life.

Ponsford recommended three questions to ask advisers when attempting to forge a referral relationship.

And while psychology means a lot, it doesn’t mean everything. For example, the compounding growth feature of a reverse mortgage line of credit is essential for LOs to comprehend before they approach advisers. “If you can’t explain how line-of-credit growth works, you’re a nonstarter in the financial solutions industry,” Ponsford said.

Scott Harmes, national manager of reverse at C2 Financial — and his daughter Christina Harmes of Barrett Financial — are on the short list of Certified Reverse Mortgage Professionals (CRMPs), a designation earned through industry experience, a letter of recommendation and passing a complex exam.

He originated his first reverse mortgage about 16 years ago for the parents of a previous client, a deal that “changed their lives, and it changed mine,” he said. He stopped doing traditional forward mortgages about eight years ago to focus solely on reverse,

Harmes said he passed the CRMP exam on his first try and later built a detailed study guide for his colleagues to use that resulted in a “virtually 100%” pass rate. The designation, he said, has helped him to solidify more referral partnerships, to the point where he said he rarely loses deals except for when retail shops offer pricing he can’t match.

At C2 Financial, Harmes has constructed a mentorship model in which an experienced LO and a novice LO work together on three reverse mortgage files, with the trainee gaining additional responsibilities with each file. After that, they’ve typically gained enough knowledge to do the work on their own.

When it comes to borrower education, Harmes stressed that the process works best when information is offered in bite-sized chunks, rather than loan proposals accompanied by dozens of pages. Counseling is a key part of that process and there are pitfalls to be aware of.

“My policy is, I never tell them to look for a free session or a session paid for by a grant, because honestly, I think that’s too much work. We’re (sometimes) giving them three pages of counselors. I don’t want them dialing for dollars for four hours,” Harmes said.

“I originate in California, and there’s a state law that you can’t order the appraisal or any services that would cost the borrower until the eighth day after counseling. So we want to get that counseling session as soon as possible.”
