#5512. Glenn Beck Sees Record Audience Growth Following Launch of Mission-Driven Media Company, Torch

Beck rivals Joe Rogan in YouTube views and generates 446 million social media impressions in 28 days, continuing a year of record-setting digital growth.

IRVING, Texas, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Since launching his new mission-driven media company, Torch, earlier this year, Glenn Beck has experienced a remarkable surge in audience growth, repeatedly setting new digital performance records throughout 2026 and emerging as one of the most-watched personalities in online media.

The latest numbers represent a new milestone in that growth.

Over a recent 28-day period, Beck's YouTube channel generated 40.7 million long-form video views, virtually matching the 40.7 million recorded by Joe Rogan during the same period, according to internal YouTube analytics and third-party data from Viewstats.

Beck also significantly outpaced Tucker Carlson, whose YouTube channel generated just 19.4 million long-form views during the same period.

And Beck's reach extends well beyond YouTube.

Across Facebook, YouTube, X, Instagram, and TikTok, Beck's social media channels generated a combined 446 million impressions in just 28 days, according to internal platform analytics. On Facebook alone, his content delivered 200.4 million impressions and reached 34.2 million unique accounts.

While the latest figures are particularly striking, they are not an isolated spike. According to Torch's internal analytics, Beck's digital platforms have established new performance benchmarks throughout 2026, reflecting sustained audience growth since the company's launch.

That momentum is also reflected in independent research.

A Media Matters analysis identified The Glenn Beck Program among right-leaning news and politics shows experiencing substantial growth on YouTube, with Beck's channel increasing from 65.7 million to 83.9 million views between consecutive five-month reporting periods.

Meanwhile, Edison Research reported an 11% increase in the weekly U.S. audience for The Glenn Beck Program between late 2024 and mid-2026, further demonstrating the expansion of Beck's audience beyond social media.

And Beck's strong audience performance isn't limited to digital platforms. According to Nielsen ratings data provided to Torch, Beck's nationally syndicated daily radio program outperforms the average ratings of the stations that carry his show by 30% among adults ages 25â54, a key demographic for advertisers.

The growth comes during a pivotal new chapter in Beck's career as he prepares to celebrate his 50th anniversary in radio next year.

After decades in nationally syndicated radio, drawing millions of viewers to Fox News, and pioneering subscription streaming with the launch of GBTV in 2011, Beck began a new venture in 2026 with the creation of Torch.

But unlike a traditional media expansion, Torch was founded around a broader mission: helping Americans understand the deeper story behind current events, rediscover their history, and become better equipped to understand and shape the future.

"We didn't build Torch just to create another media company. We built it because I believe Americans are hungry for something bigger. They want the truth. They want to understand their history. They want to connect the dots and know what's coming so they can do something about it.

"That's the mission of Torch. It's about empowering people, building a community, and reminding Americans that they have far more power to shape the future than they've been led to believe.

"People are responding to that mission. They're looking for something worth believing in, something worth building together. And I think we're just getting started."

Beck's growing digital audience reflects a broader shift in how Americans consume news and commentary, as audiences increasingly turn to individual voices and independent platforms rather than traditional media institutions.

For Beck, who continues to host a nationally syndicated radio program carried on more than 430 stations, the growth represents another successful evolution in a career spanning multiple generations of media.

But with Torch, the ambition extends beyond audience size.

The company is building a platform centered on original programming, historical storytelling, educational initiatives, and direct audience engagement, with the goal of turning passive viewers into an informed, connected, and empowered community.

And if the audience growth of 2026 is any indication, that mission is resonating.

#5510. A military spouse’s advice for serving veteran homebuyers

Mortgage teams can better serve veteran homebuyers through VA loan education and community support. Veterans move often, and 34% had service-connected disabilities in 2025.   AI Summary

During my husband’s active duty, our family lived in five different states. We packed up our belongings 10 times, rented several homes and purchased two. We learned how to settle into a new place quickly, but making a house feel permanent was another matter.

Knowing another move was likely around the corner, we sometimes questioned whether decorating, or even unpacking, was worth the effort. It was difficult to feel connected to our neighbors and community when we knew we would eventually have to start over.

That repeated disruption is familiar to many military families. According to the Military Family Advisory Network, military families move, on average, every 2.5 years.

After more than two decades as a military spouse and, more recently, a veteran spouse, I know that finding a home is only one part of the transition from military to civilian life. A veteran may be looking for civilian work while learning to live with service-related health challenges. Their spouse may be rebuilding a career interrupted by repeated moves. Children have their own adjustments to make.

As mortgage professionals, we often meet families during this transition and have a window into some of the pressures and uncertainty they might be facing. As part of our mission of making home happen, we can also help our organizations and colleagues understand some of the unique circumstances surrounding these families and where we can collectively provide more assistance.

In August 2025, 5.8 million veterans, or 34% of all U.S. veterans, had a service-connected disability, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. For some families, access to health care may be a pressing concern. Others may need help finding work or support for a spouse or child. Mortgage lenders and other employers can contribute through organizations equipped to address those needs.

Begin by getting to know the organizations already serving military families. For example, Camp Hope provides a residential program addressing combat-related trauma, along with support for families, at no cost. Stronghold Food Pantry provides free food assistance to military families, while InDependent Wellness offers wellness resources and programs for military spouses. Ask these organizations where support is most needed before deciding what to offer. Some organizations may benefit most from a financial contribution; others may need volunteers or help reaching families who could use their services.

Employers have opportunities within their own workplaces, too. They can take action by investing in training and career opportunities for transitioning service members and veterans. The Department of War (DoW) SkillBridge program offers industry training and work experience to service members with 180 days or fewer remaining before military discharge. Becoming a program provider is one way an employer can help service members prepare for civilian careers. Employee resource groups can also give veterans a place to connect with colleagues and help others understand their experiences.

The VA home loan benefit gives eligible veterans an important financing option. According to the National Association of REALTORS®, 55% of veteran homebuyers in 2025 used VA financing. Helping a family evaluate that option requires mortgage professionals who know the program well enough to explain how it applies to their circumstances.

That requires ongoing education for loan officers and broker partners. For example, mortgage professionals should understand that the benefit is not limited to one use and that eligible borrowers may qualify for another VA-backed loan while an existing one remains active.

Lenders can put that education into practice through regular in-person or virtual training and digital resources that address program requirements and borrower questions. Mortgage originators should take advantage of those resources and guidance from the VA, rather than rely on assumptions about who can qualify. A thorough understanding of the program can help them identify options they might otherwise overlook.

The conversation should begin with a question about whether the borrower has served. From there, ask what is prompting the move and how the purchase fits their finances. Take time to understand what the family needs from the home and whether the payments will be manageable. Evaluate VA financing alongside other appropriate options so the borrower can make an informed choice.

For veterans and their families transitioning to civilian life, a permanent home can mean an end to planning around the next move. It offers the chance to build lasting connections with neighbors and become part of a community.

For our family, my husband’s service-connected disabilities and our son’s special needs have made a stable home especially important as we adjust to life after the military. I know how much it means to finally have a place where you can unpack everything, settle in and make a home your own. Finding the additional support our family needs has been part of that adjustment, too.

I still think about those moving boxes and all the times our family had to begin again. This Veterans Day, it’s my hope that employers will look at how they support military families in their communities and workplaces. Mortgage professionals can examine whether their knowledge is keeping pace with the needs of the borrowers they serve.

For those working with borrowers, one place to start is a 30-minute commitment: Study one VA guideline you don’t fully understand and learn about one aspect of military family life. Make that a starting point for ongoing learning about both the benefit and the people who use it.

Our family needed a home we could settle into. We also needed people who understood what we were adjusting to. We owe it to veterans and their families to learn about the challenges they face after military service. To honor their service to our country, we as individuals and organizations should take every opportunity to serve them too.

Brittany Boccher is the Newrez National Director of Military Strategy & Military Engagement.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5508. Stage 2 Capital Closes $100M and Puts AI-Powered Go-to-Market at the Center of Early-Stage Venture

Stage 2 Capital is bringing AI-powered access to its network of 1,000+ GTM leaders at companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and ElevenLabs, helping founders find the right expertise and connections at the point of need.

BOSTON, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stage 2 Capital today announced the close of $100 million across Venture Fund IV and Catalyst IV. Stage 2's partners work directly with every founder they back. Now the firm is adding AI to its operations via its MCP agent, allowing portfolio founders to access the talent, expertise, and connections of more than 1,000 LPs in real-time. The announcement follows three recent portfolio exits: Momentum (acquired by Salesforce), Steelhead (acquired by Mainsail) and Versori (acquired by Avalara).

Together, the two funds enable Stage 2 Capital to invest in B2B AI companies from the earliest stages. Venture Fund IV writes checks of $2 million to $5 million from Seed through Series A, while Catalyst IV makes $200,000 investments in pre-seed companies, often as part of the first institutional round. Both funds provide founders with access to experienced go-to-market (GTM) operators who help build the foundation for scalable growth.

"We started Stage 2 Capital because early-stage founders need more than capital. They need investors who can help them navigate their operational challenges. No firm solved this well for go-to-market," said Jay Po, Co-Founder and Managing Partner of Stage 2 Capital. "That's been true since day one, and these latest funds demonstrate the success of the model. We'll always be in the room with our founders. Now, with AI, we can more easily surface the collective expertise, experience, and connections across our LP network, connecting founders with the right people and insights at the moment they need them"

AI-driven access to 1,000 operators: The Right Expertise, On Demand

For almost any go-to-market problem a founder faces, someone has already solved it, and many of those operators are part of Stage 2's network. What founders rarely get from VC is a way to reach the right operator at the right moment. Early-stage companies often have to move fast, and waiting for an introduction could mean missing a critical window.

Stage 2's MCP agent is built to close that gap. It combines the Science of Scaling with the knowledge from its 1,000+ GTM leaders, matching the specific portfolio company's need with the world's modern expert. When founders need help, it connects them quickly with operators who have recently solved the same problem. The MCP agent enables Stage 2's partners to double down on their support of portfolio companies on go-to-market strategy, helping founders answer the key questions of when to scale and how fast.

The Stage 2 Model: Operators, Network, and the Science of ScalingStage 2 invests through a pod model. They pair a partner from venture with a partner who comes from a GTM background. Behind them is an LP network of more than 1,000 go-to-market leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Lovable, SpaceX, ElevenLabs and more. Founders draw on their wide range of backgrounds, spanning across sales, marketing, customer success, revops, partnerships, and forward-deployed engineering.

The firm's approach is grounded in The Science of Scaling, a framework developed by Co-Founder and Managing Partner Mark Roberge that helps founders determine whenâand how quicklyâto scale, so they can seize the opportunity without risking premature failure.

"We see founders make the same two mistakes over and over. Some scale too slowly and miss their window. Others scale before they're ready and put the entire business at risk," said Mark Roberge. "We have well-established ways to measure revenue, but very little discipline around deciding when a company is actually ready to scale or how fast it should grow. Too often, boards rely on a playbook that worked for another company ten years ago, without considering whether it makes sense for the business in front of them. We want to help founders and investors make those decisions based on evidence rather than assumptions."

"Stage 2 was with us from our Series A on, as an extension of our team," said Ashley Wilson, Co-Founder of Momentum (acquired by Salesforce). "They helped us pressure-test when we truly had product-market fit and how fast to scale from there. And every GTM problem we hit after that, they found the person who had already solved that exact problem at our stage. They introduced us to customers we couldn't have reached on our own, and connected us with experienced operators who changed our trajectory."

Stage 2 has already begun investing from the new funds, backing AI companies like Letter.ai, Qualitate, and Axle. Stage 2 led Letter,ai's $10.6M Series A last October, and four months later the company raised a $40M Series B led by Battery Ventures.

About Stage 2 CapitalStage 2 Capital is the first VC fund that combines decades of investment experience and decades of go-to-market executive experience at the partner level, supported by more than 1,000 GTM operators from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Lovable, Snowflake, Databricks, SpaceX, Harvey, ServiceNow, and dozens of other category leaders. The firm invests pre-seed through Series A in B2B AI startups with a unique specialization in helping them drive sustainable revenue growth. Learn more at Stage2.Capital.

#5507. As Kubernetes inference faces launch-day deadlines, CoreWeave deepens its open-source involvement

Cloud providers are scaling Kubernetes inference to serve frontier AI models, and the problems they encounter in production are helping shape the open-source projects they rely on.

CoreWeave Inc. sits near the center of that shift as AI agents reshape enterprise infrastructure. The company describes itself as a cloud built from the ground up for AI rather than retrofitted for it. Much of its growth traces back to the open nature of the container orchestration platform and the ecosystem around it, according to Yoshi Tamura (pictured, left), principal product manager at CoreWeave. CoreWeave has now upgraded to Platinum, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s highest corporate membership tier, to help shape how Kubernetes handles the large AI workloads its customers run.

“Without [Kubernetes], I don’t think we would’ve been able to get this kind of explosive growth,” Tamura said. “With this upgrade to Platinum, we indicate that we really mean it. We want to give back to the community. We want to be more involved.”

Tamura and Rita Zhang (right), principal software engineer at CoreWeave, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why CoreWeave upgraded to CNCF Platinum membership and what it takes to run Kubernetes inference in production. (* Disclosure below.)

Open source can get a model into a cluster, but that doesn’t guarantee it will perform at scale. CoreWeave’s inference team brings together infrastructure specialists and machine learning engineers, working with model labs and open-source inference engines to patch engines and runtimes for newly released models, according to Zhang.

“Running in production is hard,” Zhang said. “We work a lot with the open-source community, not just on the inference stack, but also with the model providers. Just because it’s on Hugging Face and you download the weights doesn’t mean it will work per your requirement. This is where we work very closely with the labs and the open-source community — like vLLM, SGLang — to make sure that for day-zero models we actually are able to patch the engines and provide our own kernels and patch the runtime.”

Kubernetes special interest groups rely on users to bring them production problems, such as finding nodes with the right devices and accounting for cluster topology when scheduling large training and inference jobs, Zhang explained. CoreWeave remains smaller than incumbent cloud providers and relies on open source more than many realize, Tamura added. Its work with leading AI model builders now gives it an early look at where frontier workloads are headed.

“We’re in a very unique position,” Tamura said. “Maybe we can actually find a way to kind of bring it back to the community and sort of lead which direction Kubernetes, a larger community, could go.”

#5506. If you own the asset, you should own the project data

Owners often inherit thousands of closeout files but lose decision context stored in contractor systems. A persistent owner-controlled record improves operations, diligence, portfolio learning and future AI analysis.   AI Summary

Real estate owners spend years making decisions before a shovel hits the ground, then decades living with the consequences of those decisions after construction is complete. Yet during construction, something unusual often happens: The most complete version of the project can end up living inside systems controlled by a project team whose role is temporary.

That is not an argument against general contractors or the technology they use. Contractors need their own systems to execute the work — to manage RFIs, submittals, drawings, schedules, changes, commitments, field activity and the hundreds of other workflows required to deliver a project. The issue is what happens to all of that information when the project ends.

For the owner, construction is only one chapter in a much longer relationship with the asset, and the information created during that chapter should remain just as durable as the building itself.

By the time a general contractor mobilizes, an owner may already have spent months or years developing the project. There has been an investment thesis, underwriting, capital planning, site diligence, entitlements, early budgeting, design development, consultant coordination, procurement decisions, lender requirements and investor approvals.

Each of these steps creates information and, more importantly, context: why one design option was selected over another, why the budget moved, which assumptions drove the underwriting, which risks were identified early and which decisions were deferred into construction.

Then the project moves into delivery, and the volume of information accelerates. Drawings are revised, RFIs are answered, submittals are reviewed, contracts are executed, schedules change, pay applications are processed and change orders are negotiated. Decisions are documented across meetings, email, project-management software and individual files.

When construction ends, the asset’s operating life continues. The asset moves into operations, warranties begin to matter, capital projects follow, systems get replaced, spaces are renovated and new teams inherit the property. The asset may later be refinanced, sold or redeveloped. The asset’s history needs to remain accessible through changes in project teams, operating staff and ownership. The way that history is maintained should reflect that reality.

During construction, it is completely reasonable for the general contractor to operate its own project-management environment; in many cases, that is where the day-to-day execution record is most complete. The problem begins when that environment also becomes the owner’s only durable record of what happened.

At turnover, owners can receive thousands of files — drawings, warranties, manuals, RFIs, submittals, schedules, photos, meeting records and closeout documents. Technically, the information was transferred, but information and usable history are not always the same thing.

A folder can tell you what the final drawing was; it may not tell you why the design changed. A change-order file can tell you what was approved; it may not clearly preserve the sequence of decisions that created the change. A final budget can tell you where the project landed; it may not preserve how the forecast evolved along the way.

The distinction matters because the value of project information is not simply in possessing the files. It is in maintaining enough structure and context to understand what happened and why. When that continuity breaks at turnover, the next team has to reconstruct the story.

The answer is not for owners to dictate every piece of software used by every project participant — that would create a different problem. General contractors, architects, engineers, consultants and trade partners all have tools and workflows that support their roles, and those systems are important to project execution and should continue to be.

What the owner needs instead is a persistent layer of information that remains under its control throughout the asset lifecycle. That record should begin before construction, remain active while the project is being delivered and continue after turnover. During construction, information can move between the owner’s environment and the systems used by the project team through workflows, integrations, APIs, exports or agreed reporting processes.

In practice, that means being able to access, export and reuse the agreed project record without depending on a former project participant’s account. Owners should define the required records, their format and responsibility for maintaining them before delivery begins.

The goal is not to duplicate every click made inside a contractor’s software. It is to make sure the information that matters to the long-term owner does not disappear when the temporary project organization dissolves.

Not everything created during construction has equal long-term value. The enduring record should focus on the information required to understand how the asset became what it is.

That starts with the financial history: approved budgets, commitments, forecast changes, contingency usage, major cost movements and the financial impact of significant project decisions. It also includes the decision history — major approvals, design changes, scope decisions, responsible parties and the supporting information behind those decisions.

Then there is the technical project record: drawings, specifications, RFIs, submittals, schedule information and other documentation that explains what was designed and ultimately built. Finally, there is the turnover record — as-builts, warranties, manuals, punch and closeout documentation and the information future teams will need to operate, maintain or modify the asset.

The important point is not the specific software used to store each item. It is continuity. Five years after completion, someone working on the property should be able to understand the decisions made five years earlier without starting an archaeological dig through old inboxes, shared drives and archived contractor accounts.

Construction information is often treated as though its usefulness peaks at closeout. For owners, the opposite may be true. A complete development and construction history can become increasingly useful as the asset ages: operations teams can use it to understand equipment, warranties and design intent and asset managers can use it when evaluating future capital work.

The same history also supports investment and portfolio decisions. Development teams can compare budgets, scopes and outcomes against previous projects, and executives can benchmark performance across a portfolio. Future project teams can understand why earlier decisions were made instead of repeating the same analysis, and the information can also support underwriting, refinancing and disposition diligence by making the history of the asset easier to understand.

This becomes even more valuable for owners with multiple properties. One project record is useful; a consistent record across 20, 50 or 100 assets begins to create institutional knowledge. Patterns become visible, assumptions can be tested, budget performance can be compared and recurring problems can be identified — lessons learned on one project can actually influence the next one. The organization’s experience stops resetting every time a project team changes.

Artificial intelligence makes this conversation more important, but not because every owner needs an AI strategy for every construction workflow today. The larger issue is much simpler: AI becomes more useful when it has access to complete, structured and trustworthy information.

An owner might want to understand why similar scopes repeatedly generated changes, how contingency usage varied across developments or which underwriting assumptions proved wrong. Answering those questions requires more than a collection of final documents; it requires a traceable history of decisions and outcomes.

If each project’s information is fragmented across contractor platforms, consultant systems, shared drives, inboxes and archived files, an AI model faces the same problem a human does: the information may technically exist, but reconstructing the story becomes difficult. The owners that preserve a consistent project history today are not simply improving document retention — they are building the information base from which future analysis becomes possible.

There is an important distinction between controlling a project and controlling the enduring record of a project. Owners do not need every contractor to abandon the systems that help them build effectively, and they do not need to centralize every workflow or capture every administrative action performed during construction. What they do need is continuity over the information that explains the asset they ultimately own.

The owner owns the building. It carries the financial consequences of the decisions made during development, operates the asset after the project team leaves, funds the next capital program, and answers the questions of the next lender, investor, buyer or development team. The information describing how that asset was conceived, financed, designed, built and changed should be treated accordingly.

Construction teams move on, and ownership can change. The project record should remain with the asset, available to the people responsible for its future.

Adam Stark is a Special Forces veteran and construction technology executive with experience spanning development, project delivery, construction management and operational systems in the built world.  This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5505. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5504. University of Phoenix supports 30th annual Phoenix Veterans Day Parade as Medal of Honor sponsor

Community event celebrates "250 Years of Freedom, 30 Years of Honor" and recognizes veterans, military families and their contributions

PHOENIX, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix is proud to support the 30th annual Phoenix Veterans Day Parade as a Medal of Honor sponsor, joining nonprofit Honoring America's Veterans and the Phoenix community in recognizing the service, sacrifice and contributions of U.S. military veterans and their families.

Held each Veterans Day, the Phoenix Veterans Day Parade brings together veterans, military families, community organizations and supporters to honor those who have served the nation. This year's milestone event commemorates three decades of community recognition and gratitude with the theme,"250 Years of Freedom, 30 Years of Honor."

"University of Phoenix is honored to support an event that has united our community in appreciation of veterans for 30 years," said Sandra Perez, vice president of Student Administrative Services and head of the Office of Military and Veterans Affairs. "As we celebrate this milestone anniversary, we recognize the courage, dedication and sacrifices of veterans and their families. We are proud to support an event that brings people together to honor their service and helps ensure their stories continue to inspire future generations."

Celebrating 30 years of honoring veterans

For three decades, Honoring America's Veterans has helped bring the Phoenix community together to recognize veterans from every era of service. The annual parade serves as an opportunity to honor the men and women who wore the nation's uniform and the families whose support helped sustain them throughout their military journeys.

From veterans of World War II to those who have served in more recent conflicts, the parade celebrates stories of service, resilience and commitment that continue to strengthen communities across Arizona and the nation. Over the past 30 years, the parade has been enjoyed by an estimated 1.5 million spectators and participants and has recognized the service of 600,000 veterans.

The University of Phoenix parade entry features a large balloon and a team of veteran employees, family members and friends accompanying the float. The event this year featured 46 parade entries, including 13 veteran service organizations, eight floats, eight military vehicles, and six high school marching bands.

A community tradition with a new parade route

This year's parade continues that tradition while introducing a new parade route designed to welcome participants and spectators for another memorable community celebration. Community members are encouraged to bring their families, wave American flags and join neighbors, veterans and supporters for a day dedicated to gratitude, remembrance and patriotism.

"The Phoenix Veterans Day Parade is about far more than marching bands, floats and celebration," said Paula Pedene, U.S. Navy Veteran and Executive Director and Founder of Honoring America's Veterans. "For 30 years, it has provided an opportunity for our community to come together and recognize the men and women who served our country and the families who stood beside them. As we celebrate this milestone anniversary, we look forward to continuing this tradition of honor, appreciation and community for generations to come."

University of Phoenix remains committed to supporting veterans, active-duty service members and military families through education and career-focused resources designed to meet learners where they are. The University's Office of Military and Veterans Affairs and Veterans Employee Resource Group support veteran-centered initiatives throughout the year and help strengthen connections among military-affiliated students, alumni, faculty and staff.

University of Phoenix has 300 veteran staff and faculty members and more than 330 members of the University's Veterans Employee Resource Group. The University of Phoenix Office of Military and Veterans Affairs and the Veterans' Employee Resource Group (ERG) collaborate to promote the event to staff, students and faculty and provide volunteer support.

University of Phoenix serves the educational goals of veterans and military students, with specially trained staff to assist service members, veterans, and military spouses and dependents. In addition to providing career-relevant education for military students and flexibility that fits military student and working adult schedules, veteran and military students' military experience and training can be assessed for possible college credit.

Active students and alumni have access to Career Services for LifeÂ® resources including career guidance and tools. For more information, visit phoenix.edu.

#5503. Winning in a buyer’s market

With inventory rising and pending sales hitting historic lows, today's buyers have leverage they haven't seen in years. Jennifer Beeston breaks down three common client hesitations—high rates, high prices and closing costs—and outlines how agents and lenders can use seller concessions and buydowns to get deals across the finish line.   AI Summary

As we head into the end of the year, we are at a truly magical moment for buyers across much of America.

Buyers have more houses to choose from, along with the ability to inspect the property, negotiate repairs and make homeownership more affordable. It is something buyers have been wanting for years, but where are all the buyers? Pending sales were recently recorded as the lowest since they started tracking pending sales!

Currently, many buyers are holding back for three main reasons. As a mortgage lender or real estate agent, knowing these reasons and how to solve them is the key to helping your buyers win right now. Would I recommend waiting for lower rates?  Absolutely not; the lower the rates, the more competition, and it is the lack of competition where true opportunity lies.

Ask the seller to pay to buy down the mortgage rate.  I like a permanent buydown as it gives certainty for the long run. Many buyers can afford the house when the rate starts at 6%, so use a seller buydown to get there.

Offer less. Many buyers do not know that you can offer less. They are waiting for the seller to drop the price when, in reality, they should just write an offer now with what they want to pay.  It is up to the seller to say yes or no.

Whether the seller agrees depends on their financial situation and their motivation to sell. I have chatted with clients who want the house, but not at the current price and are afraid to offer $10,000 less. To me, that’s a missed opportunity.  The seller could be sitting on the other side praying they get an offer.  Write the offer.

Did you know many buyers don’t realize they can ask the seller to pay for closing costs? Over 42% of recent sales have seller concessions, but many buyers still do not know you can ask for this. You could have a buyer you talked to last year who was in a seller’s market, who is saving away, who does not even know that their market is now a buyer’s market. This is your opportunity as a real estate professional to help them get home. Ask the seller to pay their closing costs and help them get home for the Holidays.

As I type this, we have buyers across the country negotiating for lower sales prices, closing costs and rate buydown covered by the seller. Does every seller say yes?  No, but that is the beauty of the buyer’s market; there are so many sellers to choose from. There is tremendous opportunity in the market right now for buyers to win. Help them seize it.

Jennifer Beeston is the EVP of National Sales at Chairman’s Circle (NMLS ID: 247743). This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5502. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5501. CargoSprint Announces Patent-Pending Dynamic Stack Management, Bringing Terminal Gate and Yard Operations Closer Together

eModal Pre-Gate feature coordinates gate appointments with yard operations to optimize import delivery, increase throughput, improve cargo fluidity, and reduce truck turn times.

ATLANTA, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CargoSprint, a technology company serving the global cargo industry, today announced that Dynamic Stack Management (DSM), a patent-pending module of its eModal Pre-Gate appointment platform, is now live at multiple major marine terminal operators (MTO) in the United States. DSM's novel solution works in conjunction with CargoSprint's payment and appointment platforms to optimize import delivery processing, increase terminal throughput, improve cargo fluidity, and reduce truck turn times.

DSM uses expanded container lifecycle data to promote optimal import appointment timeslots. Ongoing communication with terminal systems to update container status and yard position enables closer coordination between gate and yard operations while improving the overall terminal experience. Less time spent at the terminal for the trucker and fewer container rehandles produce a better experience for terminals and truckers alike â and ultimately the shippers they serve.

"Marine terminals are being asked to move more cargo with the same footprint and equipment, creating a gap between gate and yard operations is where velocity is lost," said Caro Krissman, CEO, CargoSprint. "Dynamic Stack Management (DSM) brings the two together, so appointments and yard operations work as one. The results our terminal partners are seeing show what's possible when scheduling and yard operations work together. I'm proud of our team for innovating in this space on behalf of our customers and the community."

This patent pending module is now available as an add-on to eModal Pre-Gate and configurable to fit each terminal's operational needs. By coordinating the appointment timeslots offered to truckers with yard conditions as they change, DSM helps terminals optimize import delivery processing and improve cargo fluidity while reducing truck processing and turn times. It builds on the integration already supported by the terminal operating system and is currently available for rubber-tired gantry (RTG) yard operations, with a design built to extend to other operating models.

CargoSprint is a technology innovator transforming the global cargo industry with people-first solutions since 2012. Its platform â including SprintPay, SprintPass, SprintPass Pro, SprintPort, eModal, and Dray Dog â streamlines payments and orchestrates appointments, compliance, and visibility across air, ocean, road, and rail. #5500. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5499. Homebuilders and their partners team up to salute our veterans

Builders recognized Veterans Day through nonprofit partnerships, including mortgage-free home giveaways and support for transitioning service members. Regional builders also promoted limited-time military savings, typically $1,000 to $3,000, and some offered up to $2,500 toward closing costs in select communities.  AI Summary

Each Veterans Day, millions of Americans take a moment to honor the sacrifices that our military veterans have made for generations.

On a personal note, today I’m remembering both of my late grandfathers. One served in the Navy, while the other received a Purple Heart and numerous other medals for his bravery and service during the Vietnam War.

Across the country, homebuilders are marking Veterans Day with a range of initiatives, including special promotions and discounts for military families, mortgage-free home donations and workforce development programs designed to support veterans transitioning into civilian careers.

The following are some of the ways homebuilders are recognizing and supporting veterans this year.

PulteGroup, in partnership with Operation Homefront, announced that it gifted multiple newly constructed homes to military service members in cities like Anna, Texas, Wixom, Michigan and Richmond Hills, Georgia.

Meritage Homes, also in partnership with national military nonprofit Operation Homefront, will donate a brand-new, mortgage-free home to a military family in Gulfport, Mississippi.

The lucky recipient of Meritage Homes’ giveaway was Navy Personnel Specialist 2nd Class Maggie Coleman, who served 13 years in the Navy. Coleman will receive a 2,000-square-foot home with four bedrooms and three bathrooms.

“I want to give my children everything I didn’t have. I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories,” Coleman said in a press release.

Lennar partnered with national nonprofit Operation Finally Home and country music artist and U.S. Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan to surprise two military families with brand-new, mortgage-free homes in celebration of Veterans Day. The surprises unfolded Monday evening in Austin, Texas, during a reception in which the veterans believed they were simply attending as honored guests of the foundation.

And earlier this week, Invitation Homes announced that it has teamed up with Home Builders Institute to fund hands-on training, industry credentials and job placement for transitioning service members and veterans.

Many smaller, regional homebuilders, which don’t have the resources to give away homes for free, are honoring Veterans Day by offering temporary promotions for Veterans and military service members.

Taylor Homes, which builds in Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio, announced that it doubled its “We Salute You” bonus to $2,000 throughout November, giving military members a price reduction on a new home.

Tennessee-based Pratt Home Builders, meanwhile, is offering veterans, active-duty military and reservists $3,000 in savings toward a new home during November and December. Buyers can apply the savings toward the purchase price, design upgrades or appliances.

Other builders are offering similar incentives in select markets, either temporarily or on an ongoing basis. D.R. Horton, for example, is offering up to $2,500 toward closing costs through its Home of the Brave program in select San Antonio-area communities.

Landmark Homes offers active-duty military members and veterans a $1,000 incentive that can be combined with other promotions in Northern Colorado.

In Idaho, Hubble Homes offers a $2,500 Homes for Heroes discount, as does Drees Homes in markets like Jacksonville and San Antonio.

David Weekley Homes, meanwhile, provides military personnel with $1,000 in Flex Dollars in the Charleston, South Carolina market.

Many of these programs extend beyond veterans and military personnel to include teachers, police officers, firefighters and other first responders, grouping them under broader Hometown Heroes or similar initiatives.
