#5498. A2Z Reports Third Quarter 2026 Revenue of $10.9 Million

Delivered 2,000 Smart Carts in the Third Quarter; Doubling Second Quarter Volumes

Smart Cart Revenue of $9.6 Million More Than Doubled Sequentially

Acquisition of Hedia Enhances Ability to Monetize Retail Media

Reiterates Guidance of 10,000 Cumulative Smart Carts Delivered by Year-End 2026 and At Least $25 Million in Second Half Smart Cart Revenue

Conference Call to be held at 5 PM ET Today

Third Quarter 2026 Highlights(Year-on-year comparisons reflect the Company's transition from a startup to a scalable commercial business.)

TORONTO, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A2Z Cust2Mate Solutions Corp. (NASDAQ: AZ) (the "Company" or "A2Z"), a global leader in smart retail technology, announced  its financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"We are pleased with our third quarter results, which reflect the positive momentum we are seeing for our product and our effective execution as we significantly ramped up smart cart deployments. Deliveries reached a record 2,000 units in the third quarter, surpassing our total deliveries for the entire first half of the year, and were spread across multiple customers. Additionally, we advanced the development of our retail media business with the strategic acquisition of Hedia, which closed in early October," noted Gadi Graus, Chief Executive Officer of A2Z Cust2Mate.

"Importantly, our newest customers have increased their orders after initial deployment, clearly indicating the value of our product once in-store. Following the launch of our next generation Connected In-Store Commerce Platform, we have seen increased demand from existing and potential clients, and as pilot programs evolve into full blown launches, the excitement of shoppers and value to our customers is driving increased order activity and rollouts to additional locations. As we build our installed base, the cadence of our revenue is becoming more predictable, supporting our expectation for continued growth in 2027.

"In early October, we closed the acquisition of Hedia, a profitable in-store retail media business with approximately $20 million of annual revenue. Hedia brings scale, capabilities and key advertiser relationships to our retail media inventory, smart cart technology, retailer relationships and measurement capabilities. The complementary nature of Hedia's business to AZ's growing retail media inventory will accelerate the growth of our platform and enable us to provide the full retail media value chain to our customers. We view this as a source of high margin revenue as our base of deployed units grows, offering additional avenues to profitably build our business.

"We continue to pursue relationships with vendors outside of Israel. Additionally, we see international growth potential for A2Z as a U.S. competitor plans to exit what was a non-core business for them in mid-2027. This will give us the opportunity to showcase our next-generation technology and demonstrate the benefits of what we consider to be the most advanced platform available in the market.

"Accelerating smart cart deployments, supported by our direct manufacturing capabilities and a sharper go-to-market focus following our organizational realignment, give us confidence in the fourth quarter sales step-up implied by our full year 2026 guidance.

"We expect fourth quarter deliveries to eclipse our total for the first nine months of the year and are reiterating our target of 10,000 cumulative unit deliveries by year end 2026 and 19,000 units by year end 2027. These targets are based on existing backlog, with new orders representing additional potential upside. We also continue to expect at least $25 million of smart cart revenue for the second half of 2026, which excludes any contribution from retail media."

Third Quarter Fiscal 2026 Results(Year-on-year comparisons reflect the Company's transition from a startup to a scalable commercial business.)

Revenue increased to $10.9 million, up from $5.9 million in the second quarter of 2026 and $1.5 million in the prior year period due to an increase in smart cart deliveries. Gross profit increased to $3.7 million, from $2.5 million in the prior sequential quarter and $0.5 million a year ago. Gross margin was 33.4%, compared with 42.6% in the second quarter of 2026 and 34.0% in the prior year quarter. On a sequential basis, gross profit benefited from an increase in revenue, while gross margin declined due to product mix, reflecting shipments of earlier-generation smart carts, which carry lower margins. We expect to work through this inventory of earlier-generation models by the end of the year.

Operating loss was $6.8 million, compared to a loss of $7.6 million in the prior sequential quarter and a loss of $4.1 million in the prior year quarter. Operating loss narrowed sequentially due to  increased revenues.

Net loss for the period was $6.6 million compared to a loss of $7.3 million in the second quarter of 2026, and a loss of $1.4 million in the prior year quarter. The decrease in net loss compared to the second quarter of 2026 is primarily due to higher revenues.

Management will host a conference call on November 11, 2026, at 5 PM Eastern Time to discuss the company's third quarter financial results.

The conference call may be accessed by dialling 1-877-317-6789 (U.S. toll-free), 972 3-374-1008 (Israel Tel Aviv), or 1-412-317-6789 (International). The live webcast of the call can be accessed using the following link: https://event.choruscall.com/mediaframe/webcast.html?webcastid=dpTlCFUn

A2Z Cust2Mate Solutions Corp. (NASDAQ: AZ) is transforming in-store retail through a connected in-store commerce platform that brings together shopper engagement, retail media, data and in-store intelligence.

At the center of A2Z Cust2Mate's connected in-store commerce platform is its AI-powered Smart Cart, which creates a continuous digital connection with shoppers throughout the in-store journey. The platform enhances and simplifies shopping, enables retailers and brands to engage shoppers, delivers targeted retail media and offers at the point of decision, and captures real-time data and intelligence on in-store shopper behavior.

Retail media is a growing part of A2Z Cust2Mate's business, building on its digital in-store touchpoints, media inventory, shopper journey data and measurement capabilities. A2Z Cust2Mate brings together technology, data and commercial capabilities to create new ways for retailers and brands to engage shoppers, monetize the physical store and measure impact closer to the point of purchase.

A2Z Cust2Mate combines advanced software, AI, computer vision and purpose-built hardware in a modular platform designed for enterprise-scale deployment and chain-wide operations. The company works with retailers, brands and partners across multiple markets to bring connected, data-driven personalized experiences to physical stores and create new opportunities for revenue growth, retail media monetization, operational efficiency and loss mitigation.

For more information on A2Z Cust2Mate Solutions Corp. please visit: www.cust2mate.com.

#5497. Red Hat and Nvidia’s OpenShell puts AI agents on a deny-by-default leash

Prompt injection attacks and silent data exfiltration have turned AI agent security from a theoretical worry into an urgent enterprise concern.

As agents move from developer laptops into data centers, companies need guardrails that don’t strip away what makes agents useful. Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp. have expanded their partnership to tackle that problem through OpenShell, an open-source project that sets limits on what agents can do. The threat model for agents differs sharply from that of traditional software, so the industry has to build a shared standard to secure them, according to Derek Carr (pictured, left), senior distinguished engineer at Red Hat.

“Agents can’t get access to your secrets. They need deny-by-default networking, and you need a rich policy framework for what happened and when for this class of apps,” Carr said. “Nvidia had reached out to us and noted that they were seeing the same problem domain. No one wants to work on this alone. It’s better to work together.”

Carr and Mrunal Patel (right), distinguished engineer at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how OpenShell helps enterprises run AI agents in production with safeguards against prompt injection and data leaks. (* Disclosure below.)

Viral projects such as OpenClaw showed the industry that agents could take real actions on their own. Of course, that power also bred anxiety about agents leaking secrets or spending company money, with concrete warning signs appearing early, Patel noted.

“As soon as we started hearing about the prompt injection attacks and how like folks were seeing the data getting exfiltrated outside, that was scary,” Patel said. “We realized we needed a solution.”

To that end, OpenShell lets operators give agents access to specific endpoints while keeping credentials hidden from the agents and scoped to those endpoints, according to Carr. A policy advisor asks agents to justify blocked actions in plain language, while operators can update policies as workloads change. With OpenShell now under open governance at the Cloud Native Computing Foundation following Nvidia’s contribution, Red Hat aims to make deploying agents on OpenShift as routine as running traditional apps, with prompt injection defenses built into the platform.

“Many companies are struggling to get to one agent in production, let alone thousands or millions,” Carr said. “By having a project like OpenShell in the ecosystem, it provides a blueprint for companies to follow — to get from their first idea of ‘I want to do something with agents’ to a point where they’re safely doing one, 10 or 20 in production.”

#5496. A Veterans Day reflection for building leaders and the work ahead

A Veterans Day editorial urging the housing and homebuilding community to pair gratitude with action. It spotlights two mortgage-free home commitments in Texas and outlines leadership traits tied to durable affordability progress.  AI Summary

Today, amid the quickened pulse of our nation’s political and cultural divisions, Veterans Day gives Americans a chance to take stock of something that transcends the moment’s disputes and divides.

We have inherited something incalculably, extraordinarily valuable.

Generations of men and women who served in the United States Armed Forces have helped preserve and protect a nation where we can live, work, worship, disagree, build businesses, raise families and decide what kind of future we want for ourselves and for those who come after us.

Those freedoms don’t exist in a vacuum. They’re neither inevitable nor self-sustaining, though we may act as if we take them for granted. They exist only because people before us accepted duties, endured pain, and made sacrifices for beneficiaries they didn’t know and ultimately never would.

Our children. Our children’s children. Their children. And on and on.

That generational commitment deserves more than our gratitude, though gratitude is where we begin today. And where we need to begin each day. A salute and a deeply felt debt of gratitude are an open invitation. It asks each of us to examine what we do with our hard-won inheritance. It asks us all what we are willing to do to preserve and improve it for generations beyond our own.

For those of us whose livelihoods center on making homes and neighborhoods for people to live in, that searching examination resonates. We work in a business community whose homes, neighborhoods, infrastructure and institutions endure. They’re a bedrock for generations. They profoundly nurture and shape the possibilities, the very dreams, available to American families and households.

Military service and homebuilding are not equivalent sacrifices. Still, much to learn from the commitment to mission, dependence on others, the discipline of preparation, and the willingness to serve a purpose larger than oneself that distinguishes the best traditions of military service.

This Veterans Day, we have a moving example of what happens when gratitude becomes a commitment to act. In Austin, Texas, this week, Lennar and nonprofit Operation Finally Home, joined by country music artist and U.S. Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan, surprised two military veterans and their families with the promise of new, mortgage-free homes.

Marine Corps Sgt. Kevin Gallmeier served a decade in uniform, including combat deployments to Iraq, before retiring medically after sustaining service-related injuries. Army Spc. Jordan Taylor served in Baghdad and later continued serving his community as a firefighter and EMT until a serious injury forced him to retire.

For Taylor, his wife Aylynn, and their four children, financial hardship meant selling their family home and moving in with relatives. The promise of a new home offers a chance to regain stability and independence.

For Gallmeier and his family, a groundbreaking this week at Lennar’s Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas, marked the start of a new chapter.

Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath describes the organization’s mission as fighting with hammers, nails, and humility to restore dignity and peace of mind.

Nothing magical makes these homes a reality. Land must be secured, capital committed, plans developed, materials and products donated and skilled people coordinated through hundreds of decisions and handoffs before families receive their keys.

What makes the effort extraordinary is that people across organizations commit their capabilities and resources to a shared purpose, with the needs of two families at its core.

That is gratitude expressed through action.

And as HousingWire TBD reporter Tyler Williams chronicles in his Veterans Day reporting, this spirit of service spans the nation’s homebuilding community, from West to East and from South to North. From PulteGroup and Meritage Homes donating mortgage-free homes to regional builders offering military families financial assistance, and industry partners helping veterans transition into civilian careers, the commitment takes many forms.

Behind these named initiatives are countless unheralded builders, tradespeople, suppliers, employees, and volunteers who contribute their skills, resources, and time in communities across America. Their efforts reflect a deeply rooted conviction that building homes and communities also means honoring those whose sacrifices have made our freedom to do so possible.

Human beings have an extraordinary capacity to imagine a better future. That capacity is among our greatest strengths, enabling us to conceive of possibilities that do not yet exist and to organize our efforts to make them real.

We also tend toward magical thinking: believing that our wishes, convictions, or the triumph of our preferred outcomes will somehow deliver the future we envision without the difficult work required to bring it about.

Housing affordability offers a case in point.

For years, builders, developers, investors, policymakers, and families have wrestled with the interrelated constraints of lots, labor, lending, local approvals, and lumber — shorthand for the broader building-products supply chain. These five L’s often pull against one another. Improvement in one area does not necessarily lead to meaningful progress overall. In reality, getting one right often comes at the expense of one or more of the others.

And then there’s the sixth L: leadership. No single technological breakthrough, policy initiative, favorable interest-rate cycle, or election result will solve the interconnected problems of producing homes more Americans can afford.

There is no abracadabra. Only the sustained work of learning, adapting, cooperating, and improving remains.

The traditions of military service provide a useful standard for leaders in our industry to examine their own responsibilities. Five interdependent qualities stand out: character, capability, collaborative culture, customer centricity, and competitive fire.

Character means doing what is right even when it is difficult or costly. Capability is the accumulated knowledge, judgment, training, and practiced skill that enables people to perform under uncertain conditions. A collaborative culture recognizes that complex missions depend on people with different strengths coordinating their efforts toward shared objectives.

Customer centricity keeps the needs of those being served at the center of decisions. Competitive fire is the determination to keep improving, refusing complacency while adapting intelligently to adversity.

These qualities reinforce one another. Competitive fire without character becomes recklessness. Capability without collaboration becomes isolated expertise. Customer commitment without operating discipline leads to promises you can’t keep.

They also take time to develop. The strongest organizations invest in people, relationships, processes, and productive capacity, whose value can endure long beyond any individual leader’s tenure.

That is especially important now, as housing’s affordability, capital, and demand challenges strain the industry’s capacity to withstand adversity while preparing for the opportunities ahead.

Our country’s political divisions can make it mightily tempting to believe that progress requires defeating those whose beliefs differ from our own rather than finding ways to work with them. But the nation’s hardest problems will not yield simply because one side has won an election or one set of leaders has replaced another.

Nor can we assume that the good will inevitably prevail if we simply wait long enough.

Housing’s challenges remind us why cooperation matters. No single builder, developer, lender, investor, trade partner, or government agency can solve the affordability problem alone. People and institutions with different interests must find enough common ground to accomplish what none can achieve alone.

We may first need to slow the deterioration of some problems, then stabilize conditions, and only then make sustained progress toward better outcomes. That may not satisfy our appetite for quick solutions, but it is how durable improvements are achieved.

Generations of Americans have taken oaths of service without knowing whether they would live to see the fruits of their sacrifices. Their service has helped secure and preserve a nation in which we are free, individually and together, to decide what kind of future we want to pursue.

That freedom is a gift. What we do with it is our responsibility.

For those of us who build homes, develop communities, and invest in America’s future, that responsibility includes creating places where families put down roots, neighbors form communities, and children grow up with opportunities that may surpass those available to their parents.

We will not achieve those objectives through good intentions alone or by waiting for a more favorable economic cycle or a less divided political environment.

We must refuse to do nothing. We must not tolerate inaction. And we must recognize that a bigger tent, built on mutual respect and shared purpose, can accomplish more than one defined by animosity and division.

To the veterans of our United States Armed Forces, and to their families: Thank you for the freedoms you have helped protect, the sacrifices you have made, and the example of commitment to people you may never meet.

May we honor that inheritance through what we choose to build together – for our children, our children’s children, and all the generations to come.

#5495. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5494. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5492. Housing demand shows signs of stabilizing. Does your market?

Housing demand may be stabilizing nationally, but the housing market looks different from one community to the next. In Florida's Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area, new pending listings rose 20.2% year over year in October 2026, even as some neighboring cities experienced declines. The divergence shows why local housing market trends, including buyer activity, new listings and pricing conditions, matter more than regional averages alone when evaluating market momentum.  AI Summary

Lower mortgage rates are helping stabilize housing demand even as inventory has declined, according to Logan Mohtashami’s latest Housing Market Tracker.

But a national housing demand signal doesn’t mean every local market is following. And even within the same metro area, buyer activity can tell very different stories.

The Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area in Florida offers a useful example.

New pending listings across the metro area increased 20.2% year over year in October, according to HousingWire Data. A closer look at individual cities, however, reveals that the improvement was far from uniform.

In Ormond Beach, Fla., new pending listings increased 116.7% year over year in October, rising from 72 in 2025 to 156 in 2026.

Nearby Port Orange recorded an 80% increase, while Daytona Beach saw a 63.2% gain.

But Deltona, one of the cities that gives the metro area its name, experienced a 24.3% decline. New pending listings fell from 136 to 103. New Smyrna Beach also recorded a decline of 25.3%.

Different patterns of buyer activity. This chart compares weekly new pending listings in Ormond Beach and Deltona over the past six months. While both cities experience fluctuations in weekly activity, their October year-over-year trends tell different stories. Adjust the date range or select YoY to explore how each city’s activity compares with its historical performance.

For housing professionals, the distinction matters. A regional market can be gaining momentum while individual communities within it are moving in the opposite direction.

Fall typically brings a slowdown in housing activity, but the timing and magnitude can vary significantly by market.

That’s why a change in new pending listings needs seasonal context.

Consider the average weekly new pending listings in three Volusia County cities between September and October 2026:

Historical trends add another layer. Ormond Beach also experienced an increase in average weekly new pending listings between September and October in 2025, but the increase was smaller. Deltona experienced an increase during that period in 2025 before reversing direction this year.

The lesson isn’t that one city is stronger than another. It’s that seasonal changes can play out differently even in neighboring communities.

A decline in new pending listings may be consistent with a market’s typical seasonal pattern. A smaller-than-usual decline could signal improving momentum. And an increase in activity deserves a closer look to determine whether it represents a sustained shift or a short-term fluctuation.

The Florida example raises a useful question: Are changes in buyer activity consistent across the communities you serve, or is the broader market trend masking important differences?

Four metrics can help you recognize changes, understand what they might signal and put that information to work.

What to watch: Compare new pending listings with the same period last year and track changes over several consecutive weeks. Look for activity that differs from the market’s typical seasonal pattern.

What it could mean: Sustained increases may indicate strengthening buyer activity, while declines can signal weakening demand. A smaller-than-usual seasonal decline may also be an early sign of stabilization.

How to use it: Identify communities where buyer activity is changing. Agents can use that information to set expectations with buyers and sellers, while loan officers can help referral partners understand where transaction opportunities may be improving.

What to watch: Compare the number of new listings entering the market with new pending listings. Is the gap between them widening or narrowing?

What it could mean: When new pending activity increases relative to new listings, buyers may be absorbing a greater share of incoming supply. When new listings grow faster than new pending activity, more homes may be competing for buyers’ attention.

How to use it: Evaluate whether buyers are likely to encounter more competition or more choices. For agents, that can inform pricing and offer strategies. For lending teams, it can help identify markets where purchase activity may be gaining momentum relative to available opportunities.

What to watch: Track the share of active listings with price reductions and whether that share is rising or falling over several weeks.

What it could mean: A rising share may suggest sellers are having difficulty attracting buyers at their initial asking prices. A declining share could indicate better alignment between pricing and buyer expectations, although changes in listing mix and seasonality can also influence the metric.

How to use it: Bring evidence into pricing conversations rather than relying solely on recent comparable sales. Loan officers can use the same information to help referral partners understand negotiating conditions and where pricing expectations may be changing.

What to watch: Compare median days on market with recent weeks and the same period last year. Look for whether homes are spending more or less time on the market.

What it could mean: Shorter marketing times alongside stronger new pending activity may reinforce evidence of improving demand. Longer marketing times, particularly when new pending activity is declining, may indicate that buyers are becoming more selective or that listings are taking longer to find the right price.

How to use it: Set more realistic expectations for listing timelines, buyer urgency and transaction pipelines. Brokerage and lending leaders can also use changes in market pace to inform team planning and activity forecasts.

If new pending listings are increasing, new listings are flat and days on market are declining, the combination provides stronger evidence of improving buyer activity than new pending listings alone.

But if new pending listings are rising alongside increasing price reductions and longer marketing times, the market may be experiencing a more complicated adjustment.

Consider Port Orange, Fla., where the share of listings with price reductions has declined since late September, but weekly new pending listings have fluctuated without a sustained increase. Fewer price reductions may be an encouraging sign, but they don’t necessarily indicate stronger buyer activity.

Different signals, different stories. In Port Orange, the share of listings with price reductions has fallen while weekly new pending listings have remained uneven. Adjust the date range to explore how these trends have changed over time.

Then compare neighboring communities. As the Florida example demonstrates, the same combination of metrics can tell different stories within a single metro area.

You can track these metrics and customize charts by city or ZIP code in HousingWire Intelligence.

The objective isn’t to predict the next market shift. It’s to recognize what is changing, understand what the evidence suggests and bring a more informed perspective to conversations with clients, referral partners and your team.

Logan’s national analysis suggests housing demand is finding some stability as mortgage rates ease. But the Florida data shows why that broader trend is only the starting point.

The more useful question isn’t simply whether the housing market is improving. It’s whether your market is improving, how you know and what that means for your business.

National trends provide context. Local data helps you make better decisions.

Methodology: The analysis uses HousingWire Data and covers single-family residential listings in the Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area in Volusia County, Florida.

October year-over-year comparisons use five weekly reporting periods in both 2025 and 2026. September-to-October comparisons use average weekly new pending listings to account for the different number of reporting weeks in each month.

New pending listings measure properties newly entering pending status during the reporting period, rather than the total number of properties under contract or completed sales.

All figures reflect data available through Nov. 6, 2026.

#5491. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5490. CPC Biotech Launches the Quattroflow HTX All-in-One Pump Drive for Bioprocessing

DOWNERS GROVE, Ill., Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CPC Biotech, part of PSG and Dover (NYSE: DOV) and a leading manufacturer of connectors, pumps, and flow sensors used in biopharmaceutical processing, today announced the launch of the Quattroflow HTX, an all-in-one pump drive featuring touchscreen control, flexible remote operation, and fluid-specific calibration.

The HTX pairs with the same four-piston diaphragm pump heads used across the Quattroflow range, in single-use and multiple-use configurations. The new drive includes an upgraded motor, drive electronics, software, control functions, and interfaces designed to enhance operations.

The HTX was created with the operator in mind. A five-inch capacitive touchscreen replaces the keypad and small display of the previous generation and has been tested with several types of gloves, including cleanroom gloves. Speed, flow rate, and dispense volume can be adjusted directly on the screen using the operator's preferred units, and the drive displays speed, temperature, run hours, alarms, and fault codes.

"Ease of use was the starting point for the HTX. Its intuitive touchscreen and integrated, space-saving design eliminate the need for a separate inverter, so it works as a standalone unit on a laboratory bench or in bioprocessing applications," said Andreas Frerix, Product Manager Quattroflow at CPC Biotech.

The HTX connects over Modbus TCP via Ethernet, with analog and digital inputs and outputs available as a hardware alternative. Firmware updates and pump configurations can be transferred by USB, allowing configurations to be replicated across pumps.

It also offers fluid-specific calibration to support accurate flow control across a range of viscosities and densities. Operators can perform a test dispense, measure volume using a scale or a flow meter, and enter the result, allowing the software to recalculate its internal curve.

"The accuracy of the Quattroflow pump is what makes the HTX so versatile. Because each motor revolution displaces a defined volume, the HTX can reliably calculate flow rates and dispense precise amounts of fluid, for example, when filling bottles or containers," added Frerix.

Dispensing mode enables repeatable, measured volume dispensing on demand. With a foot switch connected, the operator fills a container, moves the next one into place and fills again. The pumping principle is unchanged, producing low-pulse, low-shear transfer that supports the range's established use in tangential flow filtration and chromatography.

Additional features include motor fault and overpressure alarms, timestamped alarm logging, and configurable user access controls with PIN-protected permissions. The interface is available in English, German, and French. Applications include media and buffer transfer, precise dispensing and small-batch filling, and small-scale filtration.

The HTX represents the next generation of the HT platform introduced in 2016 and is available to order in three sizes. For more information about the performance and versatility of the Quattroflow HTX Drive Series, please visit the HTX webpage.

#5489. British inference chip developer Fractile raises $720M in funding

Fractile Ltd., a British startup that develops artificial intelligence inference chips, has raised $720 million in funding.

Reuters reported today that the Series C round was led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint. They were joined by about a dozen others including the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund, the British Business Bank and Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG investment arm. Fractile is now worth $7 billion.

Fractile was founded in 2022 by AI researcher Walter Goodwin (pictured), who serves as its chief executive. The company reportedly expects its chips to provide up to 100 times better performance than current silicon. Furthermore, Fractile is promising a 90% reduction in energy use. The chips deliver those improvements by removing the need for AI models to move data to off-chip HBM memory.

Large language models generate prompt responses through a workflow that involves numerous steps. When an LLM completes a processing step, it sends the results to an off-chip HBM memory chip. It then retrieves those results to lay the groundwork for the next step. Those repeated data round-trips take a significant amount of time, which slows down inference.

Fractile is not the only AI chip supplier tackling that bottleneck. Cerebras Systems Inc., which went public in May, offers wafer-size accelerators that reduce data movement by keeping information in a large onboard cache. That cache is faster than off-chip HBM modules. The company’s newest processor, the WSE-3T, can hold 44 gigabytes of data.

Cerebras’ on-chip cache is based on SRAM, a type of memory that was historically added to processors in only small quantities. SRAM cells, the technology’s basic building blocks, have six transistors apiece. Those transistors read and write data faster than the single transistor found in HBM cells. At the same time, SRAM’s speed comes with certain trade-offs: it’s expensive and has limited capacity.

Fractile is taking a different approach to reducing data movement. Instead of integrating SRAM into its inference chips, the company is stacking standard DRAM memory on top of them. Placing a memory module immediately above a processor’s logic circuits minimizes the distance that data has to cover. That speeds up traffic while lowering the amount of electricity needed to shuffle it back and forth.

Samsung Electronics Co. is developing a similar technology. In August, the company debuted an HBM variant called zHBM that can be stacked atop AI accelerators. It uses tiny copper wires to move data to and from the host chip. Samsung says the technology will be eight times faster than HBM5, a future iteration of HBM more performant than the versions in use today.

Fractile, for its part, estimates that its chips will enable LLM to process several thousand tokens per second. It plans to ship the processors as part of rack-scale systems that will also include custom software. Many AI chipmakers offer custom compilers, software tools that automatically turn customers’ LLMs into a format compatible with their silicon.

Fractile expects to start shipping its chips next year.

#5488. Education, not operations, are holding back reverse for purchase deals

Reverse mortgage for purchase loans often close in seven to 25 days, panelists said at NRMLA Annual. Down payments typically run from 45% to 65%, and early counseling plus contract management can prevent delays.  AI Summary

Reverse mortgage for purchase loans work much like other types of home purchase financing. Even so, many real estate agents, financial advisers and loan officers don’t know how they work, according to experts who spoke this week at the National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA)’s Annual Convention & Expo in San Antonio.

Peter Morris, an Arizona-based senior vice president at Revolution Mortgage, said the ideal reverse for purchase prospects are seniors who want to upsize, downsize or relocate. He also frequently works with borrowers who don’t qualify for traditional 30-year loans or home equity products due to debt-to-income or credit constraints.

Morris said he’s seeing rising interest in these financing options among real estate partners. He recently hosted a continuing education course where “I had the most Realtors that I’ve ever had in a CE class.”

Senior homeowners with high levels of equity and a need to move are able to utilize the federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) program or proprietary programs to purchase their next primary residence. The typical down payment ranges from 45% to 65%, depending on the appraised value, interest rate and age of the borrower. For example, an 80-year-old buyer has a smaller down payment requirement than a 70-year-old buyer since they have a shorter life expectancy.

Morris relayed a story about an agent partner in North Carolina with five listings between $400,000 and $800,000. While an all-cash buyer with $400,000 — typically a highly coveted buyer — could afford only some of these listings, a reverse for purchase borrower with the same $400,000 might be able to afford each of them, he told the agent.

“You have to educate your Realtor and show them that they are losing out, and they have the potential of making a lot more money with such a simple product,” Morris said. “I can show you how you can do less transactions and make more money, because you can buy more of a house in a reverse purchase.”

Shain Urwin, national reverse mortgage director for C2 Financial Corp., and Agi Glukhovskiy, SVP of business support and operations for Rate, explained some of the differences between traditional and reverse for purchase deals.

Borrower counseling through an independent third party is required on all HECM for Purchase deals insured by the Federal Housing Administration and for most proprietary reverse mortgages. Reverse transactions also have unique forms, including a Good Faith Estimate (GFE) and a HUD-1 form, rather than the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure forms commonly associated with forward mortgages.

Glukhovskiy said the absence of conventional forward lending documents are actually an advantage for reverse deals since they won’t have a mandatory federal waiting period. Urwin noted that a handful of states, such as California and Idaho, have implemented their own waiting periods. Beyond that, however, the steps are largely the same as any traditional deal as the process moves from application to underwriting, appraisal, title and approval.

The panelists sought to dispel ideas that reverse purchases are slow to close. Glukhovskiy said her team has wrapped them up in seven to 10 days, and although the average is 20 to 25 days, the idea that the process takes 45 days is “absolutely nonsense,” she added. Neil Sweren, a Baltimore-based reverse division manager for Atlantic Coast Mortgage, recalled a recent deal that closed in seven calendar days.

Angel Booth, national sales manager for title and settlement services provider Premier Reverse Closings, clarified to HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily that the typical 10- to 15-day process cited by lenders is “absolutely attainable” once the loan is clear to close.

Glukovskiy said the keys to a quick closing are finishing counseling prior to the start of the home search process, collecting income documentation, and setting expectations with agents and lending operations staff. Loan officers should read the purchase contract and know every contingency date, Urwin said, as trouble begins when they overpromise. And Sweren pointed to timing: If a closing date gets pushed back and falls within six months of the borrower’s birthday, the amount of cash needed to close can change.

Simultaneous closings, where the borrower sells one home and buys another, can be difficult but not impossible to pull off. Glukovskiy recommended that sale proceeds should go straight to the title company handling the property being purchased, rather than going to the borrower.

Urwin told a cautionary tale about a borrower who took their sale proceeds and paid down a home equity line of credit on another property, leaving them ineligible to use the borrowed funds to buy their new house. “I learned from that very painfully, but those kinds of nuances matter when tracking those funds,” he said.

For loan officers who are new to reverse for purchase deals, panelists urged them to study up before they present the benefits to agents.

Continuing education courses are a prime way to teach agents, with Sweren saying they often come to his classes to help their own parents or grandparents. Many agents happen to be senior homeowners and may need assistance for themselves. Being the go-to loan officer when a listing includes a reverse mortgage should be part of everyone’s market strategy.

The panelists admitted that financial advisers may be a harder sell. Urwin noted that because these referral partners focus on cash and assets under management, they may not recommend a client put their cash into a home. But he relayed a success story where an adviser partner took out a reverse mortgage on his own home, then began sending referrals to Urwin when he had older clients who wanted to pay cash for a house.

The goal in these situations, Urwin said, should be to avoid an all-cash purchase. Clients should consider long-term tax strategies and the choice between leaving illiquid home equity or highly liquid cash to their heirs.

Sweren also mentioned the advantage of reverse mortgages in planning for rising healthcare costs, something he believes the industry “has not gotten past the tip of the iceberg” with. HECM lines of credit serve as “the most flexible borrowing instrument in the market by far,” he said, as borrowers can qualify for relatively large amounts, withdraw funds as needed, and have available proceeds grow over time based on the interest rate and annual mortgage insurance premium.

Sweren said reverse mortgage professionals should remember that “this is a very emotional transaction for seniors” as they may be leaving a home they’ve lived in for decades. They also may be widows or widowers who didn’t handle their family’s finances, meaning they’ll need additional support to get the deal over the line.

“Respecting that and understanding the emotional journey your client is on — and explaining that to the rest of the team that’s involved — is super helpful,” he added.

#5486. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5485. Why the 2026 fake foreclosure crisis never happened

Foreclosure activity in 2026 rose off low levels but did not signal broad credit stress. With 9- to 18-month timelines and LTV at 44.2%, the data points to normalization, not a crisis.  AI Summary

The 2026 foreclosure crisis that some people predicted has failed to materialize, and now those people look silly. We should be thankful for the regulations and laws enacted that laid the foundation for such a sound housing credit market: The 2005 bankruptcy reform law and the 2010 Dodd-Frank laws that established qualified mortgage guidelines were historically positive for the U.S. economy.

Looking at the New York Fed’s Household Debt and Credit Report for Q3, we can clearly see that the anticipated foreclosure crisis hasn’t happened. All the headlines showing a high percentage of year-over-year growth in foreclosure data didn’t amount to anything near a crisis.

For those who expected a situation worse than what we experienced in 2008, it has been an embarrassing year. This highlights the dangers of listening to economic discussions from those without the necessary expertise. So let’s talk about where these doomers get it wrong.

The idea that the FHA foreclosure moratorium, which ended in October 2025, would lead to a surge in distressed listings has been a popular topic this year. It’s gotten a lot of headlines, but has fallen flat on its face, since that isn’t how the foreclosure-to-listing process works in America. At minimum, it takes 9-18 months from the start of the foreclosure process to finally add that supply to the marketplace.And foreclosure data has not, at any point since 2014, shown any material sign of credit stress building up in the pipeline. Always remember, 1%-4% of all mortgages are always going to be in delinquency; it’s when that data breaks above historical norms that it should get everyone’s attention.To illustrate what a true foreclosure crisis might look like, we can consider the historical context: since World War II, we have experienced 13 recessions with an average unemployment rate of 7.8%, but only one significant foreclosure crisis, which was the run-up to the 2008 Great Recession.

It took four years for the foreclosure credit market to build up before the 2008 recession hit. As we finish Q3 of 2026, we still haven’t returned to pre-COVID levels of foreclosure credit stress, as the data below has always shown for anyone who believes in reading.

The New York Fed foreclosure credit stress data line moves slowly, and unless this index is above 200, there isn’t much activity out of the norm. The many posts this year predicting a foreclosure crisis have proven to be exaggerated. The scale of the situation is small, and it’s clear that many commentators lack the experience to accurately discuss the current market conditions.Additionally, I want to highlight HousingWire’s new listing data. During the previous housing crisis, credit foreclosures directly impacted new listing data, pushing weekly listings to between 250,000 and 400,000 — for years. These listings represented distressed sellers who were forced to sell in an underwater market. All those increases from 2005-2008 in foreclosures eventually became distressed sales, and none of that is happening today. Let’s compare the new listings data for last week to the same week from 2009-2011:

The 2008 massive credit boom and bust took many years to create. We have not seen this kind of credit boom in housing from 2010-2026, so it’s impossible to have a credit bust like 2008 — or “worse than 2008,” as many untrained fake housing analysts have talked about for years. A lot of people can’t let go of the past, as they’re still dancing with the ghost of the 2008 housing crisis. They should relax, have a glass of wine, and reflect on their bad takes.In contrast, over the last 16 years, FICO scores in America have remained strong. Most homeowners have 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, and qualification guidelines are much more stringent and effective now. Rising wages and homeowners staying in their properties longer have contributed to the overall financial health of American households.

Despite claims of an impending foreclosure crisis, the reality is quite different. In 2010, over 23% of homes in America were underwater, with loan-to-value ratios reaching nearly 86% in 2011. Currently, the loan-to-value figure is down to 44.2%, as the chart below shows.

It’s crucial to be cautious about who you listen to, as the narrative of a looming crisis has been overstated for many years. If someone tells you it’s housing 2008 or a foreclosure crisis is here, tell them to read a book instead of burning it, and read HousingWire.

#5483. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”
