#5482. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5481. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5480. CAE reports second quarter fiscal 2027 results

MONTREAL, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- (Nasdaq: CAE) (TSX: CAE) - CAE Inc. (CAE or the Company) today reported its financial results for the fiscal second quarter ended September 30, 2026. For more information, please refer to the annex for the second quarter fiscal 2027 available at cae.com/investors.

"We delivered another solid quarter in Q2, with improved adjusted profitability, strong free cash flow and continued progress on our transformation priorities," said Matthew Bromberg, CAE's President and CEO. "Given our performance year-to-date and increased confidence in our ability to execute our second-half plan, we are raising our full-year fiscal 2027 outlook for adjusted EPS and adjusted segment operating income margin. We remain focused on advancing our transformation and building a higher-growth, higher-return CAE.

In Q2, Civil results were in line with our expectations, with strong business aviation performance and higher yearâoverâyear utilization across both commercial and business aviation training offset by a lower contribution from Civil products. Defense delivered another strong quarter, with double-digit year-over-year growth in adjusted segment operating income and continued underlying margin expansion.

We also made progress across each of our three transformation priorities: portfolio, capital discipline, and operational performance. In October, we announced an agreement to sell Flightscape to SITA for US$500 million. We expect the transaction to close in the first half of calendar year 2027 and intend to deploy the proceeds in accordance with our disciplined capital allocation priorities, including funding our transformation, supporting growth in our core businesses, and returning capital to shareholders. In Q2, we accelerated our share repurchase activity, bringing year-to-date repurchases through the second quarter to approximately 3.0 million shares for $106.1 million.

Overall, our second quarter performance included strong execution, Defense margin expansion, higher free cash flow, increased share repurchases and meaningful progress on our transformation. We are building a more disciplined CAE, with stronger margins and cash generation supporting long-term value creation. We look forward to providing further details on our strategy, transformation and growth opportunities at CAE's Analyst and Investor Day on February 25, 2027."

(1) This press release includes non-IFRS financial measures, non-IFRS ratios, capital management measures and supplementary financial measures. These measures are not standardized financial measures prescribed under IFRS and therefore should not be confused with, or used as an alternative for, performance measures calculated according to IFRS. Furthermore, these measures should not be compared with similarly titled measures provided or used by other issuers. Refer to the "Non-IFRS and other financial measures" section of this press release for the definitions and a reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable measure under IFRS.

The Company is increasing its fiscal 2027 outlook for adjusted EPS and adjusted segment operating income margin.

Fiscal 2027 consolidated financial outlook

Adjusted segment operating income margin(1)

In fiscal 2027, management continues to expect consolidated revenue to increase by a low-single digit percentage, with Civil revenue expected to be flat to slightly down and Defense expected to grow at a mid-single digit rate.

Management now expects fiscal 2027 adjusted segment operating income margin of 14.9% to 15.4%, up from 14.6% to 15.1% previously, reflecting higher expected margins in both Civil and Defense and increased confidence in the Company's ability to execute its second-half plan. Adjusted EPS is now expected to be $1.28 to $1.35, up from $1.21 to $1.28 previously, reflecting the stronger operating outlook as well as lower expected finance expense and a lower effective tax rate.

In Defense, for the full year, CAE continues to expect higher year-over-year profitability, supported by bid discipline, structural cost reduction and strong program management. In Civil, for the full year, profitability is still expected to remain below prior-year levels, reflecting lower revenue, the near-term impact of network optimization actions and elevated investment levels intended to support stronger long-term performance.

The total cost of the transformation plan is anticipated to be approximately $200 million to $250 million, with approximately $100 million arising from non-cash charges. Of the total cost, $42.6 million was incurred in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, bringing the total costs incurred to date to $175.3 million. The majority of the remaining costs are expected to be incurred in fiscal 2027. We remain on track for our transformation targets, including $125 million to $150 million of annual transformation run-rate savings.

Ongoing geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East continues to put pressure on the global aviation industry. The Company has undertaken mitigation actions, including redeploying certain training activities within its global network. To date, these actions have been effective at mitigating the direct operational impacts from the conflict. Our outlook assumes that these mitigation actions remain effective for the balance of fiscal 2027. However, an intensification of the conflict or a further deterioration in regional conditions, including sustained increases in fuel prices or disruptions to airline activity, customer operations, or supply chains, could result in additional pressure on performance.

This outlook is provided as at November 11, 2026, to assist analysts, investors and shareholders in forming their respective views on CAE's expected performance for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027. This outlook constitutes forward-looking information and is based on multiple estimates and assumptions, including those set out in the "Forward-Looking Statements" section below, and are subject to the risks and uncertainties summarized therein. As such, the reader is cautioned that using this information for other purposes may be inappropriate and these measures are subject to change as conditions evolve and actual results may differ, and such differences may be material. The Company cautions that the assumptions used to prepare the outlook could prove to be incorrect or inaccurate.

Civil Aviation (Civil)Second quarter Civil revenue was $652.3 million compared to $670.0 million in the second quarter last year. Operating income was $61.3 million (9.4% of revenue) compared to $108.7 million (16.2% of revenue) in the same quarter last year. Adjusted segment operating income was $103.9 million (15.9% of revenue) compared to $124.1 million (18.5% of revenue) in the second quarter last year. The decrease in adjusted segment operating income was mainly due to a lower contribution from simulator sales, primarily due to a lower contribution from contracts accounted for based on progress toward completion, and lower contribution from the sale of simulator capacity structured as finance lease arrangements. The decrease was also due to higher selling, general and administrative expenses. The decrease was partially offset by a higher contribution from business training services, driven by higher utilization. During the quarter, Civil delivered 11 full-flight simulators (FFSs) and second quarter Civil training centre utilization was 65.0%.

During the quarter, Civil signed training solutions contracts valued at $580.6 million for a range of long-term commercial and business aviation training agreements, including 7 FFS sales.

The Civil book-to-sales ratio(1) was 0.89 times for the quarter and 1.07 times for the last 12 months. The Civil adjusted backlog at the end of the quarter was $8.3 billion.

Defense and Security (Defense)Second quarter Defense revenue was $552.4 million compared to $566.6 million in the second quarter last year. Operating income was $53.1 million (9.6% of revenue) compared to $46.6 million (8.2% of revenue) in the same quarter last year. Adjusted segment operating income was $75.4 million (13.6% of revenue), compared to $52.6 million (9.3% of revenue) in the second quarter last year. The increase in adjusted segment operating income was mainly due to higher profitability from products recognized upon delivery and increased profitability on our contracts in North America. The increase was also due to the recognition of $11 million in investment tax credits identified and claimed in the current period in respect of prior years.

Defense booked orders for $586.0 million this quarter for a book-to-sales ratio of 1.06 times. The ratio for the last 12 months was 1.03 times. The Defense adjusted backlog, including unfunded contract awards and CAE's interest in joint ventures, at the end of the quarter was $11.3 billion.

Finance expense â net this quarter was $44.6 million, down from $56.9 million in the second quarter last year. The year-over-year decrease was mainly due to lower finance expense on long-term debt reflecting a lower level of borrowings during the period.

Income tax expense this quarter amounted to $9.1 million, representing an effective tax rate of 13.0%, compared to 22.7% for the second quarter last year. The adjusted effective tax rate(1), which is the income tax rate used to determine adjusted net income(1) and adjusted EPS, was 18.7% this quarter compared to 22.9% in the second quarter of last year. The decrease in the adjusted effective tax rate was mainly attributable to the change in the mix of income from various jurisdictions.

Net cash provided by operating activities was $215.5 million for the quarter, compared to $214.0 million in the second quarter last year. Free cash flow(1) was $179.9 million for the quarter compared to $109.8 million in the second quarter last year. The increase was mainly due to lower capital expenditures.

Capital expenditures(1) totaled $48.9 million this quarter compared to $107.6 million in the second quarter of fiscal 2026.

Net debt(1) at the end of the quarter was $2,534.6 million for a net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA(1) of 2.16 times. This compares to net debt of $2,646.2 million and a net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA of 2.27 times at the end of the preceding quarter.

Adjusted return on invested capital(1) was 7.7% this quarter compared to 7.5% last quarter and 7.6% in the second quarter last year.

Potential transition to U.S. GAAPAs part of our ongoing transformation and in an effort to align the Company's financial reporting with aerospace and defense peers, CAE is exploring a potential transition from IFRS to United States generally accepted accounting principles ("U.S. GAAP"). If adopted, the change would be applied for the fourth quarter and fiscal year ending March 31, 2027, on a full retrospective basis. We have established a project team and a project plan, and we are currently evaluating the potential impact that a transition to U.S. GAAP may have on our consolidated financial statements.

Non-IFRS and other financial measuresThis press release includes non-IFRS financial measures, non-IFRS ratios, capital management measures and supplementary financial measures. These measures are not standardized financial measures prescribed under IFRS and therefore should not be confused with, or used as an alternative for, performance measures calculated according to IFRS. Furthermore, these measures should not be compared with similarly titled measures provided or used by other issuers. Management believes that these measures provide additional insight into our operating performance and trends and facilitate comparisons across reporting periods.

Certain non-IFRS and other financial measures are provided on a consolidated basis and separately for each of our segments (Civil Aviation and Defense and Security) since we analyze their results and performance separately.

Reconciliations and calculations of non-IFRS measures to the most directly comparable measures under IFRS are also set forth below in the section "Reconciliations and Calculations of this press release".

Changes to non-IFRS measuresAs announced in May 2026, we revised the composition of certain non-IFRS measures in the first quarter of fiscal 2027:

In addition, we refined the measurement of simulator utilization rates, full-flight simulators (FFSs) in CAE's network and Simulator equivalent unit (SEU), which are no longer adjusted for factors such as relocations, downtime or storage.

Comparative figures have been adjusted to conform to these changes.

Performance measuresGross profit margin (or gross profit as a % of revenue)Gross profit margin is a supplementary financial measure calculated by dividing our gross profit by revenue for a given period. We track it because we believe it provides an enhanced understanding of our operating performance and facilitates the comparison across reporting periods.

Operating income margin (or operating income as a % of revenue)Operating income margin is a supplementary financial measure calculated by dividing our operating income by revenue for a given period. We track it because we believe it provides an enhanced understanding of our operating performance and facilitates the comparison across reporting periods.

Adjusted segment operating income or lossAdjusted segment operating income or loss is a non-IFRS financial measure that gives us an indication of the profitability of each segment because it does not include the impact of any items not specifically related to the segment's performance. We calculate adjusted segment operating income by taking operating income and adjusting for restructuring, integration and acquisition costs, amortization of acquisition-related intangible assets, and impairments and other gains and losses arising from significant strategic transactions or specific events. Impairments and other gains and losses arising from significant strategic transactions or specific events consist of the executive management transition costs (as described in Section 5.4 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2026 and Section 5.6 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2025), the gain on fair value remeasurement of SIMCOM (as described in Note 7 of our consolidated financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2025) and the shareholder matters (as described in Section 5.5 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2025). We track adjusted segment operating income because we believe it provides an enhanced understanding of our operating performance and facilitates the comparison across reporting periods. Adjusted segment operating income on a consolidated basis is a total of segments measure since it is the profitability measure employed by management for making decisions about allocating resources to segments and assessing segment performance.

Adjusted segment operating income margin (or adjusted segment operating income as a % of revenue)Adjusted segment operating income margin is a non-IFRS ratio calculated by dividing our adjusted segment operating income by revenue for a given period. We track it because we believe it provides an enhanced understanding of our operating performance and facilitates the comparison across reporting periods.

Adjusted effective tax rateAdjusted effective tax rate is a supplementary financial measure that represents the effective tax rate on adjusted net income or loss. It is calculated by dividing our income tax expense by our earnings before income taxes, adjusting for the same items used to determine adjusted net income or loss. We track it because we believe it provides an enhanced understanding of the impact of changes in income tax rates and the mix of income on our operating performance and facilitates the comparison across reporting periods.

Adjusted net income or lossAdjusted net income or loss is a non-IFRS financial measure we use as an alternate view of our operating results. We calculate it by taking our net income attributable to equity holders of the Company from continuing operations and adjusting for restructuring, integration and acquisition costs, amortization of acquisition-related intangible assets, and impairments and other gains and losses arising from significant strategic transactions or specific events, after tax, as well as significant one-time tax items. Impairments and other gains and losses arising from significant strategic transactions or specific events consist of the executive management transition costs (as described in Section 5.4 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2026 and Section 5.6 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2025), the gain on fair value remeasurement of SIMCOM (as described in Note 7 of our consolidated financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2025) and the shareholder matters (as described in Section 5.5 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2025). We track adjusted net income because we believe it provides an enhanced understanding of our operating performance and facilitates the comparison across reporting periods.

Adjusted earnings or loss per share (EPS)Adjusted earnings or loss per share is a non-IFRS ratio calculated by dividing adjusted net income or loss by the weighted average number of diluted shares. We track it because we believe it provides an enhanced understanding of our operating performance on a per share basis and facilitates the comparison across reporting periods.

EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDAEBITDA is a non-IFRS financial measure which comprises net income or loss from continuing operations before income taxes, finance expense â net, depreciation and amortization. Adjusted EBITDA further adjusts for restructuring, integration and acquisition costs, and impairments and other gains and losses arising from significant strategic transactions or specific events. Impairments and other gains and losses arising from significant strategic transactions or specific events consist of the executive management transition costs (as described in Section 5.4 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2026 and Section 5.6 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2025), the gain on fair value remeasurement of SIMCOM (as described in Note 7 of our consolidated financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2025) and the shareholder matters (as described in Section 5.5 of the MD&A for the year ended March 31, 2025). We use EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA to evaluate our operating performance, by eliminating the impact of non-operational or non-cash items.

Free cash flowFree cash flow is a non-IFRS financial measure that assesses our ability to generate cash from our ongoing operations after considering ongoing investments required for property, plant and equipment and intangible assets. It demonstrates our ability to generate cash to repay debt obligations, make strategic investments and return cash to shareholders through either dividends or share repurchases. We use it as an indicator of our financial strength and liquidity. We calculate it by taking the net cash generated by our continuing operating activities, subtracting property, plant and equipment expenditures, intangible assets expenditures and other investing activities and adding proceeds from the disposal of property, plant and equipment, dividends received from equity accounted investees and proceeds, net of payments, from equity accounted investees.

Cash conversion rateCash conversion rate is a non-IFRS ratio calculated by dividing free cash flow by adjusted net income. We use it to assess our performance in cash flow generation and as a basis for evaluating our capitalization structure.

Liquidity and capital structure measuresInvested capitalInvested capital is a non-IFRS financial measure we use to evaluate and monitor how much we are investing in our business:

Adjusted return on invested capital (ROIC)Adjusted ROIC is a non-IFRS ratio calculated over a rolling four-quarter period by taking adjusted net operating income after tax, divided by the average invested capital from continuing operations. Adjusted net operating income after tax is calculated by taking adjusted net income and further adjusting for finance expense â net, after tax. We use adjusted ROIC to evaluate the profitability of our invested capital.

Net debtNet debt is a capital management measure we use to monitor how much debt we have after taking into account cash and cash equivalents. We use it as an indicator of our overall financial position, and calculate it by taking our total long-term debt, including the current portion of long-term debt, and subtracting cash and cash equivalents.

Net debt-to-EBITDA and net debt-to-adjusted EBITDANet debt-to-EBITDA and net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA are non-IFRS ratios calculated as net debt divided by the last twelve months EBITDA (or adjusted EBITDA). We use net debt-to-EBITDA and net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA because they reflect our ability to service our debt obligations.

Growth measuresAdjusted order intakeAdjusted order intake is a supplementary financial measure that represents the expected value of orders we have received:

Adjusted backlogAdjusted backlog is a supplementary financial measure that represents expected future revenues and includes obligated backlog, joint venture backlog and unfunded backlog and options:

Book-to-sales ratioThe book-to-sales ratio is a supplementary financial measure calculated by dividing adjusted order intake by revenue in a given period. We use it to monitor the level of future growth of the business over time.

Supplementary non-financial information definitionsFull-flight simulators (FFSs) in CAE's networkA FFS is a full-size replica of a specific make, model and series of an aircraft cockpit, including a motion system. In our count of FFSs in the network, we generally only include FFSs that are of the highest fidelity and do not include any fixed based training devices, or other lower-level devices, as these are typically used in addition to FFSs in the same approved training programs.

Simulator equivalent unit (SEU)SEU is a measure we use to show the total average number of FFSs available to generate earnings during the period. For example, in the case of a 50/50 flight training joint venture, we will report only 50% of the FFSs under this joint venture as a SEU.

Utilization rateUtilization rate is a measure we use to assess the performance of our Civil simulator training network. While utilization rate does not perfectly correlate to revenue recognized, we track it, together with other measures, because we believe it is an indicator of our operating performance. We calculate it by taking the number of training hours sold on our simulators during the period divided by the practical training capacity available for the same period.

Forward-looking financial measuresTransformation run-rate savingsTransformation run-rate savings is a supplementary financial measure we use to show the targeted total cost savings from the activities and initiatives associated with our transformation plan and their anticipated contribution to adjusted segment operating income. We use it to track and measure the success of our transformation plan.

At CAE, we exist to make the world safer. We deliver cutting-edge training, simulation, and critical operations solutions to prepare aviation professionals and defence forces for the moments that matter. Every day, we empower pilots, cabin crew, maintenance technicians, airlines, business aviation operators, and defence and security personnel to perform at their best and when the stakes are the highest. Around the globe, we're everywhere customers need us to be with sites and training locationsâ¯in over 40 countries. For nearly 80 years, CAE has been at the forefront of innovation, consistently seeking to set the standard by delivering excellence in high-fidelity flight simulators and training solutions, while embedding sustainability at the heart of everything we do. By harnessing technology and enhancing human performance, we strive to be the trusted partner in advancing safety and mission readiness - today and tomorrow.

#5479. Google tests Tabletop, letting groups build planning tools with an AI agent

Google LLC today began testing Tabletop, a Google Labs experiment in which groups share an online space and ask an artificial intelligence agent to build the planning tools they need.

In a blog post, Roman Nurik, design and engineering lead at Google Labs, wrote that coordinating a family trip or a potluck goes more smoothly when the whole group can pitch in from one place. Whoever sets up a space adds the links, files and ideas the group has collected, and from there a request to @tabletop produces the tool.

Tools Google lists include itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets, and there is a set of starter templates that Tabletop users can access as well. Once the space is shared through an invite link posted in the group’s existing chat, everyone can work on those tools at the same time, “like in a Google Doc,” Nurik wrote.

When a guest at an office party in one of Google’s demos ends up seated next to the boss, a request to @tabletop turns the seating chart into one where name badges can be dragged between tables. Any tool can be reworked the same way, according to the Tabletop site.

Google did not say which of its models run Tabletop. When Labs released its Disco browser experiment last December, Gemini 3 was the model it used to turn a person’s open tabs into small web apps.

Tabletop also follows Google’s move in September to let up to six members of a household share the division’s CC agent. Rival OpenAI Group PBC added group chats to ChatGPT a year ago, and up to 20 people can now talk to the chatbot in one thread.

In ChatGPT the chatbot sits inside the conversation as one more member, and OpenAI said at launch that it had taught the model to judge when to join in. Replies in those chats initially came from GPT-5.1 Auto, which chooses a model based on the prompt and on the subscription of whoever ChatGPT is answering. OpenAI also kept personal memory out of group chats entirely.

Tabletop is limited for now to U.S. users 18 and older who sign up through the waitlist at tabletop.google, with Google saying it will let more people in each week. Google’s announcement does not mention pricing or a release outside the U.S.

#5478. BloombergNEF warned data center gas plants could raise U.S. power emissions 10%

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The report counts 181GW of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of it in the U.S.

BloombergNEF warned in a new report released Wednesday that on-site gas plants proposed for U.S. data centers could add emissions equal to 10% of 2025 U.S. power-sector emissions if all of them were built. Bloomberg Philanthropies commissioned the report.

Under BNEF's assumptions, every on-site gas plant announced for U.S. data centers would get built and run, and together they would release roughly 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent per year. That is 152 million metric tons higher than the level the same amount of data center capacity would produce if it ran on the typical U.S. grid mix.

Developers have put forward plans for 181 gigawatts of gas-fired generation to accompany data centers, BNEF said, with more than 90% of that capacity located in the U.S. The pipeline includes projects at very different stages and on different schedules, and BNEF said it signals how large the buildout could get, not a prediction of the projects that will end up completed.

Many of the projects are meant to supply power while data centers wait for grid connections, BNEF said. After they come online, the economics may favor keeping them running, which creates a longer-term risk of locking in fossil fuels.

"The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand," Mark Daly, head of data centers and emerging tech at BloombergNEF, said in a statement.

BNEF expects data center electricity demand to reach 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, equal to 7% of global electricity consumption. In the U.S. and Europe, grid-connected data centers are the more sustainable option, and faster connections would limit near-term emissions and lock-in risk, BNEF said. In emerging markets where power systems depend heavily on coal, grid-connected data centers can be worse than those powered by on-site gas.

"The grid performs well on reliability and cost and sustainability, but it has a major weakness: It fails on speed, and that's the one thing we care about today," Musfika Mishi, a BloombergNEF associate covering data centers and emerging technologies, said at the BNEF Summit in Houston, according to Bloomberg.

Grid operators are exploring options for shortening interconnection waits, Mishi said, according to Bloomberg, such as handling applications more quickly and making flexible transmission service legal. With flexible arrangements, data centers could move computing workloads to off-peak hours or pull less grid electricity by relying on backup generation. Mishi said that approach results in lower emissions than operating on-site gas all year, even if the backup runs on diesel.

Other companies have moved toward gas for their data centers. SpaceX is proposing a natural gas power station and supercomputing site in Starbase, Texas, with an estimated $24 billion in initial capital investment. The Starbase City Commission will consider a tax abatement agreement for the project on Dec. 9.

Oracle $ORCL has been delivering compressed natural gas by truck to several AI data centers while it waits for pipeline connections.

#5477. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5476. 8 underwater sculpture parks and museums worth the dive

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 8 underwater sculpture parks and museums, from Grenada and Mexico to Italy, Cyprus and Australia, put statues and art on the seafloor for visitors to find

The sculptures in this selection were made to be seen through seawater rather than across a gallery floor. Light, weather and tide change how each piece looks from one day to the next. Some of the works serve as memorials. Others take up themes such as migration and the bond between people and the sea. At least one was installed partly to steer divers away from a natural reef.

That aim belongs to the Museo Subacuático de Arte, or MUSA, off Cancún and Isla Mujeres in Mexico. Its first sculptures went into the water in 2009. One stated goal of the project was to draw divers away from natural reefs and toward the sculptures. The artwork, in other words, doubles as an alternative dive site.

The oldest entry here is far older than MUSA. In 1954, a bronze statue by Guido Galletti known as Christ of the Abyss was lowered into the Bay of San Fruttuoso in Liguria, Italy. A replica followed in 1965 on the Key Largo Dry Rocks reef off Florida. Molinere Underwater Sculpture Park, created in Grenada in 2006, is widely described as the first park of its kind. The newest site in this selection, the Museum of Underwater Sculpture Ayia Napa in Cyprus, opened in 2021.

The sculptor Jason deCaires Taylor created or co-created most of the sites covered here. His work ranges from large groups of life-size human figures to a single sculpture of a girl holding up the surface of the sea. Off Lanzarote in Spain's Canary Islands, one of his pieces refers to migrant sea crossings. In Australia, the Coral Greenhouse sits at John Brewer Reef on the Great Barrier Reef.

The eight entries span the Caribbean, the Bahamas, the Florida Keys, the Canary Islands, the Mediterranean and Australia. They form a selection, not a ranking or a complete list. A common question is whether seeing underwater statues requires scuba diving. The answer depends on depth and local conditions. Shallow pieces can sometimes be seen by snorkelers. Deeper ones generally call for scuba gear and training. Anyone planning a trip around underwater sculpture parks should confirm each site's requirements with local operators first.

Museo Subacuático de Arte, known as MUSA, put its first sculptures into the sea off Cancún and Isla Mujeres in 2009. One stated aim of the project was to draw divers away from the area's natural reefs.

The museum lies in Mexico's Caribbean waters. Its works are split between two areas: the sea off the resort city of Cancún and the sea off Isla Mujeres, a nearby island.

MUSA was not the project of a single person. Jason deCaires Taylor created it with Jaime González Cano and Roberto Díaz Abraham.

One of Taylor's works at the museum is The Silent Evolution. It is a large group of life-size human figures placed together on the seafloor. Seen from above, the figures form a crowd standing beneath the surface.

The sculptures are made from pH-neutral marine cement. That material lets coral grow on the work. As coral settles, the figures become surfaces for reef growth as well as works of art.

That design ties the art to the project's reef-protection aim. The sculptures give divers a separate place to go in the same waters as the natural reefs.

Jason deCaires Taylor created Molinere Underwater Sculpture Park in Molinere Bay, Grenada, in 2006. It is widely described as the first underwater sculpture park.

The Grenada park predates Taylor's project in Mexico. His first sculptures for Museo Subacuático de Arte, off Cancún and Isla Mujeres, went into the sea in 2009. That puts Molinere three years ahead.

The best-known work at Molinere is Vicissitudes. It shows a group of children holding hands in a ring. The figures form one connected circle on the seabed.

The sculptures at Molinere sit in shallow water. That separates the Grenada park from Museo Atlántico in Lanzarote. Taylor's figures there rest at about 14 meters below the surface.

Molinere also differs in form from Christ of the Abyss in Italy. That earlier work is a single bronze memorial by Guido Galletti. Molinere is a park made up of several sculptures.

The Grenada site came first in a run of seafloor projects by the same artist. Taylor made Ocean Atlas off Nassau, Bahamas, in 2014. Museo Atlántico followed in 2016. The Museum of Underwater Sculpture Ayia Napa in Cyprus opened in 2021.

Within this selection, Molinere is the earliest of Taylor's sites.

Museo Atlántico is an underwater museum off Playa Blanca, on the Spanish island of Lanzarote. It opened in 2016, and its sculptures rest on the seabed at a depth of about 14 meters, or roughly 46 feet.

The museum is a project by the sculptor Jason deCaires Taylor. Its works are human figures arranged in groups and placed in open water rather than in a gallery or tank.

Lanzarote belongs to the Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean off the northwest coast of Africa. Playa Blanca is a resort town on the island's southern coast. The museum's name refers to that Atlantic setting.

Rubicon is one of the site's named works. It shows a line of figures walking toward a wall. The title echoes the expression "crossing the Rubicon," which means passing a point of no return. The phrase comes from the river in northern Italy that Julius Caesar crossed with his army in 49 BC. That crossing set off a civil war in the Roman Republic.

The Raft of Lampedusa is a second named work. It depicts a boat carrying a group of figures. The piece refers to migrant sea crossings.

Its title plays on The Raft of the Medusa, a painting by the French artist Théodore Géricault. That work shows survivors of the 1816 wreck of the French navy frigate Méduse off the coast of West Africa. It hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

Lampedusa is a small Italian island in the Mediterranean, lying between Tunisia and Sicily. It has long served as a landing point for boats carrying migrants from North Africa toward Europe.

The Canary Islands are also an arrival point for migrant boats. Those vessels cross the Atlantic from the coast of West Africa, a route separate from the Mediterranean one that leads to Lampedusa.

Both named works take crossings as their subject. Rubicon draws on a crossing that could not be undone, and The Raft of Lampedusa draws on journeys made by sea.

Christ of the Abyss, known in Italian as Cristo degli Abissi, is a bronze statue by the sculptor Guido Galletti. It was lowered into the Bay of San Fruttuoso, on the Ligurian coast of northwest Italy, in 1954. It rests at a depth of about 17 meters.

The statue is a memorial. It honors Dario Gonnella, an Italian diver who died while diving. It was made to remember one person. It was not built to create habitat or to steer visitors away from natural reefs.

San Fruttuoso Bay lies on the Portofino promontory, between the towns of Camogli and Portofino. The cove is also home to the medieval Abbey of San Fruttuoso, which stands near the shoreline.

The statue depicts Christ with his arms raised toward the surface. Galletti cast the work in bronze, a metal long used for public monuments on land. Most of the underwater sculpture parks that followed decades later use cement figures arranged in groups. Christ of the Abyss stands alone, with no surrounding installation on the seabed.

Among the eight sites in this selection, it is the earliest installation. Molinere Underwater Sculpture Park in Grenada, widely described as the first underwater sculpture park, followed in 2006.

A replica of Italy's Christ of the Abyss statue stands in about 25 feet of water off Key Largo, Florida. It was installed in 1965 on the Key Largo Dry Rocks reef, inside John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park.

The Florida figure is a copy of Cristo degli Abissi, a bronze statue by the Italian sculptor Guido Galletti. The original stands in the Bay of San Fruttuoso, on the Ligurian coast of Italy. It memorializes Dario Gonnella, an Italian diver who died while diving.

Egidi Cressi, an Italian diving-equipment maker, donated the Key Largo replica. The gift brought a copy of an Italian underwater memorial to a reef in the Florida Keys.

The two figures share a design but not a setting. The original was lowered into a bay. The replica stands on a coral reef, with Key Largo Dry Rocks as its base.

That reef lies within a state park in Key Largo. John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park takes in the stretch of reef where the replica was installed.

The Museum of Underwater Art's Coral Greenhouse opened in 2020 at John Brewer Reef on the Great Barrier Reef. The museum's work also includes Ocean Siren, which stands above the water on The Strand in Townsville.

The museum takes its name from Townsville, a city on the coast of Queensland. Its pieces are not confined to a single site. Some are placed out on the reef, and at least one stands in the city itself.

The Coral Greenhouse is the museum's submerged work. It sits at John Brewer Reef, which is part of the Great Barrier Reef off the Queensland coast. The installation puts sculpture directly onto a reef system.

Ocean Siren takes a different form. It is not submerged. The figure rises above the waterline on The Strand, the seafront in Townsville.

The sculpture changes color. Those changes follow ocean-temperature data. Its appearance on a given day reflects readings taken from the sea.

That design links the shore piece to the reef. The Coral Greenhouse sits in the water itself. Ocean Siren displays information about that water to people on land.

The arrangement also means part of the museum can be seen without entering the sea. Anyone on The Strand can view Ocean Siren from the shore. Seeing the Coral Greenhouse requires a trip out to John Brewer Reef.

The Museum of Underwater Sculpture Ayia Napa, known as MUSAN, opened in 2021 in the sea off Ayia Napa in Cyprus. It is a project by the sculptor Jason deCaires Taylor.

MUSAN is the most recent opening among the eight underwater sculpture parks and museums in this selection.

The site takes Taylor's work to the eastern Mediterranean. His other installations in this group sit off Grenada, Mexico and the Bahamas. Others are off Lanzarote in Spain's Canary Islands and on the Great Barrier Reef off Townsville, Australia.

Like the Museo Subacuático de Arte off Cancún and Isla Mujeres, the Cyprus site carries the name of a museum. It does not present itself as a single statue or a sculpture garden.

MUSAN is one of two entries in this selection that sit in the Mediterranean. The other is Christ of the Abyss, a bronze statue by Guido Galletti in the Bay of San Fruttuoso off Liguria, Italy.

Ocean Atlas is a single large sculpture off Nassau, Bahamas, made by Jason deCaires Taylor in 2014. It shows a girl holding up the surface of the sea above her.

The figure stands about five meters tall. It weighs about 60 tonnes. That scale is far beyond the size of any real child. The work reads more as a monument than a portrait.

Ocean Atlas is one work, built around one figure in one pose. Many underwater sculpture sites spread a large number of figures across a stretch of seabed. This piece rests on a single image instead. With no crowd around it, the gesture of the one figure carries the whole meaning of the work.

The title comes from Greek mythology. In the myth, Atlas is a Titan who fought on the losing side of the war between the Titans and the Olympian gods. As punishment, Zeus condemns him to hold up the sky. Ancient artists often showed him bent beneath a sphere. One example is the Farnese Atlas, a Roman marble statue now in Naples.

Taylor's version swaps the sky for the ocean. A girl takes the place of the Titan. The surface of the water becomes the weight she carries.

Those substitutions change the story the image tells. In the myth, the burden is a sentence handed down by a god to a defeated warrior. In the sculpture, it falls on a child, and the load is the sea itself. The act of lifting remains, but the bearer and the burden are both new.

#5474. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5473. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5472. Edelbyte reels in $70M for its multipurpose data analytics platform

Edelbyte Ltd., the developer of a data analytics platform optimized for artificial intelligence agents, launched today with $70 million in funding.

The startup raised the capital over two rounds. The investments were led by Sequoia and Quiet Capital with contributions from Greenoaks and Swish Ventures. According to CTech, Edelbyte is valued at $500 million.

Tel Aviv-based Edelbyte was founded last year by former Microsoft Corp. executives Avner Aharoni, Evgeney Ryzhyk, Alexander Sloutsky and Yoni Leibowitz. They helped develop Azure Data Explorer, a tool for analyzing real-time information streams. Customers often refer to it as Kusto in a nod to the eponymous query language it uses to find data patterns.

The company positions its platform as an alternative to Snowflake and Databricks. It’s designed to store up to hundreds of petabytes of data per deployment. It can hold both standard records and vectors, the mathematical structures in which AI agents keep their knowledge. Vectors store not only data snippets such as product listings but also information that makes it easier to find similar items.

The platform supports a wide range of queries. A search engine can use it to find records sought by users, while a business intelligence tool can run analytics calculations. There’s also support for graph processing. That’s an analytics approach used to study data points that relate to one another in some way, for example because they were created in the same system.

Edelbyte claims that its platform can query multipetabyte datasets with under 100 milliseconds of latency. Under the hood, it uses several different optimization methods to achieve that performance .

Analyzing a dataset usually requires companies to move it to a dedicated processing environment. Edelbyte uses a technology called query federation to skip that step. Instead of requiring users to load all their data into its platform, It can run queries in the systems where the data is usually stored. It thereby speeds up processing and reduces the amount of bandwidth that must be spent on moving data between environments.

Edelbyte further optimizes queries by generating indexes. Those are collections of shortcuts that make it easier to find specific items in a large dataset. An index only works if it’s tailored to the data access patterns of the application that uses it. According to Edelbyte, its platform automates some of the manual work involved in the index customization workflow.

“The systems companies rely on to search and analyze their data were built for a world before AI,” said Chief Executive Avner Aharoni (pictured, right). “As it becomes central to how businesses operate, the volume and complexity of data queries will grow far beyond what legacy infrastructure was designed to handle. We believe this creates an opportunity to build a new market leader in search and analytics.”

Edelbyte says several Fortune 500 customers use its platform to power petabyte-scale data environments. The company will use its new funding to grow its installed base and hire more employees.
