#5471. Before the SS United States becomes a reef, 10 lessons from artificial reefs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Do artificial reefs work? Okaloosa County's plan for the SS United States raises the question, and 10 points from oil rigs to tire dumps help answer it

The SS United States won the Blue Riband for the fastest Atlantic crossing on its maiden voyage in 1952. Decades after it carried its last passengers in 1969, the roughly 990-foot liner is slated for a very different job. Under an agreement reached in 2024, Okaloosa County, Florida, is set to acquire the ship and make it an artificial reef off the Emerald Coast, near Destin and Fort Walton Beach.

The plan puts a familiar question back in front of anglers, divers and marine scientists: do artificial reefs work? The answer depends on what "work" is supposed to mean. A sunken ship can give recreational divers a new site to explore. It can give charter boats a known spot to find fish. It can also serve as a way to retire a large steel structure that has no other use. Those are three different goals, and success at one does not guarantee success at another.

The scientific debate centers on a narrower point. Fish gather around sunken structures, from oil platforms in the Gulf of Mexico to concrete modules placed on sandy seafloor. Researchers have argued for decades over whether those structures produce new fish or simply pull existing ones into a smaller area. The difference matters. A reef that concentrates fish without adding to their numbers can make them easier to catch. That result works against the goal of rebuilding fish stocks.

Environmental risk is the other half of the story. Ships can carry fuel, oils and PCBs. U.S. agencies, including the EPA and the Maritime Administration, issued guidance in 2006 on removing those contaminants before a vessel becomes a reef. Not every project has gone to plan. Off Fort Lauderdale, bundled tires dumped at the Osborn Reef starting in 1972 broke loose and scattered. A removal effort followed years later.

The 10 points below look at how artificial reefs change over time, where they can help fish and where they have failed, and how the SS United States fits into that record. They also take up a related question: whether artificial reefs are bad for the environment, and under what conditions.

The central scientific question about artificial reefs is whether they create new fish or simply gather fish that already exist. Fish crowd around sunken structure. That crowding alone does not prove a reef has added anything to the wider population.

Researchers call this the attraction-versus-production debate. Under the attraction view, a reef works like a magnet. It pulls fish in from surrounding waters and nearby natural habitat. The total number of fish in the region stays the same, and only their location changes.

Under the production view, a reef adds habitat that lets more fish survive and grow. The region would then hold more fish than it did before the structure went down. A reef that does this increases the supply of fish rather than reshuffling it.

The two outcomes look identical to a diver or an angler. A wreck crowded with snapper or grouper could reflect new production. It could also reflect fish that moved in from somewhere else. Counting fish on the reef itself cannot separate the two. Answering the question means looking at the population across a whole region, not at a single site.

J.A. Bohnsack set out the problem in a 1989 paper in the Bulletin of Marine Science. Its title asked whether high densities of fishes at artificial reefs result from habitat limitation or behavioral preference. That question set attraction and production side by side as competing explanations. It gave researchers a hypothesis to test rather than an assumption to accept.

Grossman, Jones and Seaman returned to the evidence in a 1997 paper in the journal Fisheries. The title put the debate plainly: "Do artificial reefs increase regional fish production?" The word "regional" points to the scale at which the answer has to be found.

Neither paper settled the question for artificial reefs in general. The answer varies from case to case. It depends on which species is involved, where the reef sits and how heavily the surrounding area is fished.

That conditional answer shapes how reef projects are judged. A structure that adds fish of one species at one site may only concentrate a different species at another.

For anyone asking whether artificial reefs work, attraction versus production is the starting point. A reef can draw crowds of fish without adding a single one to the ocean. Whether it also builds fish populations has to be answered one reef, one species and one region at a time.

Okaloosa County, Florida, agreed in 2024 to acquire the SS United States and turn the retired ocean liner into an artificial reef. The county has announced plans to place the ship in the Gulf of Mexico off the Emerald Coast, near Destin and Fort Walton Beach.

The agreement moves the liner from the SS United States Conservancy, the nonprofit group that had owned it, to a local government. A reef gives the hull a use that does not depend on keeping it afloat and maintained.

The Emerald Coast is the stretch of the Florida Panhandle that faces the Gulf of Mexico. Destin and Fort Walton Beach both sit within Okaloosa County. Charter fishing boats, dive shops and beach tourism are central to the local economy. The county's stated aims for the ship serve two of those groups. It wants a destination for recreational divers and a large structure that draws fish for anglers.

The ship's design shapes what kind of reef it could become. The SS United States is a multi-deck passenger liner. On the seafloor, its hull would hold decks, passageways and interior compartments stacked well above the sand. That vertical relief gives reef fish places to shelter. It also gives divers more to explore than a flat bottom offers. Farther west along the same coast, the USS Oriskany, sunk off Pensacola in 2006, already serves as a dive and fishing site built from a large retired hull.

The plan still has required steps ahead of it. Florida's artificial reef program is coordinated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which works with coastal counties on reef sites. A reef deployment in U.S. waters also needs a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. National policy on artificial reefs traces to the National Fishing Enhancement Act of 1984, which called for a National Artificial Reef Plan. The ship must also be stripped of contaminants before it can be sunk.

Until those steps are done, the SS United States reef remains a plan the county has announced rather than a finished site.

The SS United States is an ocean liner built at Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia, launched in 1951 and placed in service in 1952. It won the Blue Riband on its maiden voyage, carried passengers until 1969 and passed to the SS United States Conservancy in 2011.

The Blue Riband is an unofficial title held by the passenger liner with the fastest recorded crossing of the Atlantic. Shipping lines on both sides of the ocean competed for it. Taking it on a maiden voyage meant the SS United States set the record the first time it sailed with paying passengers.

The result carried weight for an American ship. British, German, French and Italian liners had traded the record for decades before 1952. The ship that held it immediately before the SS United States was the Queen Mary, a British liner operated by Cunard.

Naval architect William Francis Gibbs designed the liner. He gave it an aluminum superstructure to cut weight. He also used fire-resistant materials in place of wood across most of its interiors. The U.S. government helped pay for construction. In return, the ship was designed so it could be converted into a troopship in wartime.

That link to defense planning suited the builder. Newport News Shipbuilding, in Virginia's Hampton Roads region, is better known for building warships and aircraft carriers for the U.S. Navy. The finished liner is about 990 feet long. United States Lines operated it on the transatlantic route between New York and European ports.

Its passenger career ran from 1952 to 1969. By the late 1960s, jet airliners carried most travelers across the Atlantic, and ocean liners had lost much of their business. The SS United States was withdrawn from service in 1969 and never carried passengers again. Over the following decades it passed through a series of owners. Several plans to return it to service or redevelop it did not go forward.

In 2011, the SS United States Conservancy, a nonprofit formed to preserve the ship, took ownership of the liner. Okaloosa County's announced reef plan would give the vessel a different purpose. Its long steel hull, stacked decks and enclosed interior spaces are the features that plan would put to new use on the seafloor.

A ship must be stripped of fuel, oils, PCBs and other contaminants before it can be sunk as a reef in U.S. waters. The main reference for that work is a 2006 best-practice guidance document from the Environmental Protection Agency and the Maritime Administration.

The document is titled "National Guidance: Best Management Practices for Preparing Vessels Intended to Create Artificial Reefs." Congress directed the two agencies to write it. It gives agencies and reef sponsors a shared standard for getting a vessel ready to go to the bottom.

Fuel and oil come first. Tanks, bilges, engines and piping can hold residues long after a ship stops sailing. Oil left aboard can leak as the hull settles and corrodes. That would turn a habitat project into a pollution source.

PCBs are a harder problem. Polychlorinated biphenyls are industrial chemicals once used widely in electrical equipment, cable insulation, gaskets and paint. They persist in the environment and build up in the fatty tissue of fish and the animals that eat them. U.S. manufacture of PCBs ended under the Toxic Substances Control Act. Older vessels are therefore the ones most likely to carry them.

The guidance also covers asbestos, paint that can flake or leach, and loose debris. Floatable materials such as foam, plastics and wood are taken off the ship. Left aboard, they could break free and drift away after the sinking.

The USS Oriskany shows why these details matter. The retired aircraft carrier was sunk off Pensacola in 2006. Its preparation drew scrutiny because some PCB-containing materials stayed aboard under an EPA risk-based approval rather than being removed entirely. The carrier became a reference point in arguments over how clean a reef vessel needs to be.

The cleaning stage ties directly to a common question: are artificial reefs bad for the environment? A well-prepared hull offers hard structure for marine life without a chemical legacy. A poorly prepared one can release contaminants into the same food web it was meant to support.

Preparation also shapes the schedule of any ship reef project. Every cable run, fuel tank and painted surface that needs attention adds work before a vessel can be towed out and sunk.

Rigs-to-Reefs programs turn retired oil and gas platforms in the Gulf of Mexico into permanent fish habitat instead of hauling them to shore for scrap. The practice dates to the 1980s. Louisiana launched its formal program in 1986.

The idea starts with what a platform already is. A steel jacket rises from the seafloor to the surface, crossed by legs and braces. That frame offers hard structure through the entire water column.

Much of the northern Gulf seafloor is mud and sand, with little natural hard bottom. A platform adds vertical relief in a place that otherwise has almost none. Platform structures host dense fish communities. Recreational anglers and divers have sought them out for decades.

Federal rules normally require an operator to remove a platform once its lease ends and production stops. Full removal means cutting the structure free and bringing it ashore. Rigs-to-Reefs offers another path. A state agrees to take responsibility for the structure, and it becomes part of a permitted reef site.

Conversions generally follow one of three methods. In a tow-and-place conversion, the jacket is cut loose and towed to a designated reef area. In a topple-in-place conversion, it is laid on its side at the original location. In a partial removal, the upper section is cut away. That leaves enough clearance above the remaining structure for ships to pass safely.

Money shapes the arrangement. Leaving a jacket on the seafloor generally costs an operator less than full removal. In Louisiana, operators share part of those savings with the state. The state uses the funds to run its artificial reef program. Texas operates a similar Rigs-to-Reefs program off its own coast.

The approach has limits. Platform reefs can only go where platforms already stand or where they can be towed. That means site selection follows oil and gas geology more than fish biology.

Removal work also carries a cost to marine life. Some operators use explosives to sever platform legs, and those blasts can kill fish living on the structure. Tow-and-place and topple-in-place conversions still require cutting the structure loose, which can involve the same severing methods.

Reef Balls and similar purpose-built modules are concrete structures designed from the start to serve as reef habitat. Unlike sunken ships, they are shaped to stay put on the seafloor and to give marine life surfaces and openings to use.

A Reef Ball is a hollow, dome-shaped concrete unit with holes cut through its walls. The holes let water move through the structure. They also create sheltered spaces where small fish and invertebrates can hide. The rough concrete surface gives algae, sponges and other encrusting organisms a place to attach.

The design addresses a basic engineering problem. An artificial reef has to stay where it is placed through storms and strong currents. A heavy, wide-based concrete module sits low on the bottom and resists being moved. A builder can engineer that stability into a purpose-built unit from the start. It is much harder to guarantee with a structure that was designed for another use.

Material is the other difference. Concrete made for reef use contains no fuel tanks, wiring, paint or insulation. That means there is no hazardous material to strip out before deployment. Modules can also be made in different sizes and set out in planned arrangements. That lets reef managers decide how much structure goes where.

The trade-off is height and scale. A field of concrete modules generally offers low relief compared with a ship or an oil platform. Those larger structures can rise far up the water column. A low concrete reef serves different purposes than a tall wreck sunk partly to attract divers.

Purpose-built modules contrast with an older approach that relied on materials of opportunity. Texas, for example, sank decommissioned Liberty ships — the mass-produced cargo vessels of World War II — as reefs. Ships of opportunity deliver a large volume of structure in a single deployment. Designed modules give up some of that bulk in exchange for predictability.

For a reef planner, the choice between a module field and a sunken ship comes down to what the reef is for. The options are fish habitat at a chosen spot, a dive attraction or a mix of both.

Florida has turned three retired military ships into artificial reefs. The USS Spiegel Grove went down off Key Largo in 2002, the USS Oriskany off Pensacola in 2006 and the USS Vandenberg off Key West in 2009.

Each ship had a different military career. The Spiegel Grove was a Navy dock landing ship. The Oriskany was an 888-foot aircraft carrier that served during the Korean and Vietnam wars. It carries the nickname the Mighty O. The Vandenberg began as a World War II transport and later tracked missile launches for the Air Force.

The Oriskany lies off Pensacola, at the western end of the Florida Panhandle. That places it on the same stretch of Gulf coast as Destin and Fort Walton Beach. The other two ships sit at the opposite end of the state. Key Largo lies in the upper Florida Keys, and Key West sits near the end of the island chain.

The Spiegel Grove's sinking did not go as planned. The ship went down early and came to rest on its side rather than upright. Hurricane Dennis shifted the hull upright in 2005. The episode showed that a large hull does not always settle where its planners intend.

The three wrecks show what large ship reefs are meant to do. A hull this size gives divers decks, passageways and a shape they can recognize on the seafloor. It gives fishing boats a fixed, mapped target in open water. Neither use requires the ship to produce new fish. Both rely on the ship drawing people.

Backers of ship sinkings have offered a further reason. They argue that a large wreck can draw divers away from natural coral reefs already under stress. That is a stated aim, not a measured result. A ship on the bottom does not by itself show how many divers changed their plans or whether pressure on natural reefs eased.

For Okaloosa County, the Oriskany is the nearest point of comparison. The county's announced plan for the SS United States would put another large former ship off the Panhandle coast, aimed at the same divers and anglers.

The Osborn Reef off Fort Lauderdale, Florida, is a case where an artificial reef did not work. Tires bundled together and dumped on the seafloor starting in 1972 broke loose when their bindings failed, and the scattered tires became debris rather than habitat.

The project rested on a disposal rationale. Old car tires were a waste problem on land. Bundled together and placed offshore, they were expected to give fish and marine life hard structure to use. The same plan would keep those tires out of landfills.

The plan depended on the bindings. Each bundle had to stay intact for the tires to function as a fixed reef. Once those bindings gave way, the individual tires were free to move. The site no longer held together as a single structure.

Loose tires on the seafloor do not behave like a reef. A stable reef stays where it is placed. It gives organisms a fixed surface to settle on and gives fish shelter they can return to. Scattered tires offer neither of those things in a dependable way.

The failure turned a disposal project into a cleanup project. Years after the dumping began, a removal effort followed to take tires back out of the water. That work reversed the original logic of the site. Material sent to sea to avoid disposal on land had to be brought back to land.

Osborn illustrates a point that runs through artificial reef science. Whether a reef works depends partly on what it is made of and whether it stays in place. A structure that breaks apart cannot provide the stable shelter and settling surface that reef fish need.

The case also bears on a common search question: are artificial reefs bad for the environment? At Osborn, the answer was yes. The structure was not secured well enough to stay in place. The problem lay in how the reef was built and held together, which is a separate issue from whether added structure can serve as habitat.

Artificial reefs are most likely to increase fish populations where a shortage of hard habitat holds those populations down. Where heavy fishing is the main limit, added structure tends to gather existing fish in one place and make them easier to catch.

The distinction starts with how reef fish live. Many species spend their early days as larvae drifting in open water. To survive past that stage, they need to settle onto hard bottom, where crevices and ledges offer shelter from predators. Older fish also rely on structure for cover and, for some species, for feeding.

On a flat sand or mud seafloor, that kind of shelter can be scarce. If larvae arrive in good numbers but find few places to settle, the habitat itself becomes the bottleneck. Adding rock, concrete or steel in that setting can give more young fish a place to survive. That is the scenario in which a reef can add fish rather than simply move them.

The picture changes when the bottleneck is fishing. If a population is held down by how many adults are removed each year, new structure does little to raise its numbers. It can instead draw fish into tight groups at known spots. Many state reef programs publish site coordinates for anglers. That makes those groups easy to find.

Tropical tuna fisheries offer a parallel. Fishing fleets use fish aggregating devices, floating objects that tuna gather beneath, to concentrate schools and improve catches. Seafloor reefs can work the same way for bottom-dwelling species.

Red snapper in the Gulf of Mexico sit near the center of this argument. The species is commonly caught around artificial structures. How much those structures add to the stock, and how much they simply concentrate it, has been a long-running point of dispute among fishery scientists and managers.

For reef managers, structure and harvest rules interact. A reef placed in a habitat-poor area with limits on catch has a stronger chance of adding fish. A reef dropped into a heavily fished zone with no controls has a weaker one.

An artificial reef is not finished on the day it reaches the seafloor. Corals, sponges and other encrusting organisms settle on the structure over years. The reef slowly turns from bare steel or concrete into living habitat. Even so, it remains distinct from a natural reef.

The first layer is microscopic. Soon after a structure is submerged, bacteria and microscopic algae coat its exposed surfaces in a thin biofilm. That film changes the texture and chemistry of the surface. It also gives the drifting larvae of larger organisms a cue to settle.

Fast-growing filter feeders tend to arrive next. Barnacles, hydroids, bryozoans, tube worms and tunicates claim open space early. They feed on plankton carried past the structure by currents. Their shells and tubes add small-scale texture to surfaces that started out flat and smooth.

Sponges, soft corals and hard corals take longer. Reef-building stony corals grow slowly. Their colonies spread across a wreck or module over many years rather than a single season.

Which organisms take hold depends on depth, water temperature, light, current and the larvae that drift past. Reef-building corals host symbiotic algae that need sunlight to supply them with energy. On deeper or murkier sites, sponges, hydroids and other animals that do not rely on light often cover more of the surface.

The material underneath shapes the community too. Steel hulls corrode over time. Thin plating eventually weakens and collapses. That collapse changes the shape of the habitat and the shelter it offers. Concrete is more chemically stable in seawater and tends to keep its form.

A heavily colonized artificial reef still differs from a natural one. Natural coral reefs form over thousands of years. Generations of corals lay down calcium carbonate skeletons that pile into a complex framework full of crevices and caves. An artificial reef offers a ready-made shape but lacks that age and that layered structure.

The species mix differs as well. A sunken ship or platform often rises steeply from flat sand or mud, in a spot that had no hard bottom before. That tall profile and isolation can attract a different set of fish and invertebrates than a low, sprawling natural reef.

Artificial structures can also give non-native species a foothold. Tubastraea coccinea, an orange cup coral native to the Indo-Pacific, has spread across oil and gas platforms in the Gulf of Mexico.

For anyone weighing an artificial reef against a natural reef, the comparison shifts with time. A newly placed structure is mostly bare surface and visiting fish. Years later it can carry dense growth, but it remains a distinct habitat shaped by its material, depth and location.

#5469. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5468. Burial at sea as a reef: how memorial reefs work, what the law says and what they do

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A memorial reef sets cremated remains inside a concrete reef module on the seafloor, and this guide covers how it is made, U.S. burial at sea rules and ecological limits

Scattering ashes at sea ends in dispersal. The remains drift or sink with the current and leave no fixed point a family can return to. A memorial reef works the other way. It sets a person's cremated remains inside a concrete structure on the seafloor. That structure stays in one place and can become a surface for marine life to settle on.

The difference turns a farewell into a physical object with a location. Over time, algae, sponges, barnacles and corals can colonize the structure, and fish can shelter in and around it. That habitat comes from the concrete. Cremated remains are mostly bone mineral, and they do not drive the process.

Reef memorials sit within a wider set of choices for people who want a connection to the ocean after death. Ordinary burial at sea covers both scattering cremated remains and placing a body in deep water. In the U.S., it falls under a general permit from the Environmental Protection Agency. A reef memorial follows a different path. The structure counts as an artificial reef. It can be placed only at permitted artificial reef sites, under permitting that differs from the rules for a simple scattering.

The idea has taken more than one physical form. The best-known version is the Reef Ball, a hollow concrete dome with holes through its sides. That design came out of the Reef Ball Foundation, founded in 1993. Off Key Biscayne, Florida, Neptune Memorial Reef takes a different approach. It is laid out as an underwater cemetery, with gates, columns and statuary built from concrete.

This guide covers five parts of the subject. It explains what an artificial reef memorial is and where its most common design came from. It then sets out how cremated remains are cast into a concrete reef module. It describes Neptune Memorial Reef as an example of a planned underwater site rather than a set of individual modules. It lays out the U.S. legal framework for burial at sea and for reef placement. It closes with what these structures can and cannot do for marine ecosystems. That includes the scientific debate over whether artificial reefs add productivity or mainly draw fish from elsewhere.

A memorial reef is an artificial reef that contains a person's cremated remains. The Reef Ball is its best-known form, a hollow, dome-shaped concrete module with holes through its sides.

An artificial reef is a human-made structure placed on the seafloor to give marine organisms a hard surface to settle on. Such reefs are often built for fishing, diving or habitat projects. A memorial reef serves a second purpose as well. It marks the life of one specific person who has died.

That pairing makes the structure part monument and part marine habitat. On land, a headstone stands beside a grave. In a memorial reef, the marker and the remains are the same object, because the remains are built into the concrete.

The Reef Ball design came out of the Reef Ball Foundation. The name describes the shape. Each module is a dome rather than a solid block, and its interior is open. The holes through its walls let water move through the structure instead of only around it.

The design is not limited to memorials. Reef Ball modules are also used in artificial reef projects that have no connection to a burial. A memorial reef takes that existing form and attaches it to one person's remains.

Eternal Reefs, a company based in Florida, offers memorials built on the Reef Ball format. In its version, the cremated remains are part of the module, not stored in a separate container inside the dome. Nothing sits loose within the structure.

A memorial reef also asks more of the people arranging it than a scattering does. Scattering needs no manufactured object. A reef memorial needs a module to be produced and a permitted artificial reef site to receive it.

The Reef Ball is not the only shape memorial reefs take. Some sites arrange larger concrete forms into a planned underwater layout. That approach works more like a cemetery than a single monument.

Cremated remains become part of a memorial reef when they are mixed into concrete as the reef module is cast. Once the concrete sets, the remains are part of the structure itself rather than loose material in the water.

Eternal Reefs, a company based in Florida, uses this method. It adds the cremated remains to the concrete at the casting stage, when the module is formed. The concrete it uses is pH-neutral.

The remains are bound into the concrete, so they stay with the module through transport and placement. They are not released into the water at any point. What goes down to the seafloor is a single solid object that holds them. There is no separate urn or container. The reef module itself serves that role.

After casting, the finished module is taken out to sea and set on the seafloor. It goes only to an artificial reef site that has been permitted for that use. A memorial module is not lowered at an arbitrary point chosen on the day.

Relatives often join this final step. Placement is commonly paired with a boat trip that brings family members out to the site. They can be present when the module goes into the water.

Arrangements beyond the casting itself vary from provider to provider. Each program sets what a family can add to a module or arrange around its placement. No single package of options applies across every memorial reef service.

Neptune Memorial Reef is an underwater cemetery off Key Biscayne, Florida. It is built from concrete and arranged as a single designed site, with gates, columns and statuary on the seafloor.

Key Biscayne is a barrier island in Miami-Dade County. The Rickenbacker Causeway links it to the mainland at Miami. The cemetery occupies one site in the waters off that island rather than a scattered set of locations.

The layout borrows the forms of a cemetery on land. Gates, columns and statuary are familiar parts of above-ground memorial architecture. At Neptune Memorial Reef, those forms are made of concrete and set underwater as parts of one plan.

That approach separates it from a memorial reef built from individual modules. The Reef Ball, the best-known module design, is a single concrete unit placed on the seafloor as its own structure. Each module stands apart from the others, even when several share a reef site.

Neptune Memorial Reef works as an architectural whole. Its pieces follow a common design. They are not stand-alone units added one at a time and arranged after the fact.

Both forms rely on concrete. The difference lies in scale and design intent. A single module marks one memorial at one spot. A designed underwater cemetery sets each memorial inside a larger shared space. A cemetery on land does the same thing when it gathers many graves within one plan.

For a family weighing a burial at sea reef, the choice comes down to those two kinds of place. One is a standalone marker on the seafloor. The other is a place within a planned site shared with other memorials.

A memorial reef is legal in the U.S. when it goes through the proper approvals, but it follows a different path from ordinary burial at sea. Scattering ashes or burying a body falls under a general permit from the Environmental Protection Agency. Placing a reef module requires artificial reef permitting instead.

The ordinary route rests on the Marine Protection, Research, and Sanctuaries Act. Under that law, the EPA issues a general permit for burial at sea. A general permit covers everyone who meets its conditions. A family does not apply for individual approval before a scattering or a burial.

Cremated remains carry the lightest requirements. They must be released at least three nautical miles from land. The EPA must then be notified within 30 days. The notice comes after the scattering, not before it.

Non-cremated remains face stricter conditions. The burial must take place at least three nautical miles out. The water at that spot must also be at least 600 feet deep.

A memorial reef sits outside that framework. The remains are not scattered or released into the water. They are fixed inside a concrete structure that is set on the seafloor and meant to stay there. The placement becomes a matter of putting a lasting object into the ocean. Objects of that kind fall under the rules for artificial reefs.

Artificial reef permitting involves both state and federal approval. The requirements differ from one site to the next. Memorial reef modules go to sites that already hold artificial reef permits. A family does not pick an unpermitted spot on its own.

The two routes also differ in who handles the process. A scattering under the general permit ends with a single notice to the EPA. A reef placement depends on a provider working within an approved reef site and that site's conditions.

Rules outside the U.S. differ. The U.S. framework described here does not carry over to other countries.

The concrete structure in a memorial reef, not the cremated remains inside it, is what gives marine life a place to settle. An artificial reef can host organisms and shelter fish, but it does not replace a natural reef.

A concrete module on the seafloor offers a hard, fixed surface. Over time, algae, sponges, corals and barnacles can colonize that surface. Fish can use the structure, and the openings through it, as shelter.

The remains themselves play little part in that process. Cremated remains are mostly bone mineral, a form of calcium phosphate. Once mixed into concrete, they become one more ingredient in the cast. The habitat comes from the module's shape, surface and placement, not from the remains sealed inside it.

Scientists still debate whether artificial reefs add to marine life. One position holds that a new structure adds productivity. It gives organisms more surface to settle on and more places to feed and hide. The opposing position holds that artificial reefs mainly draw fish away from other areas. Under that view, a reef concentrates existing fish rather than producing new ones.

That debate applies to memorial reefs as much as to any other artificial reef. A module that holds cremated remains is built from the same material as one that does not. It serves the same physical function on the seafloor. The memorial purpose does not change how fish or invertebrates respond to the structure.

A concrete reef is also not a substitute for a natural one. Natural coral reefs are built by living corals that lay down calcium carbonate skeletons. A memorial reef does not restore a damaged natural reef, and placing a module nearby does not repair harm already done.

Two practical concerns remain open. The first is site selection. Where a module goes determines what kind of seafloor it covers and what already lives around it. The second is long-term maintenance. A concrete structure placed on the seafloor is meant to stay there long after the memorial service ends.

Families considering a cremation reef are choosing a permanent structure that marine organisms can use. They are not choosing a way to create or rebuild a reef ecosystem.

#5467. Aura Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results, Highlights Sustained Business Momentum and Transformative Platform Innovation

BOSTON, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Aura Consolidated Group, Inc. ARBN 695 488 843 (ASX: AXQ) ("Aura" or "the Company"), a global leader in online safety and wellbeing, today announced its financial results for the third quarter of 2026, the first quarter since completing the acquisition of Qoria on July 17, 2026 ("Transaction Close").

On a pro forma basis, Aura exited the quarter with $355.0 million in annual recurring revenue ("ARR"), up 24% year over year, and generated positive Adjusted FCF of $12.4 million, a $15.5 million improvement year over year. The Company reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance of 20%+ ARR growth and positive Adjusted Free Cash Flow from Transaction Close to year-end.

Reflecting on the achievements in Q3'26, Aura's Founder and CEO, Hari Ravichandran, said:

"This quarter, we laid the foundation for our expanded long-term vision for Aura while delivering sustained revenue growth and positive free cash flow. At the same time, we are accelerating our pace of innovation, and earlier this week introduced Solstice, our in-house AI engine, along with an updated Aura experience, the first product built on that foundation.

"For decades, consumer security has pushed the hard work back onto the user. We're reimagining protection from the ground up with Solstice and will unlock what no consumer security product has had: a deep understanding of the family, and the ability to help take action when the family asks."

Aura's Chief Financial Officer, Brian DeCenzo, added, "As generative AI fuels more frequent and sophisticated scams and new risks to children online, more families, schools, and employers are turning to Aura as their trusted source of protection. We are translating broad-based customer growth and strong product uptake into robust, sustainable revenue growth. That momentum, paired with our ongoing focus on operational efficiency, leaves us well positioned to deliver on both our 20%+ ARR growth and positive free cash flow targets this year, while building toward our medium-term financial objectives."

Aura is executing ahead of plan on the $55 million cost-out program outlined in February 2026, with year-to-date and planned Q4 actions representing approximately $66 million in total savings. This includes $42 million in annualized direct and operating cost savings, driven by organizational realignment that significantly reduced the Company's fixed cost base. Direct-to-Consumer ("D2C") marketing spend is expected to decline $24 million in 2026 compared with 2025, while continuing to support investment in efficient growth.

Aura's acquisition of Qoria became effective on July 17, 2026. As such, Q3'26 unaudited statutory financials reflect Aura's full-quarter results, together with Qoria's post-close results from July 17, 2026 through September 30, 2026. To provide a more representative view of the combined group's performance and facilitate period-over-period comparability, this release and the related materials focus on unaudited pro forma results, combining Aura and Qoria for the full duration of each period presented. All dollar amounts are reported in U.S. currency unless otherwise noted.

Aura continuously evaluates strategic opportunities to optimize its business. As part of that ongoing assessment, management is evaluating a potential dual listing on a U.S. stock exchange alongside its ASX listing. While the Company remains secure in its capital position, management believes a dual listing could support its objective of maximizing long-term shareholder value through an expanded investor base and improved trading liquidity. Any potential dual listing remains subject to approval by Aura's Board of Directors and the completion of required regulatory and other processes.

This conference call and related materials will be publicly available and can be accessed at investors.aura.com. A replay will also be made available after the call.

The release of this announcement was authorized by the Aura Board of Directors.

#5466. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5465. SS United States set to become a reef: 12 ways artificial and natural reefs compare

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Artificial reefs vs. natural reefs, explained through the SS United States, the ocean liner set to be sunk off the Florida Panhandle as a dive site

The SS United States is scheduled to be sunk in the Gulf of Mexico off the Florida Panhandle. The ocean liner is 990 feet long, 108 feet longer than the Titanic. Once it settles on the seafloor, it is set to become the world's largest artificial reef. The project cost $13.5 million. Its organizers want the wreck to draw more divers and fishing enthusiasts and to give tuna, marlin and swordfish a new home.

The ship's first life played out above the waterline. More than 3,000 workers built it in Virginia in 1950 and 1951. It sailed on its maiden voyage in 1952 and went on to cross the Atlantic more than 800 times. Its passengers included Grace Kelly, Elizabeth Taylor, John F. Kennedy and Britain's former King Edward VIII. A young Bill Clinton sailed on it in 1968. The liner was decommissioned in 1969. Later plans by a hotel magnate and by Norwegian Cruise Line $NCLH to reuse it went nowhere. From 1996 until recently, it sat at a dock in Philadelphia.

Its next role will be underwater. The wreck is planned to rest about 25 miles southwest of Destin, in roughly 180 feet of water. Its top deck is set to sit about 60 feet below the surface, shallow enough for inexperienced divers. It will not be alone. About 500 artificial reefs already lie in nearby waters, according to Okaloosa County spokesperson Nick Tomecek. Tomecek said the previous largest was the USS Oriskany, an aircraft carrier scuttled off Pensacola in 2006.

The sinking puts a practical question in front of divers, anglers and coastal communities. How does a steel hull placed by people compare with a reef that grows on its own? Comparing artificial reefs vs. natural reefs means looking at ecology, marine life, cost, tourism and risk.

The 12 slides that follow start with the SS United States itself: its history, how it was prepared for sinking and where it will rest. Later slides look at what artificial reefs are, how natural coral reefs form, what lives on each, what they cost and what can go wrong.

The SS United States, a 990-foot ocean liner, is scheduled to be sunk on a Wednesday in the Gulf of Mexico off the Florida Panhandle. The sinking is meant to turn it into the world's largest artificial reef. The ship is 108 feet longer than the Titanic, according to the Associated Press.

The record the liner is set to take is held by the USS Oriskany. That 911-foot aircraft carrier was scuttled in the Gulf off Pensacola in 2006.

Organizers want the wreck to attract more divers and anglers. They also aim to create habitat for tuna, marlin and swordfish.

The liner's life above water began in Virginia. More than 3,000 workers built it there in 1950 and 1951. Its maiden voyage followed in 1952.

That first crossing carried 1,700 passengers. Margaret Truman, the president's daughter, was on board. So was an AP reporter, who filed a dispatch from the trip.

The ship averaged almost 41 miles per hour on the voyage. The AP's dispatch put that pace 4.5 miles per hour ahead of the record the RMS Queen Mary set in 1938.

The crossing ended in rough conditions. The liner ran into a full gale, with winds of 69 miles per hour. AP reported the wind was strong enough to blow a ping pong table off the deck.

Over its service years, the SS United States crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times. Its passengers included Grace Kelly, Elizabeth Taylor, John F. Kennedy and Britain's former King Edward VIII. A young Bill Clinton sailed aboard in 1968.

David Lawrence, a board member of the SS United States Conservancy, said the goal was to make sure the ship "wasn't lost forever."

Susan Gibbs is the granddaughter of the ship's designer. She said the liner "represents pride and resilience and strength and beauty." Gibbs also said she was glad parts of the ship were saved.

Turning the SS United States into a reef meant taking parts of it away and cutting into its structure before it goes under. The final step is set to be flooding the hull so the ship sinks.

Organizers removed the liner's 65-foot smokestacks. The stacks will not go down with the ship. Instead, they are planned to anchor a new museum about the SS United States.

Equipment inside the hull came out as well. Organizers removed tanks tied to the seawater cooling system for the boilers.

Workers cut holes through the decks, each measuring 10 feet by 10 feet. More than 400 portholes were also removed from the ship.

The last stage is set to happen at the sinking site in the Gulf of Mexico, off the Florida Panhandle. Valves are to be opened so seawater floods the hull. The water is meant to carry the liner to the seafloor.

The SS United States is set to go to the bottom without explosives because federal rules bar them for this job, according to Okaloosa County spokesperson Nick Tomecek. He said federal environmental and explosives regulations prevent the county and its contractor from using them.

Seawater is meant to take their place. Crews plan to open valves aboard the liner so the Gulf of Mexico floods the hull and carries it to the seafloor.

The schedule has already shifted once. Tomecek said concerns about the weather moved the sinking up by a day.

The SS United States is scheduled to settle about 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida, in roughly 180 feet of water. Its top deck is set to sit about 60 feet below the surface, shallow enough for inexperienced divers.

The site lies in the Gulf of Mexico off the Florida Panhandle. It is on the stretch of coast between Panama City and Pensacola.

Okaloosa County and its contractor are handling the sinking.

The two depth figures describe a tall wreck. The seafloor sits at about 180 feet and the top deck at about 60 feet. That would put the deck roughly 120 feet above the bottom.

That vertical spread shapes which parts of the ship different divers can reach. The top deck is within range of newer divers. The lower hull extends down toward the seafloor, well below the deck.

The USS Oriskany is a 911-foot aircraft carrier that was scuttled in the Gulf of Mexico off Pensacola, Florida, in 2006. Okaloosa County spokesperson Nick Tomecek identified it as the largest artificial reef before the SS United States, which is set to take that title.

The carrier was launched in 1950. That puts it in the same era as the SS United States. One ship was built for the Navy as a warship. The other was built to carry passengers across the Atlantic.

The two hulls are close in size. The ocean liner is 79 feet longer than the carrier.

The two wrecks will also share a stretch of the Gulf. The Oriskany lies off Pensacola. The SS United States is scheduled to go down off Destin, on the coast between Pensacola and Panama City. Tomecek said an experienced diver could visit both wrecks in one day.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission manages the Oriskany reef site. The site carries no surface marker. Its GPS coordinates are public, so divers and boat operators can find it without a buoy.

An artificial reef is a human-made structure placed on the seafloor to give marine life a place to live. A ship reef starts as a retired vessel that is stripped, opened up and flooded until it settles on the bottom.

The SS United States is set to become a ship reef this way off the Florida Panhandle. Crews took parts out of the liner and cut openings in its decks.

The last step is planned to be simple. Valves are to be opened, and seawater is meant to fill the hull until the ship goes down.

A natural coral reef has no launch date, no contractor and no price tag. The SS United States is set to become a reef on a scheduled day, in a project run by Okaloosa County and its contractor off the Florida Panhandle.

The liner's start as habitat is a single, planned event. A living reef has no comparable moment that can be marked on a calendar.

The SS United States reef is being planned with tuna, marlin and swordfish in mind. A home for those three species is one of the stated aims of sinking the ocean liner off the Florida Panhandle.

That habitat goal sits beside a human one. Organizers also want the wreck to bring more divers and fishing enthusiasts to the area.

The project's stated goals name no other species. Once the liner floods and settles on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico, its hull is meant to become the structure those fish find.

The waters near Destin, Florida, already hold about 500 artificial reefs, according to Okaloosa County spokesperson Nick Tomecek. The SS United States is set to join them, in a project meant to bring more divers and anglers to the Florida Panhandle.

The liner is scheduled to settle in the Gulf of Mexico between Panama City and Pensacola. Tomecek described the existing reefs as lying in the waters near that site.

The project is aimed at two audiences. Scuba divers are one. People who fish are the other. Organizers also want the sunken hull to become habitat for tuna, marlin and swordfish.

The liner's top deck is planned to sit shallow enough for inexperienced divers.

The new reef will also sit within reach of an older one. The aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, scuttled in the Gulf off Pensacola, had been the largest artificial reef. The SS United States is set to take that title once it is sunk. Tomecek said an experienced diver could visit both wrecks in one day.

That pairing points to two levels of access. The liner's top deck is meant to be within reach of newer divers. The two-wreck day, as Tomecek described it, is for experienced ones.

Tomecek stated the county's goal plainly: "We're trying to be the best diving destination in the world."

Sinking the SS United States to create an artificial reef is a $13.5 million project. The spending is meant to bring more divers and anglers to the Florida Panhandle and to give tuna, marlin and swordfish a place to live.

Those two aims define what the money is meant to buy. The ship is not going down simply to dispose of it. Organizers want a seafloor structure that draws recreational visitors and holds large open-water fish.

Okaloosa County is carrying out the sinking with a contractor. The vessel is scheduled to go down in the Gulf of Mexico off the Florida Panhandle.

If the sinking goes ahead as planned, the $13.5 million will pay for what is set to become the world's largest artificial reef.

Federal rules govern how a ship can be sunk as an artificial reef, and they restrict the methods available. In the case of the SS United States, Okaloosa County spokesperson Nick Tomecek said federal environmental and explosives rules prevent the county and its contractor from using explosives.

Without a blast, the job falls to seawater. Valves are to be opened so the ocean floods the liner's hull and carries it to the bottom.

Almost all coral reef ecosystems face a risk of collapse, according to a study that the Associated Press linked alongside its report on the SS United States. The AP report itself does not lay out what that study found.

Restoring coral is not among the goals set for the liner. The project's stated aims center on visitors and open-water fish, not on rebuilding or replacing living reefs.

#5463. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
