#5462. 3D-printed reefs and 6 other technologies trying to save the ocean

Free daily briefing on global business news.

3D-printed reefs open a selection of seven technologies, from farm-grown coral to satellite fishing maps, that scientists and nonprofits use to restore, clean and monitor the ocean

The ocean's problems are physical, and many of them can be measured. Reefs lose the hard structure that young coral needs to take hold. Plastic drifts into open water and collects in remote gyres. Fishing fleets work far from shore, often beyond easy view of regulators. Water temperature and chemistry shift in ways that scientists track with instruments spread across entire ocean basins.

Engineers, marine biologists and nonprofits have built tools aimed at each of those problems. Some work at the scale of a single reef patch. Others operate across the whole planet. 3D-printed reefs are one example at the small end. They are structures printed from clay or similar materials and shaped to give coral larvae a surface to settle on. They belong to a broader field of coral reef restoration technology that also draws on laboratory and farming methods.

This piece covers seven of those tools. It is a selection, not a ranking, and it does not attempt to list every technology working in the ocean. The seven fall into three broad groups.

The first group restores reefs directly. It includes printed terracotta tiles and a coral-cutting technique called microfragmentation, which is paired with land-based coral farms. It also covers coral IVF, which raises larvae from spawn, and underwater speakers that play the sound of a healthy reef. Each method targets a different stage of reef recovery, from giving coral a place to grow to drawing fish back to a damaged site.

The second group deals with pollution. The Ocean Cleanup, a nonprofit based in the Netherlands, builds floating systems that gather plastic at sea. It also builds river devices that catch plastic before it reaches open water.

The third group watches the ocean rather than repairing it. This branch of ocean conservation tech relies on data. Global Fishing Watch turns ship-tracking signals into maps of fishing activity. The Argo program uses robotic floats to record temperature and salinity below the surface.

None of these tools solves an ocean problem on its own. Each addresses one piece of a larger issue, and several have clear limits. A reef sound study measured fish, not coral. A tracking system cannot see a vessel that turns its transmitter off. The slides that follow describe those limits alongside the methods themselves.

3D-printed reef tiles made of terracotta give young corals a hard, textured surface to attach to on reefs that have lost their natural structure. The aim is to rebuild the physical base a reef needs before new coral can grow on it.

Corals begin life as tiny free-swimming larvae. To survive, a larva has to find a firm surface, attach to it and turn into a polyp. That polyp then starts laying down the limestone skeleton that, over many years, becomes part of a reef. When a damaged reef breaks into loose rubble or is smothered by sediment, larvae have fewer places to take hold.

Printed tiles are designed to fill that gap. A stable tile does not shift with currents the way rubble does. A larva that settles on it is less likely to be knocked loose or buried. Texture matters too. Ridges, grooves and small hollows give larvae more surface area and more sheltered spots than a flat slab would.

That is where 3D printing helps. A printer builds a structure layer by layer from a digital design. This makes it possible to produce irregular, branching or deeply grooved shapes. Casting those shapes in a simple mold would be difficult. The digital design can also be changed from one tile to the next rather than repeating a single form.

Material is the other half of the design. Terracotta is clay that has been fired at high temperature. Potters and builders have used it for flowerpots and roof tiles for thousands of years. It does not release many chemicals into seawater. That trait matters for anything meant to sit on the seabed for years.

Archireef, a group based in Hong Kong, prints terracotta tiles for coral restoration. Reef Design Lab in Australia is another group that produces 3D-printed reef structures.

Printed reef tiles address one specific problem: the lack of a stable surface. They do not by themselves supply coral, cool the water or reduce pollution.

Microfragmentation cuts coral into very small pieces that regrow faster than larger fragments do. David Vaughan developed the technique at Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida.

That speed matters. Many of the corals that build a reef's framework, including brain corals and boulder corals, grow slowly in the wild. A large colony can represent decades of growth. Once disease or bleaching kills one, natural replacement takes a long time.

Older coral gardening methods mostly work with fast-growing branching species, snapping off branches and growing them in nurseries. Microfragmentation takes the cut much further. Pieces small enough to sit on a fingertip are cut from a parent colony.

Fragments taken from the same parent colony share its genetics. When they are placed close together on a reef or a hard surface, they can grow toward one another and fuse. The result is a single larger colony that covers a patch of reef sooner than a single fragment could.

Coral Vita runs land-based coral farms in the Bahamas. Its corals grow in tanks on shore rather than in nurseries anchored on the seafloor. They are raised for replanting onto reefs.

A land-based setting gives operators control over conditions they cannot manage in open water. Staff can adjust water temperature, light and water quality in the tanks. Young corals are also kept away from storms, predators and the marine heat waves that trigger bleaching.

Farm-grown corals still have to reach the reef. Divers carry them out and attach them to the reef surface, where they continue to grow. Cutting one parent colony into many small pieces also yields more plantable units than cutting it into a few large ones.

The method has limits. Microfragmentation increases how much coral can be grown and how fast. It does not change the warming water, disease or pollution that damaged the reef in the first place. Replanted corals face those same conditions once they leave the farm.

Coral IVF is a restoration method that collects the eggs and sperm corals release during spawning, raises the resulting larvae and then releases them onto damaged reef. Peter Harrison of Southern Cross University in Australia led work developing the approach on the Great Barrier Reef.

The method relies on how many reef-building corals reproduce. Many species are broadcast spawners. They release eggs and sperm into the open water, where fertilization takes place outside the parent colony. On the Great Barrier Reef, large numbers of corals spawn within a short window each year. The timing is linked in part to the lunar cycle.

In the wild, most of that output never becomes a new colony. Currents carry eggs and larvae away from the reef. Fish and other animals eat them in large numbers. The larvae that survive must then find a suitable patch of hard surface before they can settle and start building a skeleton.

Harrison's approach steps in at that vulnerable stage. Teams gather spawn from healthy coral and raise the developing larvae until they are ready to settle. They then deliver the larvae directly onto damaged reef areas. The aim is to put far more larvae onto degraded patches than currents alone would bring there.

The first trials on the Great Barrier Reef took place in the mid-2010s. The name coral IVF is shorthand for the fertilization and rearing steps. It borrows from in vitro fertilization, the human fertility treatment. The corals, however, still spawn on their own natural schedule.

Larval restoration differs from fragment-based methods in one basic way. A fragment is a clone of its parent colony and shares the same genes. Larvae come from sexual reproduction, which mixes genes from different parents. A reef reseeded with larvae can carry more genetic variety than one rebuilt from a few cloned colonies. That variety is the raw material a population draws on to adapt over generations.

The method also has limits set by coral biology. Collection is tied to the short annual spawning window. The supply of larvae is seasonal as a result. Larvae that reach a reef still face predators and competition for space after they settle. Newly settled corals are tiny and take years to grow into colonies that add visible structure to a reef.

Playing recordings of a healthy reef through underwater loudspeakers can draw more fish to damaged coral. A study led by Tim Gordon of the University of Exeter, published in Nature Communications in 2019, tested the idea on degraded patches of the Great Barrier Reef.

A healthy coral reef is a noisy place. Snapping shrimp produce a constant crackle. Many reef fish grunt, chirp and drum to communicate with one another. When coral dies and the animals living on it disappear, that soundscape becomes quieter and less varied.

Sound matters because many reef fish spend their earliest weeks in open water. When young fish return to settle, they use sound, along with other cues, to locate a reef. A degraded reef sends out a weaker acoustic signal than a thriving one.

The Exeter-led team used a method known as acoustic enrichment. Researchers placed loudspeakers on patches of degraded reef and played recordings made on healthy reefs. They then compared those patches with similar ones that had no playback. The patches with reef sound attracted more fish than the silent patches.

The approach does not build new structures or plant coral. Its equipment, mainly an underwater speaker, can be moved between sites. That sets it apart from restoration methods that work on the reef's physical framework or on coral itself.

Fish do work on a reef that coral depends on. Grazing species such as parrotfish and surgeonfish eat algae that can otherwise smother coral surfaces. Their return is one sign that a damaged site still supports a functioning reef community.

The study has a clear limit. It measured fish, not coral. Its results do not show that reef sound helps coral recover. Playback acts on the animal community around a reef. Any link to coral regrowth would need separate evidence from studies designed to measure it.

The Ocean Cleanup is a nonprofit based in the Netherlands. It builds equipment that removes plastic from the open ocean and catches plastic in rivers upstream. Boyan Slat founded the organization in 2013.

Its work runs on two tracks. The first deals with plastic that is already at sea. The second tries to cut off the supply.

At sea, the main target is the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. This is a zone of the North Pacific, between Hawaii and California, where floating debris collects. Circular currents in the region, known as the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, draw plastic inward and hold it there for years.

The name suggests a solid island of trash, but the patch is not one. Most of the debris is scattered across a wide stretch of open water. Some pieces are large enough to see from a boat, such as discarded fishing nets. Much of the rest is small fragments. That spread means any collection system has to sweep a large area to gather a meaningful amount.

The Ocean Cleanup builds floating systems designed to gather this debris. The collected plastic is then hauled out of the water and brought ashore. Sunlight and wave action break floating plastic into smaller pieces over time. Once plastic degrades into microplastics, it becomes far harder to recover.

The second track focuses on rivers. Rivers carry plastic from towns and cities down to the coast. That makes them one of the main routes by which waste reaches the ocean. The Ocean Cleanup builds river-based devices it calls Interceptors. They are placed in rivers to stop plastic before it flows out to sea.

Ocean collection deals with plastic that has already accumulated and can persist at sea for decades. River interception deals with the flow of new plastic. Without that second step, a cleared patch would keep receiving fresh debris from upstream.

The approach also has limits. These systems collect plastic that is already in the water or moving toward it. They do not reduce how much plastic is produced or thrown away in the first place. That depends on manufacturing, packaging and waste management on land.

Global Fishing Watch is an online platform that maps fishing activity around the world using satellite tracking data. It launched in 2016 as a partnership between the ocean conservation group Oceana, the nonprofit SkyTruth and Google $GOOGL.

Its main data source is the Automatic Identification System, known as AIS. Ships broadcast AIS messages by radio. Each message carries details such as the vessel's identity, position, speed and heading. The system was designed so ships could see one another and avoid collisions. Satellites can also pick up these signals. Satellite reception gives a safety tool a second use as a running record of where vessels travel.

Global Fishing Watch takes that stream of positions and looks for signs of fishing within it. A boat heading in a straight line toward port moves differently from one working a fishing ground. By reading those movement patterns, the platform estimates where and when vessels appear to be fishing. It does more than show where boats happen to be.

The result is a public map. Anyone with an internet connection can view it, including researchers, journalists, fisheries managers and government agencies. Fishing on the open ocean often happens far from any observer. The high seas lie beyond the jurisdiction of any single country, and few outsiders see what takes place there.

The map has practical uses. It can show whether boats appear inside a marine protected area where fishing is restricted. It can show fishing activity close to a country's maritime boundary. It can also reveal how fishing effort shifts between regions and across seasons.

The approach has a built-in limit. Global Fishing Watch can only map vessels whose AIS signals it receives. A vessel that switches off its transmitter drops out of the AIS record for as long as the transmitter stays off. A boat fishing where it should not can stay off the map this way.

Coverage also varies by vessel size. Not every fishing boat is required to carry AIS, and many small boats do not. The map shows the activity of vessels that broadcast their position, not the full picture of fishing at sea.

Argo is an international program of about 4,000 robotic floats that drift through the world's oceans. Each float records temperature and salinity as it sinks and rises, building a running picture of conditions below the surface.

The array has been in place since around 2000. Before it existed, much of what scientists knew about the subsurface ocean came from instruments lowered over the side of research ships. Those cruises followed set routes. They could not cover remote waters in every season. Argo floats fill those gaps by spreading across the open ocean and reporting on their own schedule.

A float has no propeller. It changes depth by adjusting its buoyancy, pumping oil between an internal reservoir and an external bladder. Most of its time is spent drifting with the currents at depth. On a typical cycle of about 10 days, a float descends to roughly 2,000 meters. It then rises to the surface while its sensors take readings. At the surface, it sends its data by satellite before sinking again.

Temperature and salinity together set the density of seawater. Differences in density help drive the large-scale currents that move heat around the planet. Tracking both measurements over time shows where the ocean is warming and where it is turning fresher or saltier. It also shows how those changes shift circulation.

The data are shared freely with researchers and forecasting agencies. Weather and seasonal forecasts draw on them, as do climate models and studies of sea level rise. Warmer water expands. Heat stored in the ocean therefore contributes directly to rising seas.

Newer floats carry sensors for ocean chemistry, including dissolved oxygen. These biogeochemical floats can also measure properties such as pH and nitrate. Oxygen readings help researchers track low-oxygen zones that affect fish and other marine life.

Argo's role is measurement rather than repair. The long-term record from the floats gives researchers a baseline for tracking ocean warming, acidification and oxygen loss.

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 2:01 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 7:00 am

Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.

The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.

The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game.

“Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks, along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.

Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

#5459. How retired oil platforms become artificial reefs, and why Europe mostly says no

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Rigs-to-reefs programs leave retired offshore oil platforms in the sea as artificial reefs, and these five points explain the methods, laws, marine life and debate behind them

An offshore oil platform is built to pull oil and gas from beneath the seabed. By the time its wells stop producing, its steel legs can be coated in sponges and corals and surrounded by fish. That leaves operators and regulators with a practical choice. The structure can come out of the water, or it can stay where marine life has already settled on it.

Rigs to reefs is the name for the second option. Under this approach, some or all of a retired offshore oil or gas platform's steel stays in the sea as an artificial reef. It is not hauled to shore for scrapping. The steel can be cut off below the surface, moved to a new site or tipped over where it stands.

Decommissioning is a major engineering and policy question for any region with aging offshore fields. Every platform eventually stops producing, and each one needs a plan for what happens next. The choice touches shipping safety, fisheries and cleanup costs. It also settles who is responsible for the steel once production ends.

The answer differs sharply by region. In the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, a 1984 federal law and state programs in Louisiana and Texas allow retired structures to become reefs. In the North Sea, an international agreement covering the North-East Atlantic generally requires full removal. Off southern California, researchers have studied fish on platforms for decades. The state passed a law in 2010 that created a framework for conversion.

This slideshow covers five parts of the subject. It begins with the three engineering methods used to turn a platform into a reef. It then explains the U.S. laws and Gulf state programs that make conversion possible. The third slide looks at the fish and coral living on platform legs off California and in the Gulf of Mexico. The fourth covers the European rules and the 1995 Brent Spar dispute that shaped the debate in Europe. The last examines the open scientific question of whether these structures add fish to the ocean or mostly gather fish that were already nearby.

The same steel frame can be treated as waste in one ocean and as habitat in another. The reasons show how governments weigh ecology, cost and long-term liability at sea.

Retired offshore oil and gas platforms become artificial reefs through one of three main methods: partial removal, tow-and-place or topple-in-place. Each one keeps some or all of the platform's underwater steel in the sea.

An offshore platform has two basic parts. The topsides sit above the water and carry the deck, the production equipment and, on many platforms, the crew quarters. Below them stands the jacket. This is a steel lattice of legs and cross-bracing that reaches down to the seabed and holds the topsides up. In a reef conversion, the topsides come off and go to shore. The jacket is the part that can stay in the water.

Partial removal leaves the jacket in its original spot. Crews cut the structure off at a set depth below the surface and take away the upper section. The lower part keeps standing where it was first installed.

The cut depth follows a navigation clearance rule. U.S. practice for partial removal keeps at least 85 feet of water above whatever steel remains. That clearance is meant to keep the submerged structure out of the path of passing ships. The standard follows the National Artificial Reef Plan.

Tow-and-place moves the jacket instead of leaving it where it stood. Crews free the whole jacket from its original position, tow it to a designated reef site and sink it there. The reef ends up at a chosen location, not at the spot where the platform once produced oil or gas.

Topple-in-place keeps the jacket at its original site but changes its orientation. The jacket is tipped over and comes to rest on its side on the seabed. Laid down this way, it rises less far off the bottom than it did when upright.

Full removal, the alternative to all three, takes the entire structure out of the water. The choice among the reef methods comes down to two questions. One is where the jacket ends up. The other is how much of it remains standing.

Rigs-to-reefs conversions in the U.S. rest on a federal law, the National Fishing Enhancement Act of 1984, and on state programs in the Gulf of Mexico. Louisiana and Texas each run a program that accepts retired offshore platforms as reef material.

Congress passed the National Fishing Enhancement Act to set up a national framework for artificial reefs. The law also called for a National Artificial Reef Plan to guide how reefs are sited, built and managed. Retired oil and gas platforms fall within that framework as one type of reef material.

Louisiana created its Artificial Reef Program in 1986, two years after the federal act. The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries manages it. The program takes in retired platforms and keeps their steel in the water as reef.

Texas has its own Rigs-to-Reefs program, run by Texas Parks and Wildlife. It began in 1990, six years after the federal law.

The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, known as BSEE, oversees the decommissioning of offshore platforms in federal waters. BSEE sits within the U.S. Department of the Interior. Its rules generally require an operator to remove a platform once the structure is no longer needed. Reef conversion is one approved exception to that requirement. A state reef program enters the picture when the operator donates the structure as reef material.

The state programs work through donation. An operator retiring a platform hands the structure over to the program. The operator also typically donates a share of the money it saves by not removing the platform entirely. That money goes to the state program and helps pay for its reef work.

Full removal means pulling the whole structure out of the sea and hauling it to shore. Leaving steel in place as reef skips that step for the part that stays underwater. Each conversion involves three parties: the operator that owns the platform, BSEE as the federal regulator and the state agency that accepts the steel.

Offshore oil and gas platforms can host dense communities of fish, corals and sponges. Steel built for drilling off southern California and in the Gulf of Mexico has become habitat for marine life in both regions.

A 2014 study by Claisse and colleagues, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, measured fish production at oil and gas platforms off southern California. The authors found that these platforms had some of the highest secondary fish production per unit area of any marine habitat they compared.

Secondary production describes how much new fish tissue a habitat generates through growth over a period of time. It differs from a head count of the fish present on a single dive. Expressing it per unit area lets researchers compare habitats of very different sizes on equal terms.

Milton Love of the University of California, Santa Barbara has studied fish on California platforms for decades. His work documents juvenile rockfish living on the structures. Rockfish belong to the genus Sebastes, a large group of species found along the Pacific coast of North America. Many rockfish species are targeted by commercial and recreational anglers on the West Coast. The presence of young fish shows that platforms serve these species early in life.

In the Gulf of Mexico, platform legs become covered with encrusting animals, including corals and sponges. These organisms need a hard surface to settle on. A platform's submerged steel provides one. Once that living layer forms, it draws fish to the structure. A platform's legs run from the seafloor up to the surface. That gives encrusting animals room to grow through the full depth of the water at the site.

California has taken a legal step toward keeping some of these habitats in place. A state law created a framework for converting retired platforms into reefs. That framework lays out a legal path for conversion. It does not by itself turn any platform into a reef.

OSPAR Decision 98/3 bans dumping or leaving disused offshore installations in the North-East Atlantic. For retired oil and gas platforms in the North Sea, that makes full removal the default.

The decision sits under the OSPAR Convention, the agreement that protects the marine environment of the North-East Atlantic. The North Sea falls inside that area. Its offshore oil and gas fields, including those in the U.K. and Norwegian sectors, come under the same ban.

Decision 98/3 allows limited exceptions. These apply mainly to two categories: the footings of very large steel structures and concrete installations.

Those exceptions are the main route by which any platform material may stay on the North Sea seabed. For most installations, the rule points to removal and disposal on land.

The Brent Spar episode of 1995 was a high-profile dispute over disposal at sea in the region. Brent Spar was a storage buoy, not a production platform. Shell $SHEL planned to sink it in the deep Atlantic once it was no longer needed.

Greenpeace campaigned against the plan. Shell dropped it and had the buoy dismantled onshore instead.

The rules produce a sharp contrast with the U.S. In the North Sea, rigs-to-reefs conversions are rare. In the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, the practice is established.

The difference lies in regulation, not engineering. Under OSPAR, the starting assumption is that a disused installation leaves the sea. In the Gulf of Mexico, leaving part or all of a platform's structure in the water as an artificial reef is an accepted option.

Scientists have not settled whether reefs built from retired oil platforms produce new fish or mainly gather fish that already lived nearby. The evidence differs by species and by region, and no single answer covers every rigs-to-reefs site.

The distinction shapes how these structures are judged. A reef that adds to production increases the number of fish in the sea. A reef that only pulls fish in from surrounding waters moves them to a new spot without changing the total.

The issue is known as the attraction-versus-production debate. Production is more plausible for species whose numbers are limited by a shortage of hard habitat. In those cases, extra structure gives young fish more places to settle and survive. Where food or spawning success caps a population, added steel is more likely to redistribute fish than to multiply them.

Attraction carries its own risk. A reef that concentrates fish in one known location can make them easier to catch. If fishing pressure rises at the site, a structure that gathers fish without producing more could speed the depletion of a local stock.

In the Gulf of Mexico, red snapper sits at the center of this argument. The species gathers in large numbers around platforms. It is also one of the most heavily fished reef species in the region.

The steel can also host species that do not belong there. Orange cup coral, Tubastraea coccinea, is native to the Indo-Pacific. It has spread into the western Atlantic and colonized platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, where it competes with native corals and sponges for space. Platforms left standing can serve as stepping stones that help it reach new areas.

Long-term responsibility is another point of contention. Full removal takes the steel out of the sea. When part or all of a platform stays offshore as a reef, responsibility for that structure over the following decades shifts as well.

Cost draws the sharpest criticism. Leaving a structure in place is cheaper for an operator than hauling it ashore. Critics argue those savings, rather than habitat value, are a major force behind rigs-to-reefs programs. Supporters point to the marine life already living on the legs.

#5458. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5457. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5456. A beginner's checklist for a first reef or wreck dive: 10 things to settle on land

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how to plan your first wreck or reef dive, from certification depth limits and dive shops to buddy plans, reef etiquette and safe ascents

Most of what happens on a first wreck or reef dive is settled before anyone steps off the boat. The site, the operator, the depth, the gas plan and the exposure suit are all chosen on land. By the time a new diver descends, the dive is largely following decisions already made.

Many newly certified divers notice a gap once their course ends. Training dives take place under an instructor's direct supervision, with a set plan and a controlled site. A first fun dive works differently. The diver and a buddy share responsibility for the plan, even when a guide leads the group. Knowing how to plan your first wreck or reef dive turns that responsibility into a short series of practical choices.

Reefs and wrecks draw beginners for different reasons. A coral reef offers marine life, color and, at many popular sites, a gradual slope that lets divers pick their depth. A shipwreck offers history and structure, and it often attracts fish that shelter around the hull. Wrecks also bring hazards that reefs usually lack. These include silt that clouds the water, sharp metal, loose cables and enclosed spaces that need extra training to enter.

The 10 steps below follow the order in which most of these decisions come up. They start with the limits of an entry-level certification and the choice between a reef and a wreck. They move on to picking a dive shop, reading conditions and choosing a wetsuit or drysuit. Next come the buddy plan and the separate etiquette that applies at wreck sites and on living reefs. The final steps cover gear servicing, health, flying after diving, gas management and the slow ascent that ends every dive.

None of these steps replaces formal training or the advice of a local dive professional. Agencies such as PADI, SSI and NAUI set their own standards, and those standards differ in places. Dive computers and local rules can add further limits. Treat the guidance here as a beginner reef dive checklist and a primer on wreck diving for beginners. Confirm the details with the operator and the agency that issued your card.

An entry-level Open Water Diver certification from agencies such as PADI, SSI and NAUI typically qualifies a diver for planned dives to about 18 meters, or 60 feet. A first wreck or reef site should sit inside that range.

That figure is common agency guidance, not a universal rule. Exact limits vary by agency and by country. The British Sub-Aqua Club's entry-level Ocean Diver qualification, for example, sets its limit at 20 meters.

Younger divers face tighter limits. PADI's Junior Open Water certification restricts divers aged 10 and 11 to 12 meters, or about 40 feet.

The limit follows from the training itself. Open water courses teach skills at modest depths, and the card certifies a diver for conditions similar to the course. Going deeper raises gas consumption and shortens no-decompression time. It also increases the effects of nitrogen narcosis. Later courses give divers supervised practice in managing those effects.

Before booking, read the card. Confirm which agency issued it and at what level. Dive operators generally accept cards from the major agencies. A PADI-certified diver can usually book with an SSI shop, and the reverse. Operators will ask to see proof of certification, either a physical card or a digital version.

A logbook adds useful detail. It records how many dives a diver has made, at what depths and in what conditions. Some operators ask about recent experience before assigning a site or a guide group.

Recent practice counts alongside the card. Most entry-level certifications do not expire, but skills such as mask clearing and buoyancy control fade without use. Divers who have been out of the water for a long stretch can take a refresher program, such as PADI ReActivate, before a trip.

For sites deeper than 18 meters, the usual next step is an Advanced Open Water course. PADI's version qualifies divers to 30 meters, or about 100 feet. It includes a deep dive and a navigation dive alongside other specialty dives. Many wrecks rest below entry-level limits, so check a site's depth against the card before choosing it.

A shallow reef is usually the better setting for a first dive after certification than a shipwreck. Reefs tend to have open water overhead and fewer structural hazards. That leaves a new diver room to settle in and a direct route to the surface.

Shallow reefs also sit in the brightest part of the water column. Water absorbs red light first, so reefs near the surface keep more of their natural color than deeper sites. The extra light also helps a diver keep track of a buddy and judge distance from the reef.

Most reef dives have nothing overhead. A diver who needs to end the dive early can make a controlled ascent straight up. Open Water Diver training is built around that kind of direct access to the surface. A reef site keeps that margin intact.

Wrecks add hazards that open reefs generally do not. A wreck's depth is set by where the ship came to rest, not by what suits a beginner. Some well-known wrecks lie at or beyond the depths an entry-level card covers.

Fine sediment settles on and inside wrecks. One careless fin kick can lift it into a cloud that cuts visibility within seconds. Steel hulls also corrode and break apart over the years. That leaves jagged edges, loose plating and scattered debris.

Entanglement is another concern. Old cables and rigging can hang off a wreck. Wrecks attract fish, and fish attract anglers. Lost fishing line and netting often end up snagged on the hull. Any of these can catch a hose, a fin strap or a diver's arm.

Task loading matters as well. A newly certified diver is still building buoyancy control, tracking gas use and staying close to a buddy. A reef lets attention stay on those basics. A large structure adds navigation and hazard awareness on top of them.

Reefs are not free of risk. Current, surge over shallow reef tops and marine life that should not be touched all need attention. A sheltered reef dived with a guide limits that exposure.

Wrecks make a reasonable next step after more logged dives. Some ships were deliberately sunk as artificial reefs and cleaned of hazardous materials beforehand. Shallow, protected wrecks can be viewed from the outside once basic skills feel routine.

Book your first wreck or reef dive with an operator affiliated with a recognized training agency, such as PADI, SSI or NAUI. A suitable shop gives a full pre-dive briefing and sends a guide or divemaster into the water with new divers.

Agency affiliation means the shop's instructors and dive professionals hold ratings from that agency. They are expected to work to its published standards. Shops usually display the affiliation on their website and at the counter. PADI, for example, uses designations such as PADI Dive Center and PADI 5 Star Dive Resort.

A divemaster is a professional rating that sits below instructor in most agency systems. On a guided dive, this person leads the group and knows the layout of the site. The divemaster also watches for anyone who is struggling. For a newly certified diver on an unfamiliar site, that supervision adds a second set of eyes beyond the buddy pair.

Ask the shop how many divers each guide leads. A smaller group leaves the guide more attention for each person. Ask whether newly certified divers are grouped together or mixed with experienced divers headed to more demanding sites.

Rental equipment needs its own set of questions. Ask when the regulators were last serviced. Ask whether you can check the fit of the mask, fins and buoyancy compensator before the boat leaves. Worn straps, cracked hoses or a sticking inflator are reasons to request a replacement.

Find out how the site is reached. A boat dive usually involves a giant-stride or back-roll entry and a ladder climb on the way out. A shore dive means walking in with full gear, sometimes over rocks or loose sand.

Ask about the operator's emergency setup before booking. Find out whether the boat carries emergency oxygen, a first aid kit and a radio. Ask whether the crew follows an emergency action plan that includes contact with the nearest recompression chamber.

Expect the shop to ask questions of its own. Most will want to see a certification card before the dive. Many ask divers to complete a medical questionnaire and sign a liability release. Some operators also require proof of dive accident insurance, such as coverage from Divers Alert Network. These checks let the shop match each diver to the dive it plans to run.

Conditions at a dive site change by season, and sometimes by the hour. Ask the operator about the current, visibility, surf and water temperature before you book. A site that suits a new diver one week can be a poor choice the next.

Current shapes how much effort a dive takes. A mild current can carry a diver gently along a reef. A strong one demands more kicking and uses up air faster. It can also pull a group apart.

Some operators run drift dives. On a drift dive, divers ride the current while the boat tracks the group and collects everyone at the end. That style calls for extra skills, such as deploying a surface marker buoy. A calm, sheltered site with little water movement is the usual choice for a first outing.

Visibility describes how far a diver can see underwater. Plankton blooms, river runoff, recent storms and stirred-up sediment can all reduce it. Poor visibility makes it harder to keep track of a buddy and a guide. It can also cause disorientation, because the surface and the bottom become hard to judge. Ask how far divers have been able to see on recent trips. That answer is more useful than a site's general reputation.

Surf matters most for shore dives. Walking through breaking waves with a tank on your back and fins in hand takes coordination. A fall in the surf zone can damage gear or cause injury. Boat dives avoid the surf line, but a rough sea surface can still bring seasickness. It can also make climbing back up the boat ladder harder.

Water temperature at the site can shift with the season and with depth. A thermocline is a layer where the water turns noticeably colder, and divers can pass through one on the way down. Knowing the expected temperature in advance helps with packing and rental requests.

Operators cancel or move dives when conditions turn unsafe. That is ordinary practice, not a failure of the trip. Booking a few days in one destination leaves room for a bad-weather day. A flexible schedule also removes the pressure to dive in conditions beyond a beginner's training.

Choose your exposure protection based on the water temperature at the dive site, not the air temperature on the boat. Warm tropical water often suits a thin wetsuit. Cooler water calls for a thicker wetsuit, a hood and gloves, or a drysuit.

Water draws heat away from the body far faster than air at the same temperature. A diver can feel comfortable at the start of a dive and grow chilled before the end, even in water that feels mild on entry. Cold makes it harder to concentrate, handle equipment and follow the dive plan. All three matter on a first outing at an unfamiliar site.

A wetsuit works by trapping a thin layer of water against the skin. The body warms that layer, and the neoprene foam slows the loss of heat. Thicker neoprene contains more insulating gas bubbles, so it keeps a diver warmer. Neoprene also compresses as a diver descends, which reduces its insulation at depth.

Fit matters as much as thickness. A suit that is too loose lets cold water flush through at the neck, wrists and ankles. That constant exchange undoes much of the insulation. A suit that is too tight restricts breathing and movement. Rental suits come in a range of sizes. Trying on more than one before the boat leaves helps avoid a poor fit underwater.

Thickness also changes buoyancy. More neoprene floats more, so a diver in a thicker suit needs more lead weight to descend. Anyone switching from a thin suit to a thick one, or adding a hood and vest, should do a buoyancy check at the surface before the dive.

The cut of the suit is another choice. A shorty covers the torso with short sleeves and short legs. A full-length suit also protects the arms and legs from cold, stings and scrapes. Semi-dry suits use tighter seals at the openings to limit flushing.

A drysuit keeps the diver dry inside a sealed shell, with insulating layers worn underneath. It handles differently from a wetsuit, and training agencies teach its use in a separate specialty course. Diving one without that training raises the risk of buoyancy problems, including air shifting into the legs and an uncontrolled ascent.

The local dive operator can say what suits divers typically wear at that site in that season.

A buddy dive plan is a short conversation held before descending. It settles the maximum depth, the turnaround point, the minimum gas reserve, hand signals and what happens if the pair gets separated. Both divers should be able to repeat it back before either one enters the water.

The maximum depth for the dive comes first. It should match the site briefing and stay within the training and experience of the less experienced diver. Write it on a slate if memory might slip once underwater.

The turnaround point tells the pair when to head back toward the exit, the boat's mooring line or the shore. It can be set by elapsed time, by a landmark on the site or by a gas pressure. Settling it in advance removes the need to negotiate underwater, where conversation is limited to gestures.

The minimum gas reserve is the pressure at which each diver begins to end the dive. Operators often state a figure in the briefing, and both buddies should use the same one. Each diver also needs to know where the partner's alternate air source sits and how it releases.

Hand signals need a quick rehearsal on deck. Most recreational training agencies teach a thumb-up gesture to mean go up or end the dive, not OK. The OK sign is a circle formed by the thumb and forefinger. Divers who trained with different agencies or in different countries should compare their signals. That includes the signs for low on air, out of air and a problem with an ear or equipment.

The lost-buddy procedure covers separation, which can happen quickly in low visibility or a crowded group. The protocol commonly taught in entry-level courses is to stop, turn slowly and look for bubbles or a light for about one minute. If the partner does not appear, each diver ascends and the pair reunites at the surface. Agreeing on this keeps either diver from searching alone at depth.

The plan ends with a pre-dive safety check done together. PADI teaches it with the acronym BWRAF, which covers the buoyancy control device, weights, releases, air and a final check. Each diver inspects the other's gear. That inspection also shows where the partner's weight releases and inflator sit if an emergency arises.

On a first wreck dive, stay outside the hull and any enclosed space. Swimming inside a wreck, known as penetration, requires extra training such as a wreck diver specialty course, plus dive lights and a guideline.

The main reason is the overhead. In open water, a diver with a problem can make a controlled ascent straight to the surface. Inside a hull, deck plating, bulkheads and collapsed structure block that route. The only way out is back through an opening.

Silt makes that exit harder to find. Fine sediment settles on the floors and ledges of a sunken ship over time. One careless fin kick can lift it into a cloud that drops visibility close to zero. Divers call this a silt-out, and it can happen in seconds.

Disorientation can follow quickly. A ship lying on its side or upside down no longer matches the layout it had afloat. Doorways turn into holes in the floor or ceiling, and stairways run sideways. Without a guideline fixed outside the wreck, a diver can lose track of the way out.

Specialty training addresses these problems directly. Courses teach how to lay and follow a guideline and how to carry primary and backup lights. They also teach fin kicks, such as the frog kick, that direct thrust behind the diver rather than down toward the silt. Students practice these skills under supervision before attempting any penetration.

The outside of a wreck carries its own hazards. Corroded steel can leave sharp, jagged edges. Wrecks attract fish, and they also attract anglers. Monofilament fishing line and old nets often end up snagged on the structure. Many wreck divers carry a cutting tool for that reason. Keeping hoses and gauges tucked close to the body also reduces snag points.

Some wrecks are protected by law. In the U.K., the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 covers designated military wrecks. In the U.S., the Sunken Military Craft Act of 2004 protects sunken military vessels and aircraft. Many of these sites are war graves.

Rules on removing objects from wrecks vary by country and by site. Taking artifacts can be illegal. Divers on a first wreck visit can look and take photographs while leaving everything in place.

Good reef etiquette comes down to three habits: hold neutral buoyancy, keep your hands off the coral and keep your fins clear of the bottom. Many corals are living animals, and a single kick or grab can break structures that took years to grow.

A coral head is a colony of tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp builds a limestone skeleton. In reef-building corals, algae living inside the polyp's tissue supply much of its food. A thin layer of mucus covers the living surface. Contact from a hand, knee or fin can strip that layer and leave the colony open to infection. It can also snap off branching growth outright.

Buoyancy control is the skill that makes the no-touch rule possible. A diver who is too heavy sinks toward the reef and starts kicking or grabbing to stay off it. A diver who is too light drifts upward and then overcorrects. Make small adjustments to the buoyancy compensator and use your breathing to fine-tune depth. Hover a comfortable distance above the reef rather than right at its edge.

Trim, or body position, works alongside buoyancy. A horizontal posture keeps the fins level with the torso instead of angled down toward the coral. Bicycle-style kicks and steep head-up postures push fins into the reef. They also stir up sand that settles back onto the coral. A gentle flutter kick or frog kick moves water backward rather than downward.

Loose equipment causes damage that divers often miss. A dangling alternate air source, pressure gauge or camera can drag across the reef behind you. Clip hoses and gauges close to the body before descending. Keep lights, slates and other accessories secured.

The same restraint applies to marine life. Do not feed fish. Feeding changes their natural behavior and can make some species aggressive toward divers. Do not chase turtles or rays, and do not corner animals under ledges. Take photos from a distance. Leave shells, coral and rocks where they are. Many marine parks prohibit removing anything.

Some reef protection starts before the dive. Hawaii banned the sale of sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate over concerns about harm to coral. That law took effect in 2021. Palau adopted a similar ban. Check the local rules at your destination. A rash guard reduces how much sunscreen you need to apply.

If you lose control and begin sinking toward the reef, one finger placed on bare rock or sand does far less harm than a kick through living coral. Some sites discourage or ban gloves to remove the temptation to hold on.

Service your regulator on the manufacturer's schedule, test every piece of gear before you travel and skip any dive when a cold or congestion stops you from equalizing. Then plan your flight home around the surface interval your agency and dive computer recommend.

Each manufacturer sets its own regulator maintenance interval. There is no universal rule. The paperwork from the last service usually shows when the next one is due. A regulator that sits unused between trips still needs attention. Seals and O-rings can age even without use.

A home check a week or two before departure catches problems while there is still time to fix them. Inspect each hose for cracks, bulges or worn fittings near the ends. Breathe from the second stage and the alternate air source on a full cylinder if one is available. Look over the mask strap and fin straps for perished rubber. Charge or replace the dive computer battery, and confirm the unit powers on and displays correctly.

Rental equipment deserves the same scrutiny on arrival. Ask the shop to explain its computer or gauges if they differ from the ones you trained with.

Sinus and ear health decides whether a dive can happen at all. On descent, equalizing moves air into the middle ear and sinuses to balance rising water pressure. Congestion from a cold, an allergy or a sinus infection can block those air spaces. Forcing a descent against a blocked ear risks barotrauma, which can include a ruptured eardrum.

Decongestants carry their own risk. If one wears off during a dive, expanding air can become trapped in the ears or sinuses on the way up. Divers call this a reverse block. With a stuffy head, the conservative choice is to sit the dive out.

Flying soon after diving raises the risk of decompression sickness. The cabin of a commercial jet is pressurized below sea-level pressure. That lower pressure can let nitrogen still dissolved in the body form bubbles. For a single no-decompression dive, 12 hours at the surface is a commonly cited minimum before boarding.

Training agencies differ in their exact recommendations. Repeated dives over several days call for a longer wait. Many divers leave a full day or more between their last dive and their flight. The dive computer's no-fly time and the agency's guidance should set the final schedule. Placing the last dive early in the itinerary, rather than on departure morning, keeps that interval from being squeezed.

Watch your submersible pressure gauge throughout the dive and rise no faster than about nine meters (30 feet) per minute. Pause for three minutes at roughly five meters (15 feet) before surfacing. Training agencies commonly teach these figures, but exact rates and stops vary by agency and dive computer.

The submersible pressure gauge, often shortened to SPG, shows how much gas remains in the cylinder. Check it every few minutes and before any change in depth. Regular checks keep the reading from catching you off guard.

Depth changes how fast that reading falls. At 10 meters of seawater, the surrounding pressure is about double the pressure at the surface. A breath taken there draws roughly twice as much gas from the tank as the same breath at the surface. Cold, exertion and nerves push consumption higher. A cylinder can empty faster than a new diver expects.

Plan to reach the surface with a reserve still in the cylinder. Start the ascent early enough to keep it. That reserve covers problems such as a slow ascent, a strong current near the boat or a buddy who runs low. A buddy in that position may need to share gas from your alternate air source.

Speed matters most during the ascent. Rising too quickly raises the risk of decompression sickness. Nitrogen absorbed at depth can come out of the body's tissues faster than the body can release it safely. Holding your breath while rising can injure the lungs as the air inside them expands. Breathe normally the whole way up.

Most dive computers sound an alarm or flash a warning when the ascent rate is too fast. Follow the computer when its guidance is more conservative than the general rule. Air in the buoyancy compensator device, or BCD, expands as you rise. The gas bubbles in a neoprene wetsuit expand too. Vent small amounts of air from the BCD to keep the ascent under control.

The safety stop is a precaution on dives that stay within no-decompression limits. It differs from a required decompression stop, which applies to dives that exceed those limits. The pause gives the body extra time to release nitrogen before the final stretch to the surface.

Holding steady at the stop takes practice. An anchor line, a mooring line or a sloping reef gives a visual reference for depth. Watch the computer or depth gauge rather than guessing. Once the three minutes pass, cover the last few meters slowly. Look up as you near the surface to check for boats overhead.

#5455. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5454. Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Predicts Top 3 ZK Cryptos

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Heading into 2027, three projects stand out for a combination of technical progress, real-world traction, and narrative strength: zkSync (ZK), Starknet (STRK), and Zcash (ZEC).

With all three projects at one point in time being mentioned by Ethereum’s creator, Vitalik Buterin, they are all viable picks for the top ZK-based tokens, but stick around until the end to find out which one Meta AI predicts will have a huge 2027.
