#5453. From USS Oriskany to HMCS Annapolis: 5 ships sunk on purpose between 1921 and 2015

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These ships sunk on purpose include an aircraft carrier turned artificial reef, a nuclear test target and a German battleship used for gunnery practice

A retired warship does not always end its career in a scrapyard. Some are taken out to sea and sent to the bottom on purpose. The reason behind each sinking shows what a navy or government still wanted from the hull.

Three motives run through the history of deliberate sinkings. The first is weapons testing. Firing on a real hull lets a navy see how its shells and bombs perform against actual armor and structure. The second is nuclear research. In 1946, the U.S. gathered a fleet of target vessels at Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands to measure what atomic bombs would do to ships. The third is the artificial reef. After hazardous materials are stripped out, a cleaned hull can be placed on the seabed. There it offers marine life a hard surface to settle on. It also gives recreational divers a site to explore.

Scuttling is the term for deliberately sinking a vessel, usually by its own crew or owner. Not every ship here fits that definition neatly. SMS Baden, for one, was built for Germany and sunk by Britain.

This slideshow covers five ships sunk on purpose between 1921 and 2015. It is a selection, not a complete or ranked list. The group includes two American aircraft carriers and a World War II-era transport that became a missile-tracking ship. It also includes a German battleship taken by the British after World War I and a Canadian destroyer escort. One of them, USS Oriskany, is widely described as the largest vessel ever intentionally sunk to form an artificial reef.

The five ships also trace how the purpose behind deliberate sinkings has shifted. The earliest, SMS Baden, served as a target for British naval gunnery in 1921. USS Saratoga went down in 1946 during nuclear weapons testing at Bikini Atoll. The three most recent were sunk in 2006, 2009 and 2015. They went down off Pensacola and Key West in Florida and in Howe Sound, British Columbia. USS Oriskany and HMCS Annapolis were both sunk to form artificial reefs.

Each slide below covers what the ship was, where it went down and why it was sunk.

USS Oriskany was sent to the bottom off Pensacola, Florida, on May 17, 2006, to become an artificial reef. The retired carrier is widely described as the largest vessel ever intentionally sunk to create one.

The Oriskany was an Essex-class aircraft carrier. The U.S. Navy commissioned it in 1950. Its deliberate sinking came 56 years later.

The carrier now rests in about 212 feet of water off the Florida Panhandle.

USS Vandenberg was sunk off Key West, Florida, on May 27, 2009. The former missile-tracking ship now rests in about 140 feet of water.

The vessel did not start out under that name or in that role. It was launched in 1943 as USS General Harry Taylor, a transport.

It was later converted into a missile-tracking ship and renamed USS Vandenberg.

The hull measures about 523 feet long. That length far exceeds the depth of the water where the ship now lies.

The ship went to the bottom 66 years after its launch. Over that span, one hull carried two names and filled two distinct roles before it was sent to the seafloor.

USS Saratoga, a Lexington-class aircraft carrier, sank at Bikini Atoll after the Baker test in July 1946. The carrier was one of the target ships in Operation Crossroads, the series of U.S. nuclear weapons tests held at the atoll that month.

Saratoga was not sent down to build a reef or to give gunners a practice target. Its job in Crossroads was to sit in the target area and take the effects of a nuclear detonation.

Baker was the second test of the operation. Saratoga went under only after that blast.

That sets Saratoga apart from ships scuttled with charges or placed on the seabed at a chosen depth. Its sinking was a result of the weapons test, not the goal of the operation.

The carrier's wreck remains at Bikini Atoll, where Operation Crossroads took place.

SMS Baden was a German battleship that the British took over and then sank on purpose as a gunnery target in 1921. British guns sent it down, not its own crew.

Baden was not among the German warships scuttled at Scapa Flow. Its sinking was a separate event with a separate purpose.

After the battleship passed into British hands, it was not returned to service or turned into a reef. The British used it as a target and fired on it until it sank.

HMCS Annapolis, a Canadian destroyer escort, was sunk deliberately in Howe Sound, British Columbia, in 2015 to create an artificial reef.

The HMCS prefix is used for commissioned ships of the Royal Canadian Navy. Annapolis is the only Canadian vessel in this selection. Its wreck is also the only one here that rests in Canadian waters.

The 2015 sinking makes Annapolis the most recent ship on this list.

#5452. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

Will CPI cause a sell-off across Asian stocks and Bitcoin? Asian stocks staged a sharp recovery this morning, but another US inflation report could put the rebound to the test. Investors are preparing for October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI), with expectations of slower monthly inflation offering some relief. However, rising Federal Reserve rate-hike bets and NVIDIA shareholders suing Jensen Huang have kept markets cautious.

The Korea’s KOSPI jumped 4.5% this morning trading, led by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index also advanced, while Singapore’s Straits Times Index joined the regional recovery. Bitcoin, meanwhile, remains below $75,000 ahead of the US inflation release.

South Korean stocks getting sent 📈 🤑 🥳 pic.twitter.com/KYd5V9Oh9d

Does this recovery have enough momentum to survive another inflation surprise? A hotter reading could revive concerns about borrowing costs, while weaker inflation might give risk assets room to recover. Will the latest CPI figures determine if the rebound continues, or will it cause a sell-off?

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to publish October CPI at 8:30 a.m. ET on November 10. Economists expect headline inflation to increase 0.3% month-over-month, slowing from September’s 0.6% rise. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, is forecast to increase 0.2%, compared with 0.3% previously.

Last year’s government shutdown prevented the BLS from collecting the necessary October 2025 data. Economists nevertheless estimate headline inflation would have reached 3.9% annually.

The stakes remain high because markets have increasingly priced in another Federal Reserve rate hike. Traders recently assigned an 84% to 85% probability to a December increase, following stronger employment data. The Fed’s benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75% to 4%.

A hotter-than-expected reading could strengthen the case for tighter monetary policy. Higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar would potentially pressure Asian equities, particularly technology companies with valuations sensitive to financing costs.

South Korea’s KOSPI could face the greatest exposure. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are central to the global semiconductor supply chain, making the index particularly sensitive to changes in AI investment sentiment. Both companies helped drive today’s rebound, with their shares rising 5.1% and 6.8%, respectively.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index offers another important benchmark. Its technology-heavy components could face renewed pressure if investors reduce exposure to growth stocks. Singapore’s Straits Times Index provides a useful contrast, given its greater exposure to financial institutions and dividend-paying companies.

A cooler reading could produce the opposite reaction, easing rate concerns and supporting another regional advance.

Bitcoin is trading around $74,600 ahead of the inflation release, leaving it close to a crucial support zone. Our analysts identified the $73,000 level as an important level, with a sustained break potentially exposing $70,000.

A hotter CPI reading could intensify selling pressure as investors reassess interest-rate expectations. Bitcoin’s recent weakness also reflects fading institutional demand, with US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recording $1.28 billion in outflows last week.

A softer inflation report could trigger a relief rally, but it might not guarantee a sustained recovery. Stronger ETF demand and improved liquidity would still be necessary to support a meaningful reversal.

NVIDIA adds another complication. The chipmaker and CEO Jensen Huang is being sued in a proposed shareholder class action filed in California yesterday. Investor Mark Kistenmacher alleges that NVIDIA misled shareholders about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, and Jensen Huang are being sued in a class action lawsuit, accusing ‌them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ties with a suspected Chinese spy.The lawsuit claims that shareholders were misled about Huang's alleged relationship with a woman…

The complaint claims the alleged relationship created reputational and national security risks that investors should have known about. NVIDIA’s board had already announced an independent investigation, while the company had not immediately commented on the lawsuit.

NVIDIA shares fell 4.3% on Monday, erasing $190 billion in market cap. The decline arrived just as Asian semiconductor shares were attempting to recover from last week’s technology-led sell-off.

NVIDIA remains central to the AI investment cycle, and any deterioration in confidence surrounding the company could amplify concerns about semiconductor valuations and the sustainability of AI spending. That could leave Korean chipmakers particularly vulnerable if another inflation shock hits markets.

So, will CPI cause a sell-off? It depends on a few factors. We might need to watch core prices, Treasury yields, and the dollar for clues about the Federal Reserve’s next move. A cooler report could extend the recovery, but a hotter reading may expose how fragile confidence in Asian technology stocks and Bitcoin is.

#5450. From warships to subway cars: 10 U.S. artificial reefs for fishing and diving

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Artificial reef fishing and diving in the U.S. spans sunken warships, retired oil platforms and subway cars — here are 10 places to know about

An aircraft carrier, a missile tracking ship and the steel frames of old oil platforms now sit on the U.S. seafloor. So do retired New York City subway cars. Each one was put there on purpose to give fish something to live on and divers something to explore.

These structures are artificial reefs. The term covers anything deliberately placed on the seabed to create habitat, from sunk ships and retired oil and gas platforms to concrete and quarry rock. Bare sand and mud offer marine life little to hold onto. A hull or a pile of rock adds hard surfaces, crevices and vertical relief where growth can take hold and fish can gather.

The practice has a federal framework. The National Fishing Enhancement Act of 1984 set up a national approach to artificial reef development, and coastal states run their own reef programs within it. Several of the sites below are managed or permitted through state wildlife agencies and reef programs.

For anyone planning a trip around artificial reef fishing and diving in the U.S., the range is wide. The sites in this list stretch from the Florida Panhandle and the Florida Keys to Texas, Louisiana and Alabama in the Gulf of Mexico. They also reach Hawaii, Southern California and the mid-Atlantic coast off Delaware and New Jersey.

The structures vary as much as the locations. Some are former military vessels, including Navy ships and Coast Guard cutters. One is a ship that carried troops and cruise passengers before it became a training vessel. Others are retired oil and gas platforms converted to habitat through programs known as rigs-to-reefs. One set of reefs is made from retired subway cars. One California reef was built from quarry rock and concrete to offset kelp losses rather than mainly for recreation.

Access differs just as much. One of these shipwreck dives sits at a depth reachable by recreational divers. Several others lie in deep water suited to divers with advanced or technical training. Many also draw anglers, who reach them on charter boats from ports such as Pensacola.

What follows is a selection of 10 places, not a ranking and not a complete list. Each slide covers what the structure is, where it sits and who it serves.

The USS Oriskany is a former Navy aircraft carrier that rests on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico roughly 24 miles off Pensacola, Florida. Its deep-water setting makes it a dive for advanced technical divers, while anglers fish above it from charter boats.

The Navy sank the carrier on purpose on May 17, 2006, to turn it into an artificial reef. The ship measures 888 feet long. That length is behind the nickname it often goes by, the "Great Carrier Reef."

Before it became habitat, the Oriskany spent decades in Navy service. It was an Essex-class carrier commissioned in 1950. Its name comes from the Battle of Oriskany, fought in New York in 1777 during the Revolutionary War. The ship served during both the Korean War and the Vietnam War.

The carrier's history includes a deadly accident. In October 1966, a fire broke out aboard the ship off Vietnam and killed 44 crew members. John McCain was flying from the Oriskany when he was shot down over North Vietnam in 1967. The Navy decommissioned the carrier in 1976, three decades before it went to the bottom of the Gulf.

Diving the wreck calls for more than a standard recreational certification. The carrier lies deep enough that divers need technical training and equipment suited to that depth. That puts it out of reach for newer divers who hold only an entry-level certification.

The trip out is part of the commitment. The wreck sits in open Gulf water, well away from any sheltered bay. Every visit starts with a boat run from Pensacola.

Pensacola charter boats run reef fishing trips out to the wreck. Anglers on those trips work the water around the carrier from the deck and never need to get wet.

The site serves two groups with different needs. Technical divers come to see a sunken carrier up close. Anglers come for the fish that gather around its structure.

The USS Vandenberg is a former Air Force missile tracking ship, 523 feet long, that was sunk as an artificial reef on May 27, 2009. It lies about six miles south of Key West in roughly 140 feet of water, and it is a dive for advanced divers.

The sinking ended the ship's working life. Its hull now sits as a fixed structure on the seabed near the southern end of the Florida Keys.

Distance shapes how people reach the wreck. At about six miles offshore, it is a boat dive, not a site anyone can swim to from the beach. Key West is the closest land.

Depth shapes who can dive it. The seabed around the ship sits at roughly 140 feet. That is why the Vandenberg is treated as an advanced dive and not as a site for newly certified divers.

The ship does not lie flat against the bottom. Its structure rises well above the seabed. Divers can explore parts of the wreck that stand far higher in the water column than the sand around its base.

Size places the Vandenberg among other large ships sunk as reefs in Florida. At 523 feet, it is 365 feet shorter than the 888-foot USS Oriskany, the aircraft carrier sunk off Pensacola in 2006. It is 13 feet longer than the 510-foot Spiegel Grove, a Navy landing ship dock sunk off Key Largo in 2002.

The Vandenberg also lies much closer to shore than the Oriskany. It sits about six miles from Key West, while the carrier rests roughly 24 miles off Pensacola.

The Vandenberg was the most recent of those three ships to go down. The Spiegel Grove was sunk seven years earlier, and the Oriskany three years earlier.

The water is also deeper than at the Spiegel Grove, which rests at about 130 feet. The Vandenberg site runs roughly 10 feet deeper.

The Spiegel Grove is a 510-foot former Navy landing ship dock sunk as an artificial reef off Key Largo, Florida, on May 17, 2002. It rests about six miles offshore inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, in about 130 feet of water, and is a dive for advanced divers.

A landing ship dock is built to carry troops, vehicles and landing craft. Its stern holds a well deck that can be flooded, letting smaller boats float in and out of the ship. That design gave the Spiegel Grove a long hull with large open interior spaces.

The sinking did not go as planned. The ship rolled onto its side as it went down and came to rest on its flank rather than upright on the sand. For about three years, divers explored a wreck lying on its side.

Hurricane Dennis changed that in 2005. The storm helped push the hull upright, giving the wreck the orientation its planners had intended. The episode shows that a sunken ship can keep shifting long after it reaches the seafloor, especially in a region exposed to Atlantic hurricanes.

The location adds a layer of rules. The Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary is a federally protected area managed by NOAA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Congress designated it in 1990. Its waters surround the island chain and take in natural coral reefs, seagrass beds and other shipwrecks. Activities inside its boundaries fall under federal sanctuary regulations in addition to Florida state rules.

At about 130 feet, the sand around the wreck sits at the commonly accepted depth limit for recreational scuba. Bottom time there is short before decompression becomes a concern, and nitrogen narcosis is a greater risk. Divers usually arrive with deep-diving training and recent experience.

Key Largo is the northernmost of the main Florida Keys islands. It sits at the top of the chain, which makes it the closest Keys dive hub to the Miami area. Dive boats leave from the island to reach the wreck.

The Duane and Bibb are two retired U.S. Coast Guard cutters sunk as artificial reefs off Key Largo, Florida, on November 27, 1987. The Duane rests in about 120 feet of water and the Bibb in about 130 feet. Both wrecks are dives for advanced divers.

The two ships were sisters. Both belonged to the Coast Guard's Treasury class, also known as the Secretary class. Each cutter in the group was named for a former secretary of the Treasury. The Duane honors William J. Duane, who held the post under President Andrew Jackson. The Bibb honors George M. Bibb, who served as Treasury secretary under President John Tyler.

The Duane measures 327 feet from bow to stern. Cutters of this class were built as long-range patrol and rescue ships. During World War II, both the Duane and the Bibb escorted convoys across the Atlantic. German submarines attacked Allied shipping along those routes.

The cutters went down on the same day but came to rest in different positions. The Duane settled upright on the sandy bottom. The Bibb landed on its side. That difference shapes each dive. The Duane keeps the familiar profile of a ship, with its superstructure rising toward the surface. The Bibb presents its deck and hull as a vertical wall.

Both wrecks lie near Molasses Reef, a natural coral reef off Key Largo. The sites sit inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary. Congress designated that sanctuary in 1990, three years after the cutters were sunk.

Depth is the main planning factor. Both cutters lie well below the 60-foot limit that PADI sets for its entry-level Open Water Diver certification. They also sit deeper than the 100-foot limit tied to PADI's Advanced Open Water Diver course. Divers visiting either wreck need training and gas planning suited to that depth. They also need a charter operator that runs trips to these sites.

The Texas Clipper is a former troop transport, cruise ship and training vessel that now serves as an artificial reef. It rests in roughly 130 feet of Gulf of Mexico water about 17 miles off South Padre Island, Texas.

The ship went down on November 17, 2007. The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department's artificial reef program manages the site.

Every stage of the ship's working life involved carrying people. It entered service with the U.S. Navy as a transport for troops. It later carried vacationers as a cruise ship. Its final role was as a training ship for future merchant mariners at Texas A&M University's maritime academy in Galveston.

South Padre Island sits near the southern tip of the Texas coast, close to the Mexican border. Reaching the reef requires a boat trip across open Gulf water. Offshore weather and sea conditions decide whether a trip can go ahead.

Depth shapes who can dive the site. PADI, one of the largest scuba training agencies, sets 130 feet as the maximum depth for recreational diving. The seabed at the Texas Clipper lies at roughly that depth. At such depths, no-decompression time is short and nitrogen narcosis becomes more likely. A descent to the bottom calls for deep-diving training and careful gas planning.

Upper parts of the hull sit shallower than the seabed. Divers who stay on those sections keep their maximum depth above the sand.

Anglers fish the site too. For them, the wreck is a fixed location that boats can return to with GPS navigation. The Gulf floor off South Texas is largely flat. A ship-sized structure on that bottom stands out as a place where fish concentrate.

The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department is the agency to check for current information on the reef's exact position and any rules that apply to fishing or diving there. The Texas Clipper is one of many sites in the department's artificial reef program along the Texas coast.

Retired oil and gas platforms in the Gulf of Mexico off Texas and Louisiana can stay in the water as artificial reefs instead of being hauled to shore. The approach is called rigs-to-reefs. Both states run formal programs through their wildlife agencies.

The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department oversees the Texas program. The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries runs the Louisiana program. Once a structure joins a state program, that state takes on responsibility for it as a reef site.

An offshore platform stands on a steel frame known as a jacket. The jacket reaches from the seabed up to the surface. When production ends, federal rules generally require operators to remove the structure. Conversion to a reef offers an alternative to full removal.

Three methods are common. In a tow-and-place conversion, the jacket is cut free and moved to a designated reef site. In a topple-in-place conversion, the jacket is laid on its side where it stood. In a partial removal, the upper section is cut away below the surface. The lower framework stays standing, with enough clearance left for passing vessels.

Operators that choose conversion avoid part of the cost of bringing the steel back to shore. The Texas and Louisiana programs each receive a share of those savings. That money helps pay for managing the reef sites.

The steel legs and cross-braces create vertical habitat through much of the water column. Barnacles, sponges and corals settle on the metal. Small fish gather around that growth, and larger predators follow them.

For anglers, converted platforms are a regular destination for charter and private boats. Red snapper and greater amberjack are among the fish commonly associated with Gulf platforms. Divers visit the structures as well, on boats that run out from coastal ports.

Many converted platforms sit well offshore in open water. Reaching them takes a seaworthy vessel and close attention to Gulf weather. The state programs publish coordinates for their reef sites. Those coordinates help boaters locate the structures.

The Mahi is a former U.S. Navy minesweeper resting in about 85 feet of water off the Waianae coast of Oahu, Hawaii. That depth puts it within reach of recreational divers, a contrast with the deeper ship reefs in the Gulf of Mexico and the Florida Keys.

The ship is about 185 feet long. It was sunk on purpose in 1982 to create an artificial reef. Hawaii's Department of Land and Natural Resources, the state agency responsible for the islands' land and ocean resources, was involved in the sinking.

The Waianae coast lines the leeward, western side of Oahu. That shore faces away from the northeast trade winds that dominate the island's weather. The Waianae Range rises behind it, and the leeward side receives far less rain than Oahu's windward coast.

Depth is the main planning question for a visit. Entry-level open water certification from training agencies such as PADI covers dives to about 60 feet. A dive to the Mahi generally calls for advanced certification or equivalent deep-dive training. That is a much smaller step than the technical training needed for a deep wreck such as the USS Oriskany off Pensacola, Florida.

Bottom time is short at this depth. No-decompression limits at about 85 feet are measured in minutes, not hours. Dives on the wreck are planned around that limit and around a controlled ascent. Divers reach the wreck by boat rather than from shore.

The Mahi predates the federal framework for artificial reefs. The ship went down two years before Congress passed the National Fishing Enhancement Act of 1984.

The Mahi is the only Hawaii site and the only Pacific shipwreck in this group of 10. The other ship reefs covered here lie off Florida, Texas and Alabama, in the Gulf of Mexico or the Florida Keys. For divers on Oahu, the wreck is a ship reef within reach without travel to the mainland.

Retired New York City subway cars rest on the seafloor off Delaware and New Jersey. State reef programs placed them there as fish habitat. Anglers reach the sites by boat.

The cars came from the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, the agency that runs New York City's subway. Between 2001 and 2010, the MTA sent retired cars to several states on the East Coast and the Gulf of Mexico for reef building. The Delaware and New Jersey programs are two well-known examples of where those cars ended up. Cars from the same subway system became habitat along more than one U.S. coastline.

The material sets these reefs apart from other well-known U.S. artificial reefs, many of which are decommissioned warships, Coast Guard cutters or retired oil and gas platforms. These reefs are made from mass-transit equipment. Cars that once carried commuters through New York City now sit on the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean.

A subway car is a long steel box. On the seabed, its walls give marine growth somewhere to attach. Its interior and openings give fish places to shelter.

Black sea bass and tautog are among the species anglers target on these reefs. Tautog are also widely known as blackfish. Both species tend to stay close to hard bottom and structure. The cars add that kind of habitat to an offshore seafloor that is largely sand in this part of the Mid-Atlantic. Structure that holds those species gives anglers a specific place to fish.

The program also shows where reef material can come from. The cars were public equipment that had reached the end of their service lives. The MTA sent them to state programs that could put them to use as habitat.

Wheeler North Reef is a man-made reef of quarry rock and concrete off San Clemente, California. Southern California Edison built it to offset kelp losses linked to the San Onofre nuclear plant. That makes it a mitigation project, not a site built mainly for anglers or divers.

The reef takes its name from Wheeler J. North, a California Institute of Technology marine biologist who studied kelp forests. Its goal is different from that of many reef programs, which sink ships or place structures to attract fish and give recreational boats a destination. Wheeler North Reef was designed to replace natural habitat that had been lost.

The habitat in question is kelp forest. Giant kelp, the species that forms these forests off Southern California, needs a hard surface on the seafloor to attach to. It grips rock with a rootlike structure called a holdfast. It cannot take hold on loose sand or mud.

Rock and concrete on the bottom supply that missing anchor. Once kelp attaches, it can grow toward the surface and form a forest. A mature kelp forest provides shelter and food for fish, snails, sea urchins and other marine life.

The power plant behind the project is the San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station. It sits on the coast just south of San Clemente. Kelp losses tied to the plant created the need for replacement habitat.

The structure also differs from the wreck dives elsewhere on the U.S. coast. There is no hull, deck or superstructure to explore. The reef is a spread of rock and concrete meant to support living kelp. The marine life it holds is the main feature, not the structure itself.

California sets fishing rules through the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. Anyone planning to fish or dive near the reef should check current state regulations and any local restrictions before heading out.

Alabama's offshore waters in the Gulf of Mexico hold many permitted artificial reef sites, and reef fishing is a major draw. The attraction is not a single wreck. It is a network of deliberately placed structures spread across designated reef zones off the state's coast.

The Marine Resources Division of the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources runs the state's artificial reef program. The agency oversees where reef material goes and which sites are permitted. Each placement on the seafloor is authorized rather than left to chance.

Some of the older structures in the zones are Liberty ships sunk in the 1970s. Liberty ships were cargo vessels built in large numbers in U.S. shipyards during World War II. They moved war supplies across the Atlantic and Pacific. Decades after the war ended, some of them went to the bottom off Alabama to begin a second life as habitat.

The rest of the zones hold a mix of other deliberately placed material rather than one type of structure. That spread-out model sets Alabama apart from destinations built around one named ship. A boat leaving the Alabama coast is not heading to a single landmark. Its crew can choose among many permitted sites in the same stretch of the Gulf.

Red snapper is the species most closely tied to reef fishing off Alabama. Snapper and many other reef fish stay close to hard structure on the seafloor. Permitted sites give charter crews known locations to target on a trip. Charter fleets run reef trips out of coastal towns such as Orange Beach and Dauphin Island.

Red snapper harvest is limited to set seasons, and those dates can change from year to year. Other species, including grouper and amberjack, have their own rules. Anglers heading out to the reef zones need to check current Alabama and federal regulations for bag limits and open dates before they leave.

#5449. Tech Moves: Fred Hutch leader goes to AWS; Temporal, Augmodo and Neuralwatt name execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 6, 2026 at 10:06 amNovember 6, 2026 at 10:45 am

— Amitabha “Guppy” Gupta, a Fred Hutch Cancer Center associate director who helps researchers translate their work to broader audiences, is leaving after 14 years to join Amazon. Starting Nov. 16, he will be a strategic advisor for nonprofit research and advanced AI with AWS’ Global Nonprofit Business.

Gupta said technology was often an obstacle to scientific breakthroughs at Fred Hutch.

“It’s the infrastructure, data, and tools standing between a scientist and an answer,” he wrote on LinkedIn. In his new role, “I’ll work with researchers and research institutions on using cloud, high-performance computing, and AI to remove those barriers.”

— Microsoft board member ‌Emma Walmsley has been appointed CEO of HP, effective Jan. 4. Walmsley, who led the pharmaceutical giant GSK until December 2025, succeeds Bruce Broussard. Reuters notes that her seven years serving on the Microsoft board “are her closest brush with the tech sector” prior to taking the top job at the PC maker.

— Bas Nijholt, senior staff engineer at IonQ‘s Seattle-area facility, has resigned after three years to join an AI startup that’s still in stealth mode. At IonQ, the theoretical quantum mechanics expert built MindRoom, an open-source collaboration and knowledge-sharing platform that he calls “a company brain.”

“With this new opportunity, I get to keep building and turbocharging MindRoom with a team of people who are just as excited about AI as I am,” Nijholt said, adding that the tool will remain freely available.

Before IonQ, Nijholt spent nearly four years at Microsoft.

— Bellevue, Wash., startup Temporal, whose software keeps AI agents running reliably, has named Sean Heneghan as vice president of sales for the Americas. The company ranks No. 1 on the GeekWire 200, a list of the top Pacific Northwest startups. In September it raised $550 million, putting its valuation at $12.55 billion.

Temporal is fully remote, and Heneghan is based in the Chicago area. He joins the company from MongoDB.

— Doug Heimburger, a 26-year Amazon veteran, has changed roles, shifting from chief financial officer and vice president of Worldwide Operations to CFO/VP of Worldwide Stores. In the new position, Heimburger said he’ll help oversee efforts to improve delivery speed, reduce costs and increase growth of the Stores business. His first role at the company was data mining analyst.

— Seattle startup Augmodo has named Capri Brixey as head of retail sales. The company, which sells AI-powered wearable devices with cameras, raised $21 million in July to expand from in-store applications that let workers passively track inventory into automotive, warehouse and hospital settings. Augmodo ranks No. 122 on the GeekWire 200.

Ross Finman, founder and CEO of Augmodo, called Brixey “the right leader to accelerate our expansion” given her experience selling to both retail and warehouse operations. Her past roles include leadership positions at Coca-Cola and Kroger.

— Meaghan Davison Praznik was named vice president of marketing for Neuralwatt, a Seattle-based startup that built a tool for calculating, in real time, the carbon emissions of individual AI requests. Her former employers include Clif Bar, AllTrails and Merino Energy.

Because the carbon intensity of grid power varies throughout the day and across regions, Neuralwatt’s technology can help customers run compute-intensive operations when clean energy is more abundant.

— BuyWander, an auction-based online marketplace for returned and overstocked retail items, has named Chris Holm as senior director of product. Holm spent nine years at Amazon, leaving in 2024 after managing last-mile and same-day delivery technology and working on Amazon Fresh delivery. He has since served as a consultant for carbon removal startup Lithos Carbon and as a founder-in-residence at the startup studio Foundations.

In August, BuyWander moved its headquarters across Washington from Spokane to Kent. The company announced $21 million in new funding in September.

— T-Mobile’s Kevin Lau has joined the advisory board at the University of Washington’s College of Engineering. Lau has been with the telecom giant for 22 years over two stints and serves as VP of digital experience engineering. He holds bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the UW.

— Christian Smith, an Issaquah, Wash.-based tech leader, has been named president of revenue for Cloudflare, which provides security and speed services for websites and online applications. He will oversee worldwide go-to-market operations. Smith previously served as chief revenue officer for Splunk and Nintex.

Prime Team Partners blends AI-powered recruiting with deep human expertise. GeekWire brings unmatched reach across the tech community. Together, we help employers cut through the noise and hire smarter, faster.

#5448. From subway cars to Civil War ships, 10 sunken objects and the reefs they became

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Ships, subway cars, oil rigs and household junk all become reefs on the seabed. Ten examples show which ones help marine life.

Whatever people lose or leave on the ocean floor becomes a place for something to live, whether anyone meant it to or not. A ship, an oil rig and an old refrigerator all count as hard ground, and much of the seafloor has little of it. Marine life begins to settle on a sunken object from the start. "From the minute it sinks, it starts to form a new habitat underwater," said Avery Paxton, a researcher with NOAA's National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science. Shipwrecks come to hold microbes, algae, corals, sponges, fish and crustaceans, according to NOAA NCCOS. A single hull can end up supporting everything from microscopic life to the animals divers come to see. The same thing happens to a ship lost in a storm and to a ship sunk on purpose, and the difference between accident and plan matters far more to people than to the fish. With nearly any hard object able to turn into habitat, the real choice people face is which objects belong on the bottom.

People usually make the case for artificial reefs in terms of fish, and those who run reef programs say the benefit is real. The Post and Courier reports that Bob Martore, who oversees the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources' artificial reef program, credits the reefs with spreading anglers across more spots and sparing natural reefs from heavy fishing. Yet Paxton says it remains unclear whether the fish on artificial reefs are drawn away from nearby natural habitat or newly produced over time. A busy reef is not proof of a good one. If the fish are only moving from one spot to another, a reef can make them easier to catch without adding to their number. The fairer test is what each object does to the sea around it, and the answer depends on what the object is made of and where it sits.

Smithsonian Ocean set out to show how many different things become homes for marine life on the seabed, including retired New York City subway cars, fridges people toss into the sea, a Navy ship sunk with explosives off the Florida Keys and offshore oil platforms where anglers now find fish. Some went down on purpose and some by accident, and at least one wreck was later hauled back out. Some reefs now arrive with permits and careful cleanup, while others still form from dumping that nobody approves. Each object deserves the same measure: what it left behind on the seafloor.

Many of the ships that now support sea life were never meant to sink. Roughly three million wrecks lie on the seabed, according to Smithsonian Ocean, and marine life thrives on many of them. Nobody chose where those ships would land or planned for fish to move in, yet the habitat formed anyway.

That total counts ships lost, not reefs formed. It takes in every kind of wreck, from warships to small dinghies, and not all of them host reef life. "Many" is the most anyone can honestly say about how often a wreck becomes a thriving reef. The figure shows how often marine life has had a chance to settle on a sunken hull, not how often it actually did.

Whether a wreck helps the water around it is settled at the moment it goes down. Nobody can clean a ship before an accident sinks it, so its fuel, cargo and fittings go to the bottom with it. Fish can gather along a hull while the fuel inside it leaks into the same water. What a wreck leaves on the seafloor depends on what it was built from and what it carried, and in an accident nobody made those choices. That is the whole difference between a wreck and a planned reef. When people sink a ship on purpose, they decide which ship goes down, what gets stripped out first and where it comes to rest.

Building homes for fish began as a fishermen's answer to a poor seabed, long before anyone engineered a reef. Fishermen in South Carolina were sinking log huts in the 1830s to raise their catches, Smithsonian Ocean reports, and the seafloor they fished explains why the work seemed worth the effort. In 2021, Scott Whitaker, executive director of CCA South Carolina, put the share of sand on the seabed off the state at 90%, according to The Post and Courier. On a bottom that is almost all sand, hard structure is rare, and a pile of logs could look like a real way to change a day's haul. The huts were built on purpose, while most of what reached the seabed got there by accident. Their aim was narrow, and it never reached past more fish for the people who built them.

For generations, reef-building off South Carolina was something fishermen did on their own, and the state started its artificial reef program only in 1973, according to The Post and Courier. By 2021, South Carolina had approved 43 locations for reefs, so the state rather than a lone angler had signed off on each one. A permit means someone other than the builder decides where a reef goes and what it is made of. The log huts never faced that check.

The sandy coast that made logs worth sinking also sets a hard bar for anything meant to stay in place. "Couple that with hurricanes, big storms, heavy currents and big tides, and you need a substantial structure to make a big impact and have any kind of longevity," Whitaker told The Post and Courier in 2021. Reef builders have changed what they sink since the 1830s, even though their reason for sinking it has stayed the same. In 2021, Bob Martore, who runs the state's reef program, said both the kinds of material going into the water and how good that material is had shifted over time.

The fishermen had the right idea, which was to put hard ground where there was none. Later builders added the durability and oversight to make that idea last on a coast this rough.

Offshore platforms went up to pump oil and gas, yet anglers came to prize them for another reason. As oil and gas drilling spread offshore, the platforms became fishing hotspots, according to Smithsonian Ocean. Lawmakers from both parties now want to keep more of that fishing ground in place. E&E News reports that a House bill, H.R. 5745, the Marine Fisheries Habitat Protection Act, would keep retired platforms in the water as reefs. Democrats make up four of the bill's five co-sponsors, and its sponsor is a Republican. A House panel has taken up the measure, which remains a proposal rather than law.

The bill's sponsor pitches retired rigs as a gain for more than fish. "Instead of tearing down structures that have become vibrant marine ecosystems, we can repurpose them to benefit the environment, fishermen, and taxpayers alike," Rep. Mike Ezell, R-Miss., told E&E News. Ezell names taxpayers alongside the environment and fishermen, which makes fish habitat one benefit among several in his pitch rather than its sole aim. With motives that mixed, the outcome for the sea deserves a closer look than the pitch gives it.

The idea that rigs help fish rests on assertion rather than measurement. Ezell's view of fishing near the platforms comes from advocacy and personal experience, not from a study. Good fishing beside a platform shows that fish gather there, but it does not show what the steel does for the sea over the years it stays in place.

Until someone measures the steel's long-term effect on the sea, support for the bill rests on how the fishing looks beside the rigs.

Some reefs begin when someone throws away things they no longer want, with no permit and no plan. Smithsonian Ocean reports that individuals dump fridges, shopping carts and car frames into the sea, creating unsanctioned reefs full of fish and coral. Nobody approved those sites or answers for what happens on them, and marine life settles on them anyway. The same kind of household gear turns up on the other side of the world. In 2017, prawn trawlers off Queensland, Australia, hauled up stoves, tool boxes, outdoor furniture and buckets of cement, according to ABC News. None of these objects was made to serve as a reef, whoever put them there.

A sunken fridge is a reef or a menace depending on who works the water above it. Queensland's trawling grounds are mud and sand, according to ABC News, and crews drag their nets across that soft, open floor. Any heavy object there can catch a net. "I call them amateur bombs now," Peter Nebe-Kerridge, a prawn trawler fisherman in far north Queensland, said. Junk works as fish habitat because it is hard and stays in place, and those same qualities make it a hazard to anyone fishing that bottom.

Off Queensland, the question of who dumped the junk and why remains open. In 2017, trawler crews made allegations about who was responsible, according to ABC News, and John Robinson of Sunfish Queensland says those allegations were not substantiated. Robinson also finds it hard to picture anyone dumping on trawled mud and sand, where he says nobody would come out ahead. A pile of junk on the seabed proves only that someone dumped it.

In law, this is dumping, not reef-building. In 2017, individuals who dumped illegally at sea faced fines of up to $50,000, according to ABC News. A fine deters only people who expect to be caught. Elaine Lewthwaite, a prawn trawler operator, doubts that authorities can watch every private boat on the coast unless those boats carry the same vessel tracking system that trawlers do.

A reef that nobody permits is also a reef that nobody monitors, and it can shelter fish while it snags the next crew's nets.

The Duane became a reef because people chose it, not because of a storm or a dumping run. Someone picked the ship and picked the place to put it down. The vessel was deliberately sunk after fifty years at sea, according to Smithsonian Ocean, so its end was planned rather than left to chance. The National Park Service reports that the wreck lies inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, so the reef rests in protected waters. The ship's working life went down with it. Crews aboard the Duane took part in four rescues at sea and picked up 346 survivors. The hull that marine life now covers once helped pull people out of the sea. The sinking added more than hard ground to the seafloor. It turned a service record into a place people can visit.

The Duane is a reef for trained divers rather than casual swimmers. Even the top of its mast sits 60 feet below the surface, according to the National Park Service, far beyond a snorkeler's reach. Thousands of people make the dive each year anyway, so divers and fish use the same structure. Avery Paxton, a researcher at NOAA's National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science, says artificial reefs can serve fish extremely well as habitat. The Duane adds a steady stream of visitors to that benefit. Judged by what it left on the seafloor, this planned sinking pays off in three ways: as habitat, as a destination and as a piece of history kept in view rather than scrapped.

A ship that once picked survivors out of the water now gives fish a home and thousands of divers a reason to visit.

The Hoyt S. Vandenberg was placed on the seafloor on purpose, inside waters set aside to protect the ocean. The retired Navy transport ship was sunk with explosives in 2009 within the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, according to Smithsonian Ocean. A protected area usually works by keeping things out, but here protection meant putting a whole ship in. The goal was to spare the sanctuary's living coral by giving visitors somewhere else to go. Joe Weatherby, the project organizer at Reefmakers, told The Associated Press that the ship was "giving the reef a breather, which is what it needs." The Vandenberg is one of 61 artificial reefs in the sanctuary, which shows that building reefs on purpose is a regular part of managing these waters.

Most of the work of turning the Vandenberg into a reef took place above water, in making the ship safe to sink. The project cost about $8.6 million from the purchase of the ship through its cleanup, according to The Associated Press, and that cleanup meant hauling 193 tons of material that could potentially cause cancer off the ship before it went into the sanctuary in 2009. Without that work, all of that material would have gone to the bottom inside the hull. The price therefore reflects the preparation of the ship and not only the sinking. The Vandenberg is reef-building as an engineered public project, with millions spent to give the seafloor new habitat without the ship's toxins.

The people who backed the project measured its return in visitors as well as in fish. Officials in 2009 expected the reef to bring in up to $8 million a year from tourism, according to The Associated Press. That figure was a forecast, not a measured result. The case for marine life also rests on potential, since Avery Paxton, a researcher with NOAA's National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science, says artificial reefs are capable of giving fish an excellent home. The Vandenberg's value therefore rests on two hopes, one for divers' spending and one for the life that settles on the ship.

The Vandenberg should be judged as a dive destination that keeps visitors off fragile coral as much as a home for fish, and its success will show up in visitor counts as well as in the water.

When New York City retired a generation of subway cars, thousands of them went to the bottom of the ocean instead of to a scrapyard. More than 2,500 of the cleaned, retired cars were sunk along the Atlantic coast from 2001 to 2010, according to Smithsonian Ocean. Delaware took a large share, and CBC Radio reports that New York donated more than 600 of the cars to that state in 2001 alone. Delaware wanted the cars because its own waters offered fish so little.

The seabed off Delaware gives fish little natural shelter. CBC Radio reports that Jeffrey Tinsman, project manager for Delaware's artificial reefs, considers the mid-Atlantic poorly supplied with habitat. The cars went down onto a sandy bottom, and their value begins with that placement. Hard structure does the most for fish where the seafloor has almost none of its own.

The cars were cleaned before they were sunk, and marine life settled on their frames. On the reefs off Delaware, a blue mussel community supports a food web that sand alone cannot. "There are about 30 or 40 other species of invertebrates, shrimp, crabs and worms and so forth, that are all associated with that blue mussel community. And in total, there's about 400 times as much food for fish per square foot as there is in the natural sand bottom," Tinsman told CBC Radio. A food supply on that scale is stronger evidence of benefit than a crowd of fish. A reef where food grows does more for the sea than gather fish in one place, even if it does not prove the water holds more fish overall.

Subway cars are only one of the materials Delaware has sunk, and concrete is another. Tinsman says an automobile body that rusts away quickly costs as much to place as concrete that lasts for centuries. Reef managers judge a material by how long it keeps working, not by how interesting it is.

By that measure, the worth of a subway car on the seafloor depends on how long its frame holds up, not on the years it spent carrying New York riders.

The reef off Key Largo, Fla., began with a towing accident rather than a plan. The SS City of Washington spent years hauling passengers and cargo, went down off the island in 1917 and today gives fish a place to live, according to Smithsonian Ocean. By its last voyage the ship no longer carried passengers. NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary reports that it was a coal barge, towed by the tug Luckenbach #4, when it ran aground. Its cabins and steam machinery had been removed when it was converted to a barge in 1911, so the ship that reached the seafloor was already stripped of much of what it once held. No one put it there for marine life, and fish settled on it anyway.

More than a century after the grounding, the wreck's condition is on record rather than left to guesswork. A 3D model of the site was built from photographs taken on June 1, 2017, according to NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary. The iron hull rests in shallow water, at a depth of 25 feet. The sanctuary lists the wreck on the Florida Keys Shipwreck Trail. That listing gives the City of Washington value as a historic site in addition to its value as a home for fish.

The City of Washington became a reef through bad luck and through no one's effort. It now serves both as fish habitat and as a documented piece of maritime history. A wreck that nobody chose to sink can still leave something useful on the seafloor.

Some objects that land on a reef make the seafloor worse. Smithsonian Ocean blames a harmful "black reef" at Palmyra Atoll on the iron chains of a ship that ran aground there in 1991. The wreck was removed in 2013. The harm fell on a protected reef, because Palmyra Atoll, south of Hawaii, is a U.S. National Wildlife Refuge. Nobody chose to sink anything there. The wreck earns its place here for the damage that grew around it, not for any fish it attracted.

The black reef was a local animal that grew out of control. The corallimorphs that covered the coral around the wreck belong to a species native to the atoll, according to a 2020 report in the Honolulu Star-Advertiser. The same report described corallimorphs as animals that settle in disturbed areas of reef and then dominate them. A ship crashing onto living coral creates exactly that kind of disturbance. In 2020, iron leaching from the hull was only one theory for the spread and not a confirmed cause, even though Smithsonian Ocean pins the black reef on iron from the ship's chains. The firmer lesson concerns placement. Dropping anything heavy onto a healthy reef can start a takeover that nobody planned.

Removing the wreck helped the spot where it had lain. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service led a multimillion-dollar project to haul the ship away. Afterward, corallimorph growth near the ship site greatly slowed, according to a 2020 report in the Honolulu Star-Advertiser. Elsewhere on the atoll the growth increased, and the outbreak did not end when the ship left.

Sailors have sunk objects on purpose to stop ships, not only to give fish a home. Smithsonian Ocean reports that Roman and Persian sailors sank objects to trap or divert enemy ships. They acted for naval strategy rather than to attract fish. These sinkings should be judged by the result their builders wanted, and that result was a blocked passage for the enemy. The fair question is whether the tactic ever delivered it.

The Union still trusted the tactic enough during the Civil War to commit a whole fleet to it. It bought dozens of vessels, called the Stone Fleet, for the purpose of scuttling them off Charleston, S.C., according to the Post and Courier. The barrier did not hold. James Spirek, an underwater archaeologist at the University of South Carolina Institute of Archaeology and Anthropology, says blockade runners got past the obstructions with little change of course once the ships broke apart. The Union paid for a fleet to block a harbor and got scattered wreckage instead.

The failed barrier still matters off Charleston, because the wrecks now count as a piece of history. Isle of Palms, S.C., is spending $32 million to renourish its beach with sand taken from an offshore site, according to the Post and Courier. Patrick Barrineau, who works in coastal science with CSE, considers the wrecks a cultural resource. The project was once barred from that entire stretch of seabed, Barrineau says, and his team now coordinates with the state's historic preservation office so the sand work can go ahead while leaving the wreck sites alone.

Union sailors sank those ships to close a harbor, and coastal planners still have to work around them more than 150 years later.

#5447. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

Avalanche (AVAX) climbed on Tuesday after the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) selected its blockchain technology to power settlement for a new tokenized securities platform. The move gives Avalanche a significant role in Wall Street’s push toward blockchain-based financial infrastructure.

AVAX price reached $8.60, gaining 5.2% over 24 hours. The token had climbed as high as $8.99, putting the psychological $9 resistance level back within reach.

Investors could eventually trade tokenized US stocks and exchange-traded funds outside traditional market hours.

Avalanche will provide the underlying blockchain infrastructure through a dedicated network built around institutional requirements. Meanwhile, NYSE will retain its existing Pillar matching engine to process buy and sell orders.

The announcement shows Avalanche’s growing appeal among traditional financial institutions seeking faster and more flexible settlement infrastructure.

The timing is particularly interesting as Wall Street increasingly explores tokenization. Nasdaq is developing its own tokenized securities infrastructure, while the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) is advancing blockchain-based settlement initiatives.

NYSE’s decision gives Avalanche a prominent position in that competition. The exchange operates one of the world’s largest stock markets, making the partnership a significant endorsement of Avalanche’s technology.

AVAX price is approaching a critical technical level after yesterday’s explosive rally. The token climbed from an intraday low near $7.82 toward $8.99, putting $9 within striking distance. A decisive breakout could open the door toward $9.10, the next resistance area.

Trading volume provides another encouraging signal. The sharp increase suggests renewed interest in AVAX as investors react to the NYSE announcement. If buyers maintain momentum above $9, Avalanche could extend its recovery toward higher resistance levels. Conversely, $8 remains the first important psychological support if traders take profits.

The rally also arrives as Avalanche works to strengthen its position in institutional finance. Its blockchain infrastructure is increasingly competing for attention alongside established networks seeking to capture the growing tokenized asset market.

The NYSE announcement gives that narrative considerable weight. Rather than simply attracting another crypto partnership, Avalanche has secured a role in the infrastructure plans of a major traditional stock exchange.
