#5445. 8 Florida artificial reef dives, from the SS United States to the Keys

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These eight Florida artificial reef dives range from sunken Navy ships and Coast Guard cutters to a memorial reef and the planned SS United States reef off Destin

The ocean liner that set a transatlantic speed record on its 1952 maiden voyage is slated to spend its next chapter underwater off Florida's Panhandle. The SS United States, a 990-foot ship, left passenger service in 1969. It then spent decades tied up at a pier in Philadelphia while preservation groups searched for a way to save it. In 2024, Okaloosa County, Florida, agreed to acquire the vessel and sink it as an artificial reef off the Destin–Fort Walton Beach area.

The ship left Philadelphia under tow in February 2025, bound for Mobile, Alabama. Crews there were to clean it and prepare it for sinking. The county intends the liner to serve as habitat for fish and coral and as a draw for visiting divers.

Florida has used retired ships this way for decades. The state's artificial reef program is run by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission in partnership with coastal counties and cities. It places steel, concrete and decommissioned vessels on the seafloor. Hard structure gives corals, sponges and algae a surface to grow on. That growth draws small fish, which in turn attract larger predators. Before any ship goes down, it must be stripped of fuel, oils and other contaminants so it does not pollute the surrounding water.

For divers, the result is a set of Florida artificial reef dives that combine marine life with naval and maritime history. Former military ships, Coast Guard cutters and a cargo freighter now rest off Pensacola, Key Largo, Islamorada, Key West and Southwest Florida. One reef off Key Biscayne was built as an underwater memorial rather than from a ship. Some sites sit within recreational diving limits. Others reach depths suited to divers with advanced training.

This list covers eight of those sites. It opens with the SS United States, a planned reef that has not had decades to collect marine growth the way the older wrecks have. The rest are established sites. They include the aircraft carrier USS Oriskany off Pensacola and the USS Spiegel Grove off Key Largo. The Coast Guard cutters Duane and Bibb sit nearby, also off Key Largo. Farther south are the freighter Eagle off Islamorada and the USNS General Hoyt S. Vandenberg off Key West. The list also includes the USCGC Mohawk in Southwest Florida's Gulf waters and the Neptune Memorial Reef off Key Biscayne.

The SS United States, a 990-foot ocean liner built in the early 1950s, is slated to become an artificial reef in the Gulf off Florida's Panhandle, near Destin and Fort Walton Beach. Okaloosa County plans to sink the hull as a dive site and a habitat for marine life.

The liner was built at Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia to a design by naval architect William Francis Gibbs. It entered service in 1952. On its maiden voyage, it took the Blue Riband for the fastest Atlantic crossing from the Cunard liner Queen Mary. The eastbound run lasted three days, 10 hours and 42 minutes, at an average speed of 35.59 knots.

Cold War priorities shaped the design. The U.S. Navy helped fund construction on the condition that the liner could be converted into a troop transport if needed. Gibbs also kept wood aboard to a minimum as a fire-safety measure. Much of the furniture and fittings were made of metal instead.

Jet airliners took over most transatlantic passenger travel during the 1960s, and the liner's commercial career ended before the decade was out. It then passed through several owners over the following decades. Its interiors were stripped, and a series of redevelopment plans failed to return it to sea.

From 1996, the ship sat at Pier 82 on the Delaware River in Philadelphia. The SS United States Conservancy, a nonprofit, bought it in 2011 and searched for a new use. A rent dispute with the pier's owner ended in a 2024 federal court ruling that the ship had to leave its berth. The Okaloosa County agreement followed later that year.

Cleanup in Mobile, Alabama, follows national best-management-practices guidance issued in 2006 by the Environmental Protection Agency and the Maritime Administration. The document applies to vessels sunk as reefs anywhere in U.S. waters, not only in Florida.

The Associated Press has reported on the ship's conversion into a reef. Divers cannot visit the wreck until it reaches the seafloor. The final depth, the site's distance from shore and the deployment date are details to confirm with Okaloosa County before planning a trip.

The USS Oriskany is a retired U.S. Navy aircraft carrier that was sunk as an artificial reef in the Gulf, about 24 miles southeast of Pensacola, in May 2006. Divers call it the Great Carrier Reef. It is the largest ship ever deliberately sunk to create a reef.

The Oriskany began as an Essex-class carrier at the New York Naval Shipyard, where construction started in 1944. World War II ended before the ship was finished, and work on it was suspended in 1947. The Navy later completed it to an updated design and commissioned it in 1950. It never saw action in the war it was built for.

Its combat record came later. The carrier launched aircraft during the Korean War and again during the Vietnam War. In October 1966, a fire broke out aboard while the ship operated in the Gulf of Tonkin. The fire killed 44 crew members. A year later, Navy pilot John McCain was flying from the Oriskany when he was shot down over Hanoi. He was taken prisoner. The Navy decommissioned the ship in 1976.

The carrier spent the following decades out of service before it was chosen for reef duty. On the day of the sinking, explosive charges sent it to the bottom in about 37 minutes.

The Oriskany came to rest upright on a sandy bottom in roughly 212 feet of water. The top of its island, the command tower that rises above the flight deck, sits about 80 feet below the surface. The flight deck lies near 135 feet.

That vertical profile shapes who can dive it. Divers with advanced recreational certification generally stay on the upper island structure. Reaching the flight deck and the hull below it calls for technical dive training and planned decompression stops.

The wreck sits in open water well offshore. Current and visibility can change from one day to the next, and trips depend on sea conditions.

The steel hull now supports fish common to the northern Gulf, including red snapper, greater amberjack, gag grouper and barracuda. Sponges and corals have also settled on the superstructure since the sinking. The wreck adds tall structure to a stretch of seafloor that is mostly flat sand.

The USS Spiegel Grove is a former U.S. Navy dock landing ship that was sunk off Key Largo in 2002 to create an artificial reef. It came to rest on its side after a troubled sinking. Hurricane Dennis pushed the hull upright in 2005, leaving it in the position divers explore today.

The ship was built for amphibious operations. Dock landing ships carry landing craft in a floodable well deck at the stern. That design lets troops and vehicles move from ship to shore. The Spiegel Grove served the Navy from the mid-1950s until it was decommissioned in 1989. Its name comes from Spiegel Grove, the Fremont, Ohio, estate of President Rutherford B. Hayes.

The vessel is 510 feet long. Its sinking did not go to plan. The hull flooded earlier than expected and settled upside down, with its bow still above the surface. Salvage crews then worked the wreck down to the seafloor, where it came to rest on its starboard side.

That position held for about three years. During that period, divers swam along decks that ran vertically and through passageways turned on their edge. When Hurricane Dennis passed through the region, the storm's surge and currents shifted the hull until it sat upright on the sand.

The righting changed the dive. The decks, superstructure and cranes now sit as the shipbuilders intended. That orientation makes it simpler for divers to track where they are on a structure of this size.

The wreck lies within the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, the federal marine protected area that covers the waters around the island chain. Dive boats tie into mooring buoys attached to the wreck rather than dropping anchor on it.

The Spiegel Grove is a deep dive by recreational standards, and currents across the site can run strong. Divers need to plan their air supply and bottom time around both. Entering the interior is a separate skill that calls for wreck penetration training and suitable equipment.

After more than two decades on the bottom, the hull carries a growth of sponges and corals. Schools of fish gather around the superstructure. Goliath grouper and barracuda are among the larger species seen at the site.

The USNS General Hoyt S. Vandenberg is a retired military tracking ship that was scuttled about seven miles south of Key West on May 27, 2009. At more than 500 feet long, it gives divers in the lower Florida Keys a large steel wreck with depths suited to several levels of training.

The vessel began as something else. It was built during World War II as a troop transport and served under the name General Harry Taylor. The Navy commissioned it in 1944. Its job then was moving service members.

Its second career began in the early 1960s, when the U.S. Air Force took it over. The ship was renamed for Gen. Hoyt S. Vandenberg, the second chief of staff of the U.S. Air Force. Crews fitted it with tracking equipment to follow missile and spacecraft launches from Cape Canaveral. That work tied the ship to the early U.S. space program.

After its military service ended, the ship sat for years in the reserve fleet on Virginia's James River. It also appeared on screen. The 1999 science fiction film Virus used it as a setting, with the hull repainted under a fictional Russian name.

The wreck now sits upright on a sandy bottom in about 140 feet of water. Its upper decks and superstructure rise well above the seafloor. That layout lets recreational divers explore the top of the ship without going to full depth. The lower hull and any interior penetration call for advanced or technical training.

The site lies within the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, which covers the waters around the island chain. Mooring buoys over the wreck let boats tie up without dropping anchor on the structure. Currents can run across the site, and divers commonly descend and ascend on lines tied to the ship. Barracuda, grouper and other fish have moved onto the hull since the sinking.

The Duane and the Bibb are two retired U.S. Coast Guard cutters that were sunk as artificial reefs off Key Largo in November 1987. They lie near Molasses Reef in deep water with strong currents. Depth and current make both of them dives for advanced, experienced divers.

The two ships are sisters from the Coast Guard's 327-foot Treasury class. The class was named for former secretaries of the Treasury. The Duane entered service as the William J. Duane, and the Bibb as the George M. Bibb. Both names were later shortened.

Their wartime records overlap. Both cutters escorted Allied convoys across the North Atlantic during World War II. In 1943, the Bibb rescued survivors of the torpedoed troop transport Henry R. Mallory. In 1944, the Duane served as a flagship during Operation Dragoon, the Allied landings in southern France.

The Coast Guard decommissioned the pair in 1985. Two years later, they were scuttled a short distance apart. The site now falls within the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary.

The two dives differ mainly in how each hull landed. The Duane settled upright on a sand bottom at about 120 feet. That posture lets divers follow the deck, the bridge and the mast in a layout that still resembles a working ship.

The Bibb came to rest on its starboard side in about 130 feet. Its exposed port hull and sideways deck give it a different profile from its sister. Divers breathing standard air get limited bottom time at those depths. Many visitors see only part of either wreck on a single descent.

Currents are the other defining factor. Boats typically tie into mooring buoys. Divers then descend and ascend along the line rather than swimming freely in open water. Entering the interior of either cutter requires specialized wreck-penetration training.

Decades underwater have coated both hulls in corals and sponges. Barracuda, schools of jacks and large groupers are common sights around the superstructures.

The USCGC Mohawk is a World War II Coast Guard cutter resting on the Gulf floor off Lee County in Southwest Florida. Lee County sank it in 2012 as an artificial reef and dedicated the site to the veterans of that war.

The cutter was commissioned in 1935. It belonged to the Algonquin class, a group of six cutters the Coast Guard built in the mid-1930s. Each measured 165 feet, far shorter than the aircraft carrier and ocean liner behind Florida's largest reef projects.

During World War II, the Mohawk served on the Greenland Patrol. The patrol guarded Greenland, which the U.S. agreed to defend in 1941 while Denmark was under German occupation. The Mohawk also escorted convoys across the North Atlantic, the supply route between North America and Europe that German submarines targeted throughout the war.

That service is the basis for the reef's memorial role. A dive on the Mohawk doubles as a visit to a veterans memorial.

The Coast Guard decommissioned the cutter in 1948. It later spent years as a museum ship on the Key West waterfront. Its final assignment moved it north from the Keys to the waters off Lee County.

Lee County sits on Florida's southwest coast and includes Fort Myers Beach, Sanibel and Captiva. The Mohawk lies offshore in open Gulf water. Divers reach it by charter boat rather than from the beach.

Much of the Gulf seabed off Southwest Florida is flat sand and limestone. The Mohawk's steel hull rises from that bottom as hard vertical structure. On an otherwise open plain, it gives fish and invertebrates a fixed place to gather and settle.

Among the eight dives in this selection, the Mohawk is the only one off Florida's southwest coast. It pairs a Gulf Coast location with an Atlantic convoy history. That puts a World War II wreck within boat range of the Fort Myers area.

Neptune Memorial Reef is an underwater memorial site in the Atlantic off Key Biscayne, near Miami, where cremated remains are mixed into concrete and set into the reef's structures. Work on it began in 2007. The site works as both a burial place and an artificial reef open to recreational divers.

The reef lies about 3.25 miles east of Key Biscayne, on the seafloor roughly 40 feet down. That depth sits within the 60-foot limit that training agencies such as PADI set for divers with entry-level open water certification.

Its structures were cast and lowered to the seabed rather than sunk as a whole vessel. There are no enclosed decks, hatches or passageways to penetrate. Divers stay in open water, moving around and between the pieces.

Miami artist Kim Brandell designed the layout around the legend of Atlantis, the lost island Plato described. Columns, archways, gates and sculpted figures are arranged to suggest the ruins of a sunken city. The result looks more like an underwater sculpture garden than a shipwreck.

Each memorial placement holds the remains of a person whose ashes were combined with cement to form part of the structure. Plaques mark the individuals memorialized. Families can visit the site by boat, and those who dive can see the placements in person. The reef was designed to keep expanding as new placements are added over time.

Over time, the concrete has picked up encrusting growth. Reef fish now gather around the columns and arches.

For divers, the draw is the sculpture and the memorial plaques, along with the marine life settling on them. The shallow depth also allows longer no-decompression time than deeper wrecks do.

The site's location off Key Biscayne puts it a short boat ride from Miami. Reaching the Keys wrecks farther south means a drive down the Overseas Highway before the boat trip begins.

The Eagle is a cargo freighter that was sunk on purpose off Islamorada in 1985 to create an artificial reef in the Florida Keys. Hurricane Georges split its hull in two in 1998. Divers today visit a wreck that lies in two separate sections.

Islamorada is a village in the Upper Keys of Monroe County. It sits along the Overseas Highway between Key Largo to the north and Marathon $MPC to the south. Its offshore waters lie inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a federal marine protected area managed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Sanctuary rules cover the wrecks within its boundaries as well as the natural coral reefs. Those rules bar divers from taking or damaging coral.

Congress designated the sanctuary in 1990, five years after the Eagle went down. The freighter was already on the bottom when those federal protections took effect.

The Eagle has been on the seafloor longer than several other Keys wrecks. It reached the bottom 17 years before the Spiegel Grove was scuttled off Key Largo. It also predates the Coast Guard cutters Duane and Bibb by two years. Among the Keys ships on this list, the Eagle has spent the most time on the bottom.

Hurricane Georges crossed the Florida Keys in late September 1998 and made landfall near Key West. The storm broke the Eagle apart 13 years after the ship was placed on the bottom. The two pieces now rest near each other. Divers who visited before 1998 saw a single intact hull. Divers today move between two sections. The break shows that a sunken ship keeps changing after it is placed. A strong hurricane can still reshape steel lying well below the surface.

The Eagle sits on the Atlantic side of the Keys, where the Florida Current runs offshore. The Florida Current is part of the Gulf Stream system that carries warm water north along the U.S. East Coast. That current can push water across deeper sites. Conditions change from day to day.

#5444. Nvidia board’s idolatry of Jensen Huang could open the door to shareholder lawsuits in Delaware Chancery Court

There is no doubt that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang is a visionary genius, whose vision as the ‘Godfather of AI’ has improved billions of lives around the world and contributed greatly to American prosperity and innovation. He has attended our Yale CEO forums and has been revered by CEOs across sectors and around the world for his bold, entrepreneurial vision and his revolutionary technological triumphs, plus he is a showcased contributor to our new, upcoming book, When Machines Act: The Promise and Perils of our Agentic AI Future, published by MIT Press and written with Two Sigma Co-Founder David Siegel.

Yet, amid calls for Huang’s immediate resignation from top GOP voices, including Sen. Kevin Cramer of the Senate Banking Committee and others, and demands that he answer to Congress, there were some blatant red flags in Huang’s recent leadership that were apparently missed by the Nvidia board.

In October 2025, the New York Times reported that Megaspeed, a little-known Singapore firm, had bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips amid suspicion that it was helping China evade U.S. restrictions by laundering banned chips on the U.S. export restriction list to China via neutral countries. Nvidia said a review found no evidence its chips were diverted, but that reporting was followed by an explosive report by a short seller, Culper Research, alleging “uncomfortably close ties” between Alice Huang, the head of Megaspeed, and Jensen Huang, in May 2026. Jensen described the Megaspeed dealings as normal, and apparently the Nvidia board was content to leave it at that.

Late last month, the Times reported that U.S. intelligence believed that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset. A company spokesperson said the diversion claims had been debunked and described the relationship as nothing unusual. Ten days later, Jensen admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, in a message that referred to the national security concerns in the press – a troubling sequence of events after all the repeated denials.

The Caremark doctrine, established in 1996 in Delaware Chancery Court, establishes that corporate directors have a fiduciary duty of oversight, and that directors breach their duty of loyalty when they make no good-faith effort to monitor the risks central to the business, or when they consciously ignore red flags.

Under this doctrine, and derivative variants of it, several boards have run into trouble in Delaware Chancery Court for similar sins of omission when it comes to oversight. In 2019, Delaware’s Supreme Court revived a suit against the directors of Blue Bell Creameries, an ice cream maker whose board had no system for overseeing food safety before a deadly listeria outbreak. In 2021, the Court of Chancery let claims proceed against Boeing’s directors, who had no board committee responsible for airplane safety before the 737 MAX crashes. That case settled for $237.5 million. The lesson of both: on risks that can sink the company, the board must watch for itself: the board cannot simply trust management, even when those risks were unforeseeable or unanticipated.

So plaintiffs’ lawyers will ask the questions directors should have asked many months ago. Who conducted the review that cleared Megaspeed? Did it report to independent directors or to management? Did any director know the CEO had a personal relationship with an executive of the customer under review? Did the board ever discuss Megaspeed at all, or Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang? Did any board members even care to ask any questions about these topics?

The answers are in the board meeting minutes, and alarmingly for Nvidia’s board, shareholders can now get those minutes with nearly complete transparency. Nvidia knows this better than most companies for a very ironic reason. In 2022, it fought a books-and-records demand all the way to Delaware’s Supreme Court. Even after Delaware narrowed those inspection rights last year, board minutes and board materials remain within reach for plaintiffs litigation. That is how the Boeing plaintiffs built their case.

All of the major risks that have now landed on Nvidia in such dramatic fashion were exactly the risks directors should have been most alert to.

First, and most importantly, every board entrusted with protecting minority shareholders should be alert to management conflicts of interest. A Megaspeed affiliate bought about $4.8 billion of Nvidia-powered equipment in under two years. A chief executive in a personal relationship with an executive of a customer that size has an apparent conflict that Nvidia’s own code of conduct would have likely required him to disclose. And Megaspeed was no ordinary customer: by October 2025 both Washington and Singapore were investigating it.

That conflict poisons the compliance record. When the questions first surfaced, Nvidia said it had visited Megaspeed’s sites and had no reason to believe chips were diverted. That assurance came from people who report to a CEO with a personal tie to the customer being cleared, a tie no investor had been told about. Bloomberg reports that Nvidia’s general counsel went so far as to contact a senior Commerce Department official about the government’s Megaspeed probe. Did the board authorize that call? Did it even know?

Then comes national security and export-control evasion, as “mission critical” a risk as food safety at an ice cream maker or flight safety at Boeing. Nvidia makes the most strategically sensitive product on earth; and The Information reported today that companies tied to Alice Huang helped Chinese buyers obtain $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips, including banned ones that were laundered through neutral parties. That report is unconfirmed, and Megaspeed denies wrongdoing. But the penalties for export violations run from fines to criminal prosecution to the loss of export privileges, and a board should not have been waiting for verdicts before it starts asking questions. According to Nvidia’s own proxy statement, the board committee responsible for trade compliance met three times last fiscal year, and the company has no chief compliance officer. How much did they know, and when?

The national security risk is larger still. According to the Times, U.S. officials concluded that Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to get close to Jensen and to shape his views on chip sales to China – which of course, Jensen Huang has been very vocal on in Washington and in the media, arguing that the U.S. should continue to sell chips to China so that China is not building their own chips. No one has alleged that Jensen knew Huang was a spy, and Beijing calls the claims a smear. But the president was reportedly briefed in late 2025, and a secret memo circulated among policymakers this spring, the same year Jensen was appointed to the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Now three House committee chairmen want him in a closed-door briefing, and the president says the FBI is reviewing the matter. Yet not one Nvidia director, as Semafor noted, has a national security background; what questions were asked and what prudent diligence steps were taken by the board?

Then there is the risk every board dreads: that management did not tell it the truth. On Oct. 29, a company spokesman described Jensen’s interactions with Alice Huang as “not unusual or unexpected,” the routine customer contact of any CEO. The same week, Jensen called the Megaspeed dealings normal. Nine days after that he told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, and tied the admission to the national security concerns in the press. If directors approved those October statements knowing what Jensen knew, they could be in trouble. If they never asked him, that is the Caremark problem.

Shareholders have already paid. Nvidia closed today at $168.89, down almost 10% in the two sessions since the admission, a loss of more than $400 billion in market value, and about 30% below its early-October record. Nobody can attribute this recent fall merely to just the AI sell-off, as the evidence shows it was an idiosyncratic move. On Monday, as Nvidia fell 4.3%, the semiconductor index jumped nearly 7%, and direct competitors all rose, including AMD.

The last risk is one the board manufactured itself. Jensen has more than 50 direct reports and no identified successor, and one prominent analyst estimates Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less without him. That reflects poorly on the board. Succession is a director’s first duty, and these directors let one man become the company with no obvious succession plan until it is too late.

Even now, the reflex appears to be deference. The same statement that launched the board’s investigation declared, before a single interview, that the board had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” and that it had confidence in Jensen. A board that announces its conclusion on the day it opens the inquiry, makes one wonder whether the board has already predetermined what their preferred outcome would be rather than following the trail of wherever facts lead them in a way that protects all shareholders.

Readers of Fortune will know that we have been critics of Vice Chancellor Travis Laster on the Delaware Court of Chancery, who wrongly attacked us in his Cloudflare opinion as “advocates for dual class shares” and for founder control more broadly. Vice Chancellor Laster did not apparently understand that we are not advocates for anything; rather, we call it as we see it as fact-based academics with five decades’ experience as a widely recognized scholar of corporate governance.

We have published extensively on dual-class shares, on when they work, and when they don’t, with extensive academic analysis and quantitative research into performance of companies with dual class share structures.

In our extensive careful research, published widely in academic outlets such as the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance as well as FORTUNE, Chief Executive Magazine and many other outlets, we have studied instances when dual class shares work well, such as when a founder or family with real money at stake uses the protection to invest through cycles and outlast short-term activists, as at Berkshire Hathaway, Alphabet and The New York Times.

Similarly, we have studied instances when dual class shares should be retired, such as when they shield controllers with ulterior motives from consequence, as at WeWork under Adam Neumann or Paramount under the Redstones.

Critics of founder control tend to treat dual-class shares as the bogeyman behind every entrenched founder, and one share, one vote as the cure. Nvidia is the case study that breaks that outdated, prosaic theory. Nvidia has a single class of common stock, not dual class shares. Jensen owns about 3.5% of it and casts 3.5% of the votes. The board is declassified, every director stands for election every year, and a simple majority of directors could replace him as CEO at any meeting. On paper he is as removable as any hired manager. In practice, no CEO in America has been more immune from proper scrutiny and oversight.

What entrenched Jensen was not the capital structure of the company; rather, it was the apparent idolatry of a board which was in thrall socially and interpersonally to Jensen Huang. He earned the adulation honestly, building a company from a booth at Denny’s into, for a time, the most valuable on earth. But the directors whose job it was to provide effective oversight to guard shareholders’ interests, apparently effectively joined the congregation. No charter provision did that, and no proxy adviser would have caught it. Nvidia has the independent majority, the lead director, the annual elections and the single share class that the checklists of ISS and Glass Lewis reward.

Nor has one share, one vote ever been a vaccine against scandal. Enron, Tyco, Wells Fargo and Boeing all had it. One of us argued in the Harvard Business Review in 2002, after Enron, that failed boards routinely passed every structural test, and that what set great boards apart was a culture of open dissent, in which directors challenge the chief executive and each other. That was true then and Nvidia shows it is true now.

When it comes to providing effective oversight, what matters is the oversight culture of the board and the quality of the board, not the ‘check the boxes’ yardsticks so often misleading propagated by governistas, such as ‘one share one vote’.

Delaware needs no new invented legal theory for measuring whether Nvidia’s board did its duty as a board in providing oversight. If shareholders bring Caremark claims against Nvidia’s directors, the court will ask what the board knew and what it did to find out. We have called out the Delaware Court of Chancery when it overreaches, and we will be again. But failing to question a celebrated CEO about a customer under federal investigation is no business judgment at all. Nvidia’s directors were paid to provide oversight over Jensen Huang, however brilliant. And in that duty, by all outside appearances, they apparently whiffed.

Aristotle famously warned, “There is no great genius without a touch of madness.” Psychiatrists call shared disorders “folie à deux.” It is up to the board to ensure a company’s owners benefit from the genius of founders but are protected by the madness.

President Donald Trump says the Iran War is effectively over, but Bitcoin and financial markets face another potentially turbulent week. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller has warned that stubborn inflation could justify a 50-basis-point rate hike in December. Meanwhile, Kalshi traders have raised the odds of a US Treasury Bitcoin purchase this year to 13%.

The three developments put geopolitics, monetary policy and Bitcoin adoption attentions being rekindled. Trump’s latest comments could ease concerns about prolonged military escalation, while Waller’s warning raises questions about borrowing costs. Bitcoin, meanwhile, is attracting attention from prediction markets betting on a possible government purchase.

Trump told reporters on Monday that the Iran War was “militarily effectively over,” suggesting Washington sees little immediate need for further military action. Speaking at the White House after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, Trump said negotiations were moving in a positive direction. He also suggested that an agreement could bring the conflict to an end fairly soon.

However, Washington has not completely ruled out further strikes. Trump said American forces remained ready to respond if circumstances changed, keeping some uncertainty around the negotiations.

Oil prices follow with a decline. Brent crude fell 5.85% last night before slipping another 1.7% to around $90.99 per barrel this morning. The retreat reflects easing concerns over prolonged supply disruptions in the Middle East.

How could it affect crypto? With the Iran war ending, cheaper oil could offer some relief for Bitcoin by reducing inflationary pressure and giving the Federal Reserve more room to eventually lower interest rates. Energy prices influence Bitcoin primarily through inflation expectations, monetary policy, and market liquidity.

Before Trump’s statement, the conflict had already created significant pressure across energy markets. Higher fuel prices have contributed to inflation concerns, complicating the Federal Reserve’s efforts to bring price growth back toward its 2% target.

An end to the Iran War could remove one important source of energy-market uncertainty.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller has introduced another complication for investors. Just last night, Waller said the Fed could consider a 50-basis-point increase in December if October inflation data show persistent pressure in core prices.

He warned that delivering only a 25-basis-point increase could undermine the Fed’s credibility if core inflation remains stubbornly high. However, Waller currently leans toward a smaller increase if inflation improves.

FED’S WALLER BACKS DECEMBER RATE HIKE, SAYS OPEN TO 50 BPS MOVE

A 50-basis-point move would represent two standard quarter-point increases delivered in a single meeting. It would also show that policymakers remain prepared to prioritize inflation control over easing financial conditions.

The possibility matters for Bitcoin because higher interest rates generally make speculative investments less attractive. Investors may favor cash and yield-bearing assets when borrowing costs rise, and liquidity becomes more expensive.

The Iran War adds another layer to that calculation. Even if military tensions ease, energy prices and inflation could keep the Fed under pressure.

Kalshi odds for a US Treasury Bitcoin purchase this year have climbed to 13%. The market reflects speculation that Washington could move beyond its existing Bitcoin reserve framework and acquire additional BTC.

Bitcoin’s growing institutional ambitions are also creating interest in infrastructure designed to expand what BTC can actually do. Bitcoin Hyper (HYPER) is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM). The network aims to bring Solana-style transaction speeds, low fees, and near-instant finality to Bitcoin while anchoring settlement to its underlying blockchain.

The project has already raised more than $33.2 million in presale funding, with HYPER currently priced at just $0.0136. Its testnet explorer is now live, giving users an early look at network activity. The ecosystem is designed to support Bitcoin transfers, decentralized finance, payments, and smart contracts, potentially unlocking new uses for BTC liquidity.

HYPER holders can also access advertised staking rewards of up to 35% APY through the presale. The token has a fixed supply of 21 billion, with allocations covering development, treasury, marketing, community rewards, and exchange listings.

Its planned November 26 presale conclusion is approaching, leaving buyers with a narrowing window before the next stage of the project.

With more than $33 million already raised, a live testnet explorer and the token launch approaching, Bitcoin Hyper is building momentum ahead of its next milestones. The combination of early-stage pricing, staking incentives, and Bitcoin-focused infrastructure gives the project several potential demand drivers. Its upcoming launch could become an important test of investor appetite for the next generation of Bitcoin Layer 2 networks.

For now, investors have three competing forces to watch: the possibility of an Iran War resolution, a more aggressive Federal Reserve, and growing speculation about government Bitcoin accumulation.

#5441. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5440. 10 unusual artificial reefs, from subway cars and a tank to sculptures

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These unusual artificial reefs turn subway cars, an aircraft carrier, a tank, sculptures and concrete modules into habitat where corals, mussels and fish can settle

A retired New York City subway car, an American M42 Duster tank and a decommissioned U.S. Navy aircraft carrier now share the same job. Each was placed on the seafloor on purpose. Each now serves as a surface where corals, mussels, sponges and fish can settle.

An artificial reef is a human-made structure put underwater to give marine life something hard to grow on. Large stretches of ocean floor are flat mud or sand. The larvae of corals, oysters and sponges need a firm surface to attach to. Small fish need crevices where they can shelter from predators. A sunken hull, a concrete module or a cement sculpture can supply both. Once algae and invertebrates take hold, larger fish arrive to feed, and a bare patch of seabed becomes working habitat.

These projects serve people as well as wildlife. Wreck sites and sculpture parks attract recreational divers and snorkelers. Some are placed with the stated aim of drawing visitors away from fragile natural reefs. Retired ships also have to be cleared of toxic substances before they go into the water. The aircraft carrier on this list was checked for that by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency before it was sunk.

The 10 entries below, all unusual artificial reefs or reef-building methods, fall into three broad groups. Some are decommissioned machines. They include that aircraft carrier, a World War II transport ship and a military transport plane that once served in the Turkish Air Force. A tank in Jordan's Aqaba Marine Park and hundreds of subway cars off Delaware belong to the same group. Some are works of art, including two installations in an underwater museum near Cancun, Mexico. The rest are purpose-built structures. One is a reef off Key Biscayne, Florida, designed to evoke the mythical city of Atlantis. Others are hollow concrete modules used around the world and cement pyramids set beside natural coral in Indonesia.

The entries sit in waters ranging from the Gulf of Mexico and the U.S. Atlantic coast to the Caribbean, the Red Sea and Indonesia's Coral Triangle. Each offers a different answer to the same practical question: what can go on the ocean floor to give sea life a foothold?

An American M42 Duster tank rests on the seabed of the Aqaba Marine Park in Jordan. The Jordanian Royal Ecological Diving Society sank it on purpose in 1999 so that sea sponges and corals would have somewhere to settle.

The wreck lies about 15 feet below the surface, according to Daniel Keller, who compiled a list of unique artificial reefs on Medium.

At that depth, the tank sits within reach of snorkelers as well as scuba divers. Keller describes the site as a well-known spot for both activities.

The sinking was a deliberate ecological project. The diving society's stated aim was to give sponges and corals a foothold inside the marine park.

Keller writes that sea stars, lionfish and shrimp now live on and around the wreck. Those residents cover three distinct groups of sea life. Sea stars are echinoderms, lionfish are predatory fish and shrimp are crustaceans.

Neptune Memorial Reef is a 16-acre artificial reef off Key Biscayne, Florida, designed to resemble the mythical sunken city of Atlantis. Its metal and cement structures give algae and coral a hard surface to settle and grow on.

The reef takes its name from Neptune, the Roman god of the sea. Key Biscayne is a barrier island just off Miami, linked to the mainland by the Rickenbacker Causeway. The reef sits in the Atlantic Ocean off the island's shore.

Atlantis comes from Plato. He described the island civilization in two dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, written around 360 BCE. In Critias, Plato names Poseidon, the Greek counterpart of Neptune, as the god who founded Atlantis. He placed the island beyond the Pillars of Hercules. In his account, Atlantis was a powerful naval empire that was defeated by ancient Athens. He wrote that it sank into the sea in a single day and night.

The reef recreates that drowned city in architectural detail. Statues of lions, decorative gates and pillars stand across Neptune Memorial Reef. Marine growth now covers the pillars. Together they give the site the look of a city in ruins.

Arches and holes built into the structures give small fish a stable place to live. Reef-building corals lay down skeletons of calcium carbonate. Each colony that grows on the reef adds its own skeleton to the structure.

The reef also serves as an undersea burial ground. It was built so that the memorial would also support a healthy marine environment. Snorkelers and scuba divers are free to visit.

A 2012 study measured how much life the structures had drawn. It counted 195 coral colonies and 56 fish species at the site, according to Daniel Keller's list of unique artificial reefs.

Those counts come from one survey in one year. They show what lived on the reef at that point, not how its populations have changed since.

The USS Oriskany is a decommissioned aircraft carrier that was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico near Pensacola, Florida, in 2006 to serve as an artificial reef. Daniel Keller's Medium list of unique artificial reefs describes it as the world's largest artificial reef made from a sunken vessel.

Keller's post gives the carrier's weight as 30,800 tons and its length as 888 feet. Those two figures are the basis for the size claim. Most other entries on the list are vehicles, sculptures or concrete modules. The Oriskany was a warship built to launch and recover aircraft at sea.

That scale shapes what the reef offers. A single tank or sculpture gives marine life one compact patch of hard surface. A carrier hull of this length offers a long run of steel, with flat decks, vertical sides and enclosed compartments. Those surfaces sit at different depths and angles. That gives settling organisms a wider range of places to attach.

Before the sinking, the Environmental Protection Agency made sure the Oriskany was free of toxic substances, according to Keller's post. A hull still carrying toxic material would work against the purpose of an artificial reef, which is to give marine life a place to settle and grow.

Once the carrier settled on the bottom, its hull and deck became hard structure in open water. Algae, corals and mussels now grow on the ship, Keller writes. Each of those organisms attaches to a firm surface, and the wreck offers a large one. As that growth builds up, the steel outline of a warship turns into living habitat.

Divers call the wreck the Great Carrier Reef, according to Keller's post. The nickname plays on Australia's Great Barrier Reef and points back to the vessel's original role as an aircraft carrier. The name treats the wreck as a reef first and a ship second, which matches the reason it was sunk.

Redbird Reef, off the Delaware coast, includes 714 retired New York City subway cars. The reef lies 80 feet down and covers more than 1.3 square miles of seabed.

The subway cars share the site with other retired hardware. The reef also holds 86 armored personnel carriers and tanks, all retired from service. About 3,000 tons of truck tires went into the water as well. Eight barges and tugboats round out the list of materials.

That inventory draws on surplus from several different sectors. Urban transit supplied the rail cars, and the military supplied the armored vehicles. Trucking supplied the tires, and the barges and tugboats came from maritime work. None of those items was originally built with marine life in mind.

Redbird Reef is built from many objects rather than from a single wreck. Each one adds hard surfaces, edges and hollow spaces to the seafloor. That sets it apart from reefs made from one sunken ship, where a single hull supplies all the structure.

The surrounding Mid-Atlantic seabed is featureless mud and sand. The steel shells of the rail cars and military vehicles supply structure that the bottom there otherwise lacks.

Oysters grow on the sunken equipment. Blue mussels live there too, along with other invertebrates that attach to hard surfaces. Both oysters and blue mussels are filter feeders that strain plankton from the surrounding water.

The Medium post by Daniel Keller that profiles the reef also makes a claim about its output. The post says the reef has produced more than 400 times as much food for marine life as the plain seabed. It does not name a study or survey behind the comparison.

Cars that once carried commuters through New York now rest on the Atlantic floor off Delaware. They sit beside armored vehicles, truck tires and tugboats that were retired from very different jobs.

The Silent Evolution is an underwater art installation made up of 450 human figures, set inside a national marine park near Cancun, Mexico. It belongs to the Cancun Underwater Museum of Art, a collection created to improve marine ecosystems and draw more tourists to the area.

The sculptor behind it is Jason deCaires Taylor. Unlike a scuttled ship or a retired military vehicle, this reef was made for the seabed from the start. Its subject is people rather than machinery.

The installation lies on Manchones Reef in Mexico. It is one of the works in the MUSA Collection.

The figures are arranged in groups of standing people. Some tilt their faces up toward the sky. Others look down at the seafloor beneath them.

Taylor builds his sculptures from marine-grade cement. The material contains no metals or other substances that could harm marine life. He also leaves parts of each surface rough on purpose. Those textured patches give coral larvae a place to gain a foothold.

The figures do two jobs for the museum. Visitors come to see them as an exhibit. Reef organisms use the same surfaces as a place to settle and grow.

A C-47 Dakota military transport plane was sunk off the Karaada coast in 2008 to become an artificial reef. The wreck is now a dive site that supports a wide range of marine species, including giant groupers.

Before it reached the seabed, the aircraft flew as a transport plane in the Turkish Air Force.

The Dakota is an aircraft rather than a ship, a ground vehicle or a purpose-built concrete module.

Divers visit the site to see the plane itself and the sea life that now lives on and around it.

The USNS Hoyt S. Vandenberg is a World War II transport ship that was sunk on purpose off Key West, Florida, in 2009 to create an artificial reef. Daniel Keller's Medium list of unique artificial reefs calls it the world's second-largest artificial reef, after the USS Oriskany.

The ship is 522 feet long. That makes it 366 feet shorter than the Oriskany, the aircraft carrier that sits ahead of it in Keller's size comparison. The two Florida wrecks top that comparison, but the carrier is far larger.

The Vandenberg's resting place was chosen in advance. Keller writes that researchers spent months surveying the seabed before the ship went down. They were looking for a spot where the hull would not harm the natural reefs nearby.

That survey addresses a basic risk of ship reefs. A hull set down on top of living coral would destroy part of the habitat the project is meant to add to. Placing it on open seabed avoids that trade-off.

Keller describes the wreck as a popular recreational dive site.

Keller also writes that authorities hope the Vandenberg will ease the pressure heavy tourism puts on natural reefs. The aim is for some divers to choose the ship over living coral elsewhere. Keller presents this as a hope for the project, not as a measured result.

Urban Reef is a sculpture in the shape of a house, placed on the seafloor off the coast of Mexico as part of the Cancun Underwater Museum of Art. Open windows in its walls lead into enclosed spaces where fish and other marine animals can shelter.

The piece is by the sculptor Taylor, who also created The Silent Evolution in the same museum. He developed the design with marine biologists. The building is meant to be occupied by sea life rather than people.

The layout works as habitat. The open windows serve as entry points. Fish can swim from the surrounding water into the enclosed rooms and back out again. Those rooms give fish and other animals a protected place to stay.

Urban Reef shares the museum with sculpted human figures. The house takes architecture rather than the human body as its subject. It turns a familiar human shelter into one built for marine animals.

Taylor builds his sculptures from marine-grade cement. The material contains no metals or other additives that could harm sea creatures. He also leaves some surfaces rough so coral larvae can attach firmly. His forms include openings and gaps that let fish and other animals pass in and out.

Taylor placed his sculptures near the Mesoamerican Reef off Cancun. His aim was to draw visitors away from the natural reef and ease some of the pressure on it.

Taylor has said that the first layers of reef life, such as algae and mollusks, can start attaching to his sculptures within days or weeks.

Smithsonian magazine reports that scientists are divided over whether manmade sculptures on the seafloor help marine ecosystems. Some consider them too disruptive. Others expect coral to grow over the figures and hide them completely within 10 years. On that view, Taylor's sculptures would eventually disappear from sight beneath the coral growth they were made to host.

Reef Balls are a building method rather than a single reef: hollow concrete spheres with perforated surfaces, set on the seabed to give fish and corals somewhere to live. More than 500,000 of them have helped produce about 4,000 new coral colonies, according to a Medium post by Daniel Keller of Naples, Florida.

Keller places those colonies across Asia, Africa, the U.S. and the Caribbean. That geographic spread separates the modules from the other entries in this list, each of which sits at a single named location. Reef Balls were also built for no other purpose. Ships, tanks and subway cars become reefs at the end of a working life. These structures are cast from the start to serve as habitat.

Keller describes the modules as custom-designed, and the design centers on shape and material. The hollow interior and the holes in the shell are meant to attract fish. The concrete is part of the design too. Keller writes that it is environmentally safe and formulated to match the composition and pH of seawater.

Builders sometimes attach coral plugs directly to the modules, which gives coral a head start on the bare concrete. Keller says the practice speeds up the growth of habitat around the structures. Without plugs, a module depends on drifting coral larvae arriving and settling on their own.

The approach has also been used in lakes. For a project in Lake Murray, workers placed a large bladder inside each mold and filled the gap around it with concrete. The molds were bought from the Reef Ball Foundation. The finished modules are dome-shaped, with openings that let fish swim through in both directions.

In Nova Scotia, community members in Pictou Landing made the reef balls that were placed in Bras d'Or Lake. Openings in those modules give fish and lobster places to shelter and live.

At Jemeluk, Indonesia, cement pyramids were placed on the seabed on purpose to serve as an artificial reef. They stand beside natural coral at a popular dive site. Tropical fish and green sea turtles use the area.

Unlike a sunken tank or ship, the pyramids had no earlier life above water. They are cement forms built for one job: to give marine life a hard structure on the seafloor.

The pyramids sit right next to living coral reefs rather than on an open stretch of seabed. Divers at Jemeluk can see the built structures and the natural reef at the same site.

The Jemeluk pyramids are part of a national program. Indonesian authorities installed artificial reefs as part of a wider effort to protect the country's marine ecosystems, according to Daniel Keller.

Indonesia's coastline lies within the Coral Triangle. Keller writes that the region has recently faced illegal fishing and coral degradation. The cement pyramids at Jemeluk are one of the artificial reef projects placed under that national effort to protect Indonesian waters.

#5439. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.

#5438. J. Crew debuts new AI shopping tool that’s designed to think like a stylist

Over the course of four decades, J. Crew’s style has woven cashmere cardigans, tweed jackets, and other preppy staples that have attracted high-profile fans including Michelle Obama, Demi Moore, and Meghan Markle.

Throughout the apparel brand’s history—beginning as a catalog, then growing to become a physical and omnichannel retailer—those styling decisions were made by humans. But beginning today, there’s artificial intelligence at work too.

On Wednesday, J. Crew announced a new consumer-facing, AI-enabled tool called Style Advisor, which runs on a collection of Anthropic’s models. Style Advisor is trained on data from thousands of outfit pairings from the company’s photo shoots and J. Crew’s styling principles, outfit and accessories pairings.

“It’s not just about the piece that you’re looking for, but how to style it,” says Danielle Schmelkin, chief information officer at J. Crew. “What those stylists bring to the table—and really recommend more than just the item that you may have picked up when you walked into the store—we are really looking to create that online.”

As more shoppers gravitate to agentic shopping, with more than 50% of global consumers using AI to buy goods within the past three months, new tools have proliferated ranging from Meta Platforms’ Muse agent and Alexa for Shopping from Amazon to AI shopping assistants created by retailers including Lowe’s, Ulta Beauty, and Macy’s.

But while 56% of consumers say they use AI chat or search tools including Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT, only 27% are gravitating to retailer-created AI shopping assistants, according to consulting firm McKinsey.

“I think the visual piece is really important,” says Schmelkin of the distinctive edge that she promises Style Advisor will offer. In the future, the tool will also pull in data from a consumer’s past purchase history, allowing Style Advisor to make even more personalized recommendations, replicating that’s already possible during the omnichannel shopping experience.

She says Style Advisor is also grounded in contextual details, asking questions to better understand a shopper’s intent. If a J. Crew customer were to tell it that they were looking for an outfit to attend a wedding—in, say, Miami, but not too formal—the tool will make recommendations based on these nuances.

Style Advisor will debut on J. Crew’s desktop website and is expected to later be added to the retailer’s mobile app.

J. Crew’s Style Advisor runs on a variety of Claude’s models, including Fable 5.1, which is leveraged to handle the more complex and ambiguous judgment that allows the tool to think and respond like a stylist. Claude’s Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 4.5 support the speed and efficiency of the back-and-forth responses between consumers and the AI stylist, while Claude Opus 5.5 was utilized by J. Crew’s team to build a working prototype.

“What is the actual experience that we want the shopper to have, and then, how do we think about making sure that we’re mapping the right models to be able to deliver that,” says Lauren Collett, Anthropic’s enterprise go-to-market leader.

Schmelkin says J. Crew built in a back-end observation layer that allows the retailer to closely monitor the costs. “We want to make sure we are constantly refining and using these models in the right way, both in terms of the outputs for our customers, but also the efficiency we want to see to make this scalable,” says Schmelkin.

Internally at J. Crew, to bolster AI adoption, the retailer has created an AI fluency program that begins with the basics and advances up through vibe coding. An internal AI lab, called “Second Thread,” began with just the tech team but has broadened to incorporate all corporate employees to discuss AI use cases and propose other technology solutions.

For four years, J. Crew has also run a two-day tech summit that features workshops, hackathons, guest speakers, and vendor presentations. Initially, this programming was only available to the tech team, but J. Crew has more recently democratized access. Employees are also encouraged to use AI enterprise tools from Anthropic and OpenAI.

The Style Advisor was conceptualized by a J. Crew digital product designer, who developed a working prototype before engineers were pulled into the project. The fact that the tool wasn’t mandated from the top of J. Crew’s C-suite reflects Schmelkin’s efforts to encourage employees to chart their own path on AI.

“I’ve been screaming to anyone who will listen for years now to get in there and build a habit,” says Schmelkin. “You have to find your a-ha moment and then all of a sudden…this could really change the way you think about your own life, work, and team productivity.”

Nvidia’s shares rattled by CEO's affair and board probe. The biggest tech headlines swirling this week centered on an admission over the weekend that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been unfaithful to his wife and that the AI chip maker’s board was investigating reports that he had been targeted by a business executive who U.S. intelligence says was a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s shares slipped on Monday as U.S. lawmakers are also asking for more information. Fortune reports that Nvidia controls about 90% of the market for high-powered GPU computer chips used in AI data centers. And yet another issue is poor succession planning by the board: Huang, who has been CEO for 33 years, has 60 direct reports and no clear successor.

Alphabet, meanwhile, takes aim at Nvidia. On Monday, Google debuted new AI chips that Bloomberg reports are intended to take some share from Nvidia’s dominant position and represent an acceleration in product development coming from the company’s chip division. But another corner of the search giant’s AI business is facing mounting criticism. Politicians are lamenting the company’s decision to block search for K-12 student accounts if districts have enacted AI bans. Sen. Edward Markey has demanded that the company reverse a policy; while Google says its AI features are so interconnected with search that it cannot offer the service without AI.

Anthropic continues to advance plans for IPO; debuts new frontier models. Yet another AI company aiming to navigate more turbulent times is Anthropic, which is reportedly planning to go public next week even as shares of AI companies have faced pressure as investors fret about high infrastructure costs and U.S. midterm election results that are divisively more “anti AI.” Separately, on Monday, Anthropic debuted two new AI models called Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, which the company said generate outputs that are 30% faster than their predecessors. The models also cost 20% less than the prior generation. And on Tuesday, it unveiled a suite of new office productivity tools aimed at knowledge workers, putting Anthropic in closer competition with Microsoft.

OpenAI raises about $11 billion in a new funding round. The ChatGPT maker’s latest effort to raise more funds reportedly closed on Friday, with the remainder of the round, which could hit as much as $20 billion in total, expected to be completed “in the coming weeks,” according to media reports. OpenAI has reportedly sought out to raise $30 billion or more at a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but settled for a lower figure and a valuation of $1.25 trillion, amid the pressure AI companies are facing from investors. More optimistically, Business Insider reports on fresh research data from Graphite that found ChatGPT has captured 81% of worldwide AI chatbot traffic, easily outpacing rivals Google and Anthropic, who had been making some inroads.

Data and analytics, cyber jobs will see the largest headcount increase in 2027. AI’s impact on jobs have loomed over the IT industry, magnified by younger, entry-level workers that have taken to social media to lament they can’t find their first role and as Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and other tech giants have announced layoffs. Yet encouragingly, 40% of enterprises plan to increase their IT headcount in 2027, according to a survey of 2,002 CIOs and other tech leaders conducted by Gartner. The biggest changes will be for data and analytics and cybersecurity roles.

Alicia Mullery, VP analyst at Gartner, tells Fortune that much of the concern about AI in the workplace is that these systems will save organizations so much time, they’ll need less people. But that’s not always the case: AI can create a lot of so-called “slop” that workers need to rummage through. And, even when the outputs are more advantageous, there are still plenty of instances where human-machine collaboration is needed.

IT departments tend to be further along on their AI journey and this is where CIOs can continue to step in and guide, remaking workflows across other parts of the business, says Mullery. “I see the CIO as really being at the forefront of being able to say, ‘Hey our teams went through this first,’” adds Mullery. “Here’s what we learned, here’s what worked, and here’s what didn’t work.”

- FFB Bank is seeking a CIO, a remote-based role. Posted salary range: $275K-$375K/year.

- Citi is seeking a head of retail and wealth risk technology, based in Rutherford, New Jersey. Posted salary range: $250K-$500K/year.

- DBV Technologies is seeking a VP of IT, based in Bernards, New Jersey. Posted salary range: $300K-$350K/year.

- The American Board of Emergency Medicine is seeking a CIO, based in East Lansing, Michigan. Posted salary range: $200K-$250K/year.

- Hyatt named Danny Miles to serve as the hospitality company’s chief digital and information officer, leading a newly combined organization that includes engineering, digital products, enterprise technology, data, AI, and cybersecurity. Miles most recently served as CTO at athletic gear maker Under Armour and also was CTO at Dollar Shave Club and a VP at Nike.

- Fox Factory promoted Troy Henige to the newly established role of CTO, leading the manufacturer’s enterprise technology and product roadmap strategies. Henige spent seven years in engineering roles at motorcycle and ATV suspension manufacturer Progressive Suspension before joining Fox a decade ago, most recently serving as VP of engineering.

- Time appointed Michael Dugan to the role of CTO. He joins the media company from peer G/O Media, where he served as CTO. Previously, Dugan served as CTO of Hearst Magazines and spent 17 years at Forbes, including four years as CTO.

- Authentic Brands Group promoted Adnan Somani to the role of CTO, expanding his responsibilities to include overseeing the brand management company’s AI strategy and IT organization. Somani joined Authentic Brands as EVP of digital technology in May 2024 and previously, founded the technology startup Aiva Labs.

- Presidio announced Doran Stienike will join the IT services firm as CIO, effective November 9. Previously, Stienike served as CIO and chief information security officer at software-as-a-service provider CSG International. He also served as CIO and held other technology leadership roles at ConAgra Foods.

- OneTrust named Tim Mullen to serve as CIO, overseeing the governance and compliance software firm’s enterprise technology strategy and accelerating its AI efforts. Mullen joined OneTrust in 2022 and previously served as CISO. He also held information security leadership roles at Change Healthcare, InterContinental Hotels Group, and Travelport.

- DNSFilter announced the appointment of Justin Foster as CTO. Foster joins the cybersecurity company from another cyber firm, Forescout, where he most recently served as CTO and oversaw the research and development organization. He joined Forescout through its acquisition of Cysiv, where he was co-founder and CTO.

John Kell is a contributing writer for Fortune and author of Fortune’s CIO Intelligence newsletter.

#5437. Your iPhone Duo Under Attack? Binance Flags Dangerous iOS Security Flaw

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Binance has warned Apple users about a dangerous iOS vulnerability that could expose crypto wallets, private keys, and login credentials. The flaw, called worse_query, allows malicious applications to access files normally isolated inside other apps. Binance warning identifies several affected iOS software versions and urges users to remove untrusted applications immediately.

The vulnerability threatens more than crypto wallets; apps storing sensitive information locally could also expose passwords, authentication data, and personal files. That makes the latest warning particularly concerning for iPhone users who rely on their devices for banking and crypto transactions.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

Binance says the problem affects iOS itself rather than its own wallet infrastructure. Users who suspect their devices have been compromised should create new wallets on clean devices and move their funds. The exchange also recommends resetting active login sessions and updating installed software.

The vulnerability exploits Apple’s application sandbox, a security mechanism designed to keep applications separated from one another. Normally, an application cannot freely access another application’s private files. This isolation protects sensitive information even when users install multiple applications on the same device.

This is where it gets dangerous: the worse_query exploit reportedly bypasses those restrictions. A malicious application could potentially access directories containing information belonging to other installed applications.

The researcher behind the public GitHub repository describes worse_query as a sandbox escape affecting iOS 26 and iOS 27. The project identifies affected releases spanning iOS 26.0 through 26.7.2 and iOS 27.2. Binance warns that exposed information could include cryptocurrency recovery phrases, private keys, and login credentials.

The actual danger depends partly on how individual applications store sensitive information. Wallets retaining recovery phrases or other credentials in accessible local files face particular risks.

Security researchers have also highlighted the importance of protecting plaintext wallet information. SlowMist’s security chief warned that the vulnerability could undermine assumptions about isolation between application containers.

Apple’s security update schedule adds another dimension to the Binance iOS warning. Apple’s security releases list iOS 27.2 and iOS 26.7.2 among its available software versions, both released on October 26, 2026.

However, Apple’s published security advisories do not explicitly identify worse_query by name. There is currently no confirmed public statement establishing that these updates fully resolve the specific sandbox escape.

A separate GitHub project implementing the exploit also reported on November 8 that Apple’s available software releases had not patched worse_query. This leaves users with an important gap between installing the latest available update and confirming that a particular vulnerability has been fixed.

Binance recommends installing the latest official iOS release and keeping all applications updated. It also urges users to remove applications from unknown sources, including manually signed IPA files.

For us, crypto holders, the safest response to suspected compromise goes beyond simply deleting suspicious software.

The latest iPhone warning follows several security incidents involving malicious applications and crypto credentials. In September, Binance warned users about FomoPeek, a third-party application whose versions 1.1 and 1.2 reportedly contained malicious code.

Security researchers found that the software could exploit iOS vulnerabilities to obtain elevated device privileges. Potentially exposed information included recovery phrases, private keys, login credentials, and other locally stored data.

More recently, CertiK highlighted the DarkSword exploit framework, which reportedly targeted cryptocurrency applications through compromised websites and vulnerable iPhones.

#CertiKInsight 🚨 A new version of DarkSword, an iOS exploit kit, is being used to target crypto wallets on unpatched iPhones. Simply opening a malicious site in Safari can be enough: no wallet connection, no signature needed. Here's what you need to know 🧵

These incidents involve separate attack methods. Nevertheless, they demonstrate why smartphone security has become increasingly important for crypto holders.

The Binance iOS warning highlights a fundamental problem with self-custody: protecting a recovery phrase means protecting every place where that information might be stored.
