#5436. 10 stages and factors that shape how fast an artificial reef comes alive

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How long an artificial reef takes to come alive depends on material, depth and nearby habitat, and these 10 stages and factors trace its path from biofilm to coral

A sunken ship, a stack of concrete modules or a pile of quarried rock is not a reef on the day it reaches the seafloor. It is bare, hard surface in open water. What turns it into habitat is ecological succession. In that process, one group of organisms changes the surface and its surroundings in ways that make room for the next. That is why there is no single answer to how long it takes an artificial reef to grow into a living community. "Alive" can mean several different things, and each arrives on its own schedule.

The first life on a new structure is invisible: a thin film of bacteria and organic material that coats submerged surfaces. Algae follow, then encrusting animals such as barnacles, tube worms, bryozoans and sponges that settle out of the water as drifting larvae. Fish can show up early, drawn to shelter and to the way a structure breaks the current. Corals, where the water allows them to grow at all, are among the slowest major groups to establish.

The pace of that sequence depends on conditions the builders of a reef can only partly control. Material matters. Texture and surface chemistry influence what settles. Depth governs how much light reaches algae and corals. Water temperature and currents shape growth rates and the delivery of larvae and food. Distance from an existing natural reef affects how many larvae and mobile animals reach a new site in the first place.

These questions matter to a wide range of people. Coastal managers use artificial reefs to create habitat and to steer fishing and diving activity. Anglers and dive operators look to them for fish and for places to visit. Conservation groups weigh what the structures add to an ecosystem against what they change. A basic question also remains open: whether artificial reefs produce new fish or mainly concentrate fish that already live nearby.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of the stages and factors that shape an artificial reef's timeline. They run from the first microbial film to the long-term comparison with natural reefs. They end with the debate over what a successful reef looks like.

The first life on a new artificial reef is a microscopic biofilm, and it starts forming almost as soon as the structure enters the water. It arrives long before algae, barnacles or fish, and it changes the surface that every later settler encounters.

The process begins with chemistry rather than biology. Seawater carries dissolved organic matter, including proteins and polysaccharides. These molecules stick to clean submerged surfaces and build a thin coating often called a conditioning film. That coating alters the surface's charge and texture at a microscopic scale.

Bacteria come next. Free-floating cells drift against the coated surface, and some attach loosely before anchoring themselves more firmly. Once attached, they release a sticky matrix of extracellular polymeric substances, usually shortened to EPS. The matrix binds the cells together and holds nutrients close.

As the film thickens, other microorganisms join it. Diatoms, which are single-celled algae with silica shells, are common members of marine biofilms. Fungi, protozoa and other microbes can settle in as well. The result is a layered community rather than a single species.

To the naked eye, the structure still looks bare. A diver touching it might notice a slippery feel or a faint brownish tint. That slime is the same kind of material that fouls ship hulls, pier pilings and buoys. Antifouling hull coatings are designed to keep this kind of growth from taking hold.

The biofilm shapes what settles after it. Larvae of many invertebrates, including barnacles and tube worms, test surfaces before committing to them. Chemical cues from the bacterial film can encourage or discourage that settlement. The tube worm Hydroides elegans, a widely studied fouling species, settles in response to particular marine bacteria in the film.

The film also feeds the reef's first grazers. Snails, limpets and other small grazing animals scrape biofilm from hard surfaces as food.

The pace and makeup of the film vary from site to site. Water temperature, nutrient levels, light and the material of the structure all influence which microbes dominate. That variation helps explain why two reefs placed in different waters can follow different paths from the very start.

Algae are usually the first growth a diver or underwater camera can see on a new artificial reef. A fuzzy green or brown layer of turf and filamentous algae spreads across sunlit surfaces before most animals have built any lasting cover.

These early colonizers grow fast and reproduce in large numbers. Green algae in the genus Ulva, which includes sea lettuce, release spores into the water in great quantities and can spread quickly across new hard surfaces. That speed lets them claim bare space before slower-growing competitors arrive.

Light decides where this layer appears. Algae need sunlight to photosynthesize. The heaviest early growth forms on the tops and upward-facing sides of a structure. Shaded undersides and the interior compartments of a sunken vessel tend to stay sparser. Those darker spaces leave room for filter-feeding animals that do not depend on sunlight.

The early algal coat changes the reef in practical ways. It adds texture to smooth concrete or steel. It traps sediment and organic particles. It also creates tiny pockets where small crustaceans and worms can shelter. Amphipods and other small grazers feed directly on the algae.

Larger grazers follow that food supply. Sea urchins and snails scrape algae from hard surfaces. In tropical waters, parrotfish and surgeonfish crop algal turf as well. Their feeding keeps turf short and opens patches of bare space that other settlers can occupy.

Crustose coralline algae play a separate role. These red algae deposit calcium carbonate in their cell walls and grow as pink or purple crusts over hard surfaces. They help cement loose material together. On coral reefs, certain coralline species provide chemical cues that prompt the larvae of some corals to settle.

Algal cover does not stay fixed. Early filamentous species are often replaced by larger seaweeds, coralline crusts or encrusting animals as the community matures. In temperate waters with enough light, kelp and other large brown seaweeds can establish on reef structures.

Heavy algal growth is not always a sign of a healthy reef. When nutrient levels are high or grazers are scarce, fleshy seaweeds can smother surfaces. That dense cover can crowd out the corals and invertebrates that reef managers often aim to attract.

Barnacles, tube worms and other encrusting animals reach an artificial reef as drifting larvae that settle on the bare surface and cement themselves in place. Their hard shells and tubes turn smooth concrete or steel into a rough, layered surface that other species can use.

The arrival of these animals has no single fixed date. It depends on which larvae are in the water when the structure goes down. Many marine invertebrates release larvae in seasonal pulses. A reef placed during one spawning period can collect a different set of settlers than one placed later in the year.

Barnacles are crustaceans. They are related to crabs and shrimp rather than to snails or clams. Their larvae swim freely before reaching a final stage called the cyprid, which searches for a place to attach. A cyprid probes surfaces with its antennae and then glues itself down head-first. It then transforms into a young barnacle. The barnacle builds a ring of hard plates and spends the rest of its life sweeping feathery legs through the water to catch food.

Barnacle cyprids also tend to settle near other barnacles. They respond to chemical cues left by members of their own species. That behavior helps explain why barnacle cover often spreads in dense clusters rather than evenly across a structure.

Tube worms take a different approach. Serpulid worms secrete hard tubes of calcium carbonate that stay fixed to the surface. Some members of this group, the spirorbids, build tightly coiled tubes only a few millimeters across. The worms extend crowns of tentacles to filter plankton from passing water. They pull back into their tubes when disturbed.

Other encrusting animals share the same surfaces. Bryozoans form colonies of tiny linked individuals that can resemble a lacy crust. Sponges, hydroids and sea squirts also settle on submerged structures. Mussels and oysters can build thick layers of their own.

These animals compete for limited space. Faster-growing colonies can overgrow slower ones. The mix of species on a structure can shift as some die back and others take their place.

The same process fouls ship hulls, piers and pipelines. That is the reason shipping companies coat hulls in antifouling paint. On a man-made reef, the growth is the purpose. Each shell, tube and crust adds crevices, shade and food for crabs, snails and small fish.

Fish are often among the first animals to use a new artificial reef. They can arrive before the structure carries much visible growth, drawn by shelter and a break from open water rather than by food on the reef surface.

A sunken structure changes the seafloor around it. On a flat stretch of sand or mud, it may be the only hard, vertical feature for a long distance. It casts shade, offers holes and overhangs to hide in and gives fish a fixed point to orient around.

It also changes how water moves. Current flowing over and around the structure creates eddies and calmer pockets on its downstream side. Fish can hold position in these slower zones while spending less energy than they would in the open current.

The same principle underlies fish aggregating devices, the floating rafts and buoys that commercial fleets use to gather tuna and other open-ocean species. Fish collect around these objects even though the devices supply little food of their own.

Early visitors to a reef structure tend to be mobile animals already living in the surrounding area. Schools of small baitfish hover above and beside it. Small reef fish tuck into crevices and gaps. Larger predators, such as jacks and snappers in warmer waters, follow the baitfish and patrol the edges.

Fish are not the only mobile arrivals. Crabs, lobsters and octopuses move into cavities and openings, where the structure protects them from predators.

A second wave comes from the plankton. Many reef fish spend their earliest life stage as drifting larvae. When they are ready to settle, they seek out hard habitat. A new structure can become home to these young fish.

As the reef surface becomes covered with growth, the fish community shifts. Species that graze on algae or pick at small invertebrates find more to eat. The reef begins to offer food as well as shelter, and the mix of residents changes with it.

Reef-building corals are among the slowest major groups to establish on an artificial reef. Their arrival depends on a steady supply of drifting larvae, clear warm water and a surface that other organisms have already prepared.

Most new coral colonies on a man-made structure begin as larvae called planulae. Many reef-building species reproduce by broadcast spawning. They release eggs and sperm into the water in synchronized events, often timed to the lunar cycle. Fertilized eggs develop into larvae that drift with the plankton before they search for a place to attach. Other species brood their larvae internally. Those larvae are released ready to settle soon, often close to the parent colony.

Settlement is permanent. Once a planula attaches, it cannot move again. It cements itself to the surface and transforms into a single polyp. That polyp divides repeatedly to build a colony. Each polyp lays down a skeleton of calcium carbonate beneath it.

Coral larvae are selective about where they land. Many species settle preferentially on or near crustose coralline algae. These hard, pinkish red algae encrust reef rock and give off chemical cues that larvae can detect. A freshly sunk structure lacks that crust. Corals tend to appear only after the surface has gathered a community that makes it suitable for them.

Young corals are tiny and fragile. Fast-growing turf algae, sponges and other encrusting animals can overgrow or smother them before they reach a safe size. Grazers such as parrotfish and sea urchins help by keeping algae in check.

Light sets another limit. Reef-building corals host symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae inside their tissues. These algae photosynthesize and supply much of the coral's energy. A structure placed too deep or in murky water receives too little light for these corals to thrive.

Growth form shapes how quickly a reef looks coral-covered. Branching species such as staghorn coral grow far faster than massive boulder corals, which can take decades to reach large sizes.

Outside the tropics, artificial reefs rarely develop the stony reef-building corals found on tropical reefs. Their surfaces are more often claimed by sponges, anemones, soft corals and other invertebrates.

Some projects do not wait for larvae at all. They attach coral fragments raised in underwater nurseries, a practice known as coral gardening. That approach is a restoration method rather than natural colonization. The coral cover it produces reflects human effort, not the structure's own pull on drifting larvae.

The material an artificial reef is made from shapes how quickly life takes hold. How rough a surface is, what it is made of and how much shelter it offers all affect which organisms settle first and how fast a bare object becomes working habitat.

Concrete is the most common purpose-built reef material. It can be cast into modules with holes, ledges and hollow interiors. Its rough surface also gives drifting larvae many small places to attach.

Fresh concrete has a highly alkaline surface. Some reef designers adjust the mix or let modules cure before deployment. Both steps make the surface less hostile to early settlers.

Retired steel ships work differently. A sunken vessel rises well above the seafloor. Its decks, rails and superstructure reach into water with more light and stronger currents than the sand around it. Holds, corridors and engine rooms give fish and invertebrates enclosed shelter that small modules cannot match.

Ships also require heavy preparation. In the U.S., federal guidance from the Environmental Protection Agency and the Maritime Administration covers how a vessel is readied for sinking. It calls for removing fuel, oil, loose debris and hazardous materials such as asbestos and PCBs. That cleanup protects water quality, but it adds time and cost before the reef exists at all. Steel also corrodes in seawater. Over time a wreck slowly changes shape and can eventually collapse.

Limestone and other quarried rock offer a third path. Limestone is made of calcium carbonate, the same mineral that corals and many shellfish use to build their skeletons. Piles of boulders create irregular crevices that resemble natural rocky bottom. Rock does not rust, and it stays heavy and stable through storms.

Some materials have failed outright. Bundles of tires dropped off the U.S. coast in past decades proved a poor base for marine growth. Many broke loose, shifted with storms and battered nearby habitat. Florida has since carried out efforts to haul them back out of the water.

Lightweight, unstable or toxic materials tend to slow or derail colonization. Heavy, stable and textured materials give settling organisms a surface that stays in place long enough for a community to build on it.

Water depth, temperature and current strength set the pace of colonization on an artificial reef. Light fades with depth. Warmth speeds up the metabolism of most marine organisms, and moving water delivers the food and larvae that new settlers need.

Depth matters first because of sunlight. Seawater absorbs light quickly, and red wavelengths are the first to disappear. A shallow reef in clear water gets enough light for algae and other photosynthesizing organisms to spread across its upper surfaces. A structure in deep or murky water receives far less light. Filter feeders such as sponges, hydroids and anemones tend to dominate its surfaces instead.

Water clarity shifts that balance. River sediment, plankton blooms and stirred-up sand all limit how far light reaches. Two reefs at the same depth can develop very different communities. One may sit in clear offshore water while the other sits near a muddy river mouth.

Temperature controls how fast organisms grow once they settle. Most marine invertebrates and fish are ectotherms, meaning their body temperature and metabolism track the surrounding water. A reef in warm tropical water generally gains cover faster than one in cold temperate water. In cooler seas, growth slows through the winter months.

Timing within the year also matters. Many invertebrates release their larvae during particular seasons. In temperate seas, the spring plankton bloom fuels a pulse of feeding and growth. A reef placed in the water just before a spawning season can collect settlers sooner than one deployed after the larvae have already drifted past.

Warmth has an upper limit. Reef-building corals live close to the top of their temperature tolerance. Unusually warm water can trigger bleaching, in which corals expel the symbiotic algae that supply much of their energy.

Currents act as the reef's supply line. Moving water carries plankton to filter feeders and flushes away sediment and waste. It also transports the larvae that become a reef's next residents. A structure in steady flow typically supports denser filter-feeder growth than one in stagnant water.

Too much water movement works against growth. At shallow sites, storm waves and surge can scour surfaces, shift lighter materials and bury the base of a structure in sand. Deeper placement shields a reef from most wave energy, but it comes at the cost of less light on the reef's surfaces.

An artificial reef placed near natural reef or other hard-bottom habitat usually fills with life faster than one sunk on open sand far from any reef. Nearby habitat supplies a steadier stream of drifting larvae and puts mobile animals within reach of the new structure.

Most reef organisms begin life as larvae carried by currents. Corals, sponges, barnacles, sea urchins and many reef fish spend part of their early lives drifting in open water before they settle on a surface. A new structure can only be colonized by larvae that actually reach it. A natural reef close by acts as a source, releasing spawn that can land on the new surface.

Current direction matters too. A structure downcurrent of an established reef sits in the path of that reef's larvae. A structure upcurrent of the same reef, at the same distance, may receive far fewer of them.

Juvenile and adult animals offer a second route in. Crabs, lobsters, octopuses and many reef fish move along the seafloor. A structure close to existing habitat gives them a reachable new shelter. A structure ringed by a wide stretch of bare sand is harder to reach for animals that avoid open ground, where predators can spot them.

Larvae also do not settle at random. The larvae of many reef fishes can detect the sounds a reef produces. Coral larvae of many species respond to chemical signals from crustose coralline algae. These pink algae form a rock-hard crust on reef surfaces. A new structure far from any reef offers few of these cues at first.

Connectivity can carry unwanted species too. Offshore structures can work as stepping stones across stretches of seafloor that were once barriers. In the Gulf of Mexico, the orange cup coral Tubastraea coccinea, a species native to the Indo-Pacific, has spread across offshore oil and gas platforms.

Siting involves trade-offs. Reef programs generally avoid placing structures on top of natural reef or seagrass, which the material would bury or damage. As a result, many projects sit on sand some distance away. The gap between a new reef and the nearest natural one is a key factor in how quickly the structure gains a living community.

A long-established artificial reef can support a dense, varied community of fish and invertebrates. It rarely becomes a copy of a nearby natural reef, though. Its species mix and life span depend heavily on the structure underneath.

The difference starts with how each reef is built. A natural coral reef grows as living organisms lay down calcium carbonate, often over thousands of years. Its framework is full of holes, ledges, overhangs and rubble at many scales, from finger-width gaps to caves. A sunken ship or a field of concrete modules arrives on the seafloor fully formed. Its shape is the one its designers gave it.

That shape influences what moves in. Tall, vertical surfaces such as ship hulls and the legs of offshore platforms rise through the water column and sit in stronger currents. Filter feeders such as sponges, anemones, soft corals and mussels often dominate those faces. A natural reef that sits low and wide in shallow water may instead be covered by algae and reef-building corals that depend on sunlight.

Fish communities can differ for the same reason. Structures that stand high off the bottom tend to draw schooling and midwater species alongside resident reef fish. A natural reef with many small crevices may shelter more of the small, secretive species that rarely leave cover.

Time treats the two kinds of reef differently. Steel corrodes in seawater, and hulls weaken, buckle and eventually collapse. Storms can shift or bury lighter structures. Each change resets part of the community. It strips away established growth and exposes bare surface for new settlers. A healthy coral reef, by contrast, keeps repairing and adding to its own framework while water conditions allow.

Artificial reefs can also host species that nearby natural reefs do not. A hard structure placed on open sand creates habitat where none existed before. Non-native species can use that new surface as a foothold. A chain of platforms or wrecks can act as stepping stones across seafloor that would otherwise block their spread.

An artificial reef can do two things for fish: draw existing fish away from surrounding waters, or add new fish by giving them habitat to settle, feed and grow. Fisheries researchers have argued for decades over which effect dominates, and the answer changes what a "living" reef means.

The first idea is known as attraction. Under this view, a new structure works like a magnet. Fish already living in the area move to it for shelter or food. The total number of fish in the region stays the same. The reef looks busy because the fish are concentrated in one spot.

The second idea is production. Here the reef adds habitat that a population was short of. Larvae that would have drifted over bare sand and died find a surface to settle on. Juveniles find crevices that protect them from predators. Adults find prey living on the encrusted structure. If more fish survive than would have without the structure, the reef has added to the population rather than rearranging it.

The distinction has direct consequences for fishing. Fish packed around a known structure are easier to find and catch. If a reef only attracts fish, heavy fishing on it can speed the decline of a stock that is already depleted. Red snapper in the Gulf of Mexico gather around artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms. The species has long been a central example in this argument.

Attraction and production mark two ends of a range rather than an either-or choice. Where a reef falls on that range depends on the species and the site. A species whose numbers are held down by a shortage of shelter or settlement habitat is more likely to gain from new structure. A species held down by fishing, food supply or the number of larvae reaching the area is more likely to simply relocate.

Production is also hard to prove. Fish move. A diver counting fish on a reef cannot tell where those fish came from. Showing production means tracking signs such as juveniles settling and growing on the structure, fish feeding on reef-dwelling prey and adults spawning nearby.

Some reef managers respond by limiting or banning fishing on certain artificial reefs. That gives the fish that gather there a chance to grow and reproduce. Under the production view, a reef counts as fully alive not when fish first show up, but when it supports fish across their whole life cycle.

#5434. A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.

Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off.

In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period.

The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting. Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday. LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress.

Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s.

The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together.

In NY-1, the people who funded the race and the people who voted in it were often different. Both campaigns were bankrolled mostly by donors outside the district, including major Wall Street, Hollywood and tech names. Even the men on the ballot live beyond its lines: both reside near Amityville, on Long Island’s South Shore, which means neither could vote for himself.

NY-1 runs from Suffolk County’s North Shore villages to the East End, with vineyards and farms on the North Fork and the Hamptons on the South Fork. In between lie Smithtown and Brookhaven, where suburban neighborhoods give way to woods and residents are largely commuters, law enforcement and small-business owners.

Each summer, the South Fork fills with the people who run Wall Street and corporate America. That makes the district one of the country’s busiest political ATMs, where financiers and industry titans host fundraisers for both parties. Suffolk County donors gave more than $45 million to campaigns in the 2020 cycle alone, according to OpenSecrets data CNBC cited.

In August, Vice President JD Vance raised more than $5 million from young Republican donors at the Southampton home of Omeed Malik, president of 1789 Capital and a prominent Trump donor.

LaLota, a Navy veteran and former Suffolk County elections commissioner, was first elected in 2022 to succeed Lee Zeldin and was re-elected in 2024, defeating former CNN anchor John Avlon by about 11 points. In that race, LaLota criticized Avlon for his dual residency in both Sag Harbor and Manhattan.

Gallant, 37, is an Army National Guard Black Hawk pilot, a former FAA air traffic controller at JFK, a former union leader and a volunteer firefighter. He won the June primary with about 63% of the vote, defeating Lukas Ventouras, a 25-year-old law student and district resident who had raised about $124,000, mostly in unitemized small-dollar donations. Gallant later picked up endorsements from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

After the Post story, Gallant’s attorney, Sara Azari, who previously represented former Rep. Eric Swalwell after misconduct allegations, confirmed the photos were authentic and consensual. Gallant told the New York Times he hoped it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” and the campaign began selling “Make Politics Sexy Again” merchandise. LaLota stuck to calling Gallant “weak and woke” and needling him for declining to debate.

Asked by Fortune about the surge, Gallant answered through Slingshot Strategies, a consulting firm that promises “a proven track record of shifting the conversation” for candidates facing “overwhelming odds” and “difficult fights.”

He said the Post story “backfired on them” and that the Times interview let voters see “a proud gay man who refused to be ashamed of his identity, and it resonated.” On LaLota’s outside money, he said, “I never had to rely on outside interests to try and buy this seat.” About a third of his own money from named donors came from inside the district.

LaLota cast the surge as a product of the controversy itself. “On the same days my opponent was backing out of debates, he was monetizing his BDSM and pornographic modeling past,” he said in a statement to Fortune. “Instead of boasting how kinky he is, as he did to the Times, he owes Long Islanders an explanation for choosing vanity and fundraising over debates and accountability.”

Fortune analyzed itemized contributions dated in 2026 in both campaigns’ raw FEC filings through Oct. 14, so the comparison covers the same stretch of the race for both candidates. Repeat donors were counted once, refunds subtracted and conduit entries adjusted so no gift was counted twice. The FEC does not require campaigns to name individuals who give $200 or less in a cycle, so those donors are excluded. Fortune placed donors inside or outside NY-1 based on the mailing city they listed, which may differ from where they vote. Individuals may give $3,500 per election this cycle, or $7,000 for the primary and general combined. Fortune tallied the filings by hand, then used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to clean the raw files and check the calculations.

LaLota had the bigger war chest. Through Oct. 14, he had raised $4.5 million and had $2.31 million in cash on hand. Gallant had raised $1.7 million and had $426,000 on hand.

The sharper contrast was where the money came from. Of the 785 named donors in LaLota’s 2026 filings, 29% listed mailing addresses in the district. Together they gave $207,161, only 16% of what he raised from named individuals. PACs and other committees supplied $1.18 million, about a quarter of his total for the cycle.

Gallant’s support was more local, but not by much. Of his 1,031 named donors in the 2026 raw file, 390 (38%) listed addresses in NY-1 and nearly $300,000, about a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals this year. Counting gifts from 2025, his itemized individual total for the cycle is $1.15 million.

Half of that in-district money, about $159,000, came from the Hamptons and Shelter Island, the East End enclaves where wealthy New Yorkers have long kept second homes. In East Hampton Town, half of the 22,562 housing units are no one’s usual residence, according to the Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 American Community Survey, which counts second homes as vacant. In Brookhaven, the figure is only about 9%.

Outside the district, 218 Manhattan donors gave Gallant $215,600 and 85 Californians gave about $93,000. Thirteen listed San Francisco.

The photos worked as a fundraiser, just not a local one. Between Sept. 13 and Oct. 14, Gallant reported 677 itemized contributions totaling $276,055: $229,050 from 484 individual donors and $47,005 from PACs, party committees and other sources.

That haul, all in the campaign’s final month of reporting, is about 16% of the $1.7 million he raised this cycle and nearly a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals in 2026. About a third of it arrived in the first four days after the leak.

On Sept. 15, two days after the leak, the New York State Democratic Committee transferred $25,025 to the campaign. That same day, the campaign paid Sara Azari, the celebrity attorney who specializes in crisis and media strategy.

Among the contributions that followed: $500 on Sept. 15 from Howard Sacarob, head of U.S. Tax at Royal Bank of Canada, and $3,500 on Oct. 4 from Ryan Fitzpatrick, Corcoran’s regional vice president for Downtown Manhattan.

On Oct. 7, the New York Times published its own analysis of the photo scandal. That day, Robert Saum, the World Bank Group’s regional country director for Eastern Europe, a role based in Kyiv, gave $1,000. He lists an Arlington, Va., address.

Steven Holley, COO of the New York investment manager Select Equity Group and former Sullivan & Cromwell partner, gave $1,000 on Oct. 9. Sacarob, Fitzpatrick and Holley all list New York City addresses, outside the district.

The San Francisco-based CEO of Mr. S Leather, the retailer behind the photos, gave $1,000 on Oct. 10.

Not all of Gallant’s best-known donors gave after the Post story. Fortune checked the names below against the dates in his filings.

Wall Street: Stephen Mandel, who founded the Greenwich hedge fund Lone Pine Capital, gave the $3,500 maximum on Sept. 14, the day after the story ran. Susan Mandel of Greenwich, listed as not employed, gave $3,500 the same day.

Old money and real estate: Katharine Rayner, the Cox Enterprises heiress whose fortune of about $4.9 billion (Forbes) rests on her estimated 17% stake in the family company, gave $3,500 on Sept. 15. She had also given $2,000 in July, and her cycle total is listed at the $3,500 limit.

Another maximum gift came on Sept. 26 from Michael Raynes, a developer who restores architecturally significant properties in Miami. In late 2022, he sold a historic estate in Southampton for $20 million. He lists a Miami Beach mailing address.

Wall Street: Charles Myers gave the $3,500 maximum at the end of 2025, when Gallant was still facing a primary. He is founder and chairman of Signum Global Advisors, a geopolitical research firm that advises financial institutions and touts “representation across the political spectrum.” He previously served as vice chairman at Evercore ISI and advised Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign.

Jason Carroll, co-founder of the high-frequency trading firm Hudson River Trading, gave $3,500 on Sept. 8, five days before the leak. Eric Knight, a senior trader at Jane Street, gave $7,000, covering both the primary and the general.

Hollywood and media: Kevin Huvane, co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency, gave $3,500 on June 30. Jeffrey Bewkes, the former Time Warner chairman and CEO who sold the company to AT&T in 2018, gave $3,500 on Aug. 12.

Local: Nancy Goroff, an organic chemist and former chair of Stony Brook University’s chemistry department, gave the maximum on June 29, days after Gallant’s primary win. Goroff lives in a modest New England saltbox overlooking Stony Brook Harbor, valued at about $1.1 million. She ran for a similarly drawn seat in 2020, losing to Lee Zeldin, now President Trump’s EPA administrator.

Goroff also backed “Team KCQ,” North Fork educator Kathryn Casey Quigley’s progressive bid to oust Suffolk County Democratic Chairman Rich Schaffer. Casey Quigley won about 43% of the weighted county committee vote on Sept. 22. Her campaign accused Schaffer of “backroom deals” with the local Conservative Party, which had harshly condemned Gallant’s photos.

Wall Street: Charles Schwab, founder of the brokerage bearing his name, a Fortune 500 company, gave LaLota $13,600 over the past two cycles, the maximum allowed. His mailing city: Palm Beach, Fla.

Crypto and defense: Faryar Shirzad, Coinbase’s chief policy officer and a deputy national security adviser under George W. Bush, gave $3,500 from a Washington, D.C., address. Palmer Luckey of Newport Beach, Calif., who founded defense contractor Anduril after selling Oculus to Facebook for about $2 billion, gave $7,000.

Global money: Leonard Blavatnik, the Ukrainian-born British American billionaire (Forbes) behind Access Industries, gave LaLota $3,500 in March. FEC reports list another $7,000 in aggregate from his wife, Emily.

“Though I have never met him, I appreciate his support,” LaLota said. His spokeswoman suggested Blavatnik may be drawn to LaLota because Russia’s Foreign Ministry put LaLota on a May 2023 list of 500 Americans barred from the country, a distinction the congressman “wears as a badge of honor.”

Blavatnik’s recent contributions also include Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and the Equality PAC, which backs LGBTQ+ candidates.

His contribution forms give an address of 40 W. 57th St. in Manhattan, about 105 miles from the estate the press calls his.

The July 2025 sale of 408 Further Lane in Amagansett, which Behind the Hedges reported as the most expensive residential sale in Hamptons history, lists Brise Lointaine LLC as the new owner.

The seller, Terry Semel, ran Warner Bros. when Stanley Kubrick filmed his masked Long Island society for the studio. Semel had bought the property from Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman in 2005 for $43 million.

Property records from the real estate data service PropertyShark, reviewed by Fortune, list the arm’s-length price as $115,000, three zeros shy of the reported $115 million. East Hampton’s 2026 tax roll still billed Semel’s Windsor Digital Studio LLC. The town assessor’s office said it did not update the roll until July 2026.

The East Hampton Town Clerk’s office confirmed Brise Lointaine LLC’s ownership to Fortune and said deed updates take “very long” to process, along with the Suffolk County Clerk’s office.

Press accounts, though not the paperwork, identify the buyer as LaLota donor Len Blavatnik: Behind the Hedges, citing a source, and The Real Deal. Blavatnik owns Warner Music and holds a stake in A24, the arthouse studio behind Lady Bird (2017), Queer (2024), the gay BDSM romance Pillion (2026) and Backrooms (2026).

The tabloid framing of the race borrowed from Eyes Wide Shut (1999), but the sex and the masks were bait. Kubrick’s real horror was a gated order where wealth and power circulate in a closed circle, insulated from consequences.

In his year, the guest list was paper: electronic filing stayed voluntary for most committees until 2000, so a donor was a scanned page, not a spreadsheet. In NY-1, the circle is no secret.

In an age of metadata, AI-scanned social feeds and Flock cameras, nobody wears a mask for long. The leather shoot was archived, authenticated by an attorney and sold back to voters as merchandise. Every FEC filing is a digital fossil Kubrick’s guests would never have left behind.

The economics were another matter. LaLota raised about 84 cents of every named dollar from outside the district; Gallant, nearly two-thirds. What stayed masked on Election Day was not Gallant’s leather photos but the money, and how much of it came from outside NY-1.

#5433. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 9:52 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

He quipped: “Yeah, I’m coming for AI’s job.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5432. Silicon Valley’s richest outspent supporters more than 10 to one to kill California’s billionaire tax—and won

California voters rejected a proposed tax on the state’s billionaires after some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives and investors spent $378.4 million to defeat it—delivering a victory to a coalition led by Google cofounder Sergey Brin.

The Associated Press called the race on Monday, with 52.8% of voters opposing Proposition 40 and 47.2% supporting it. The votes needed to pass the measure had trailed for days.

The defeat means—at least for now—an effort to make California the first state to impose a one-time tax on its billionaires has ended. It also represents a significant win for the Silicon Valley executives who have come together to block the measure.

Approximately 52.8% of voters opposed Proposition 40, whereas 47.2% supported it. According to CalMatters, ultrawealthy opponents collectively contributed $378.4 million to efforts opposing the tax and related countermeasures like Props 41 and 42. That amount is more than 10 times the $33.5 million raised by supporters of Proposition 40.

The defeat means, at least for now, an effort to make California the first state to impose a one-time tax on its billionaires has ended. It also represents a significant win for the Silicon Valley executives who have come together to block the measure.

Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of individuals worth more than $1 billion who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026. The proposed tax covered financial assets and other forms of wealth, rather than just income.

Under the proposal, approximately 90% of the revenue would have gone toward healthcare services, with the remaining 10% allocated to education and food assistance. The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated that the measure could generate “tens of billions” of dollars.

The initiative was introduced by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which argued that California needed additional revenue to address healthcare funding shortfalls following federal spending reductions under President Donald Trump’s tax and spending legislation. The measure also received support from Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, the California Democratic party and several labor organizations.

But not every Democrat and Californian was on the same page. The proposal faced opposition from prominent Democrats including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who argued that a state-level wealth tax would push wealthy residents and their businesses out of the state. Instead, Newsom said he would support a national wealth tax. San Francisco Democrats also opposed the measure, voting 17-4 against Prop 40 in August, while U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi, a member of the local party, voted “no endorsement.”

“Here is what I support: A national billionaires’ tax,” Newsom wrote in a post on Substack in June. “A true minimum tax on billionaires—a modern Buffett Rule—that ensures the people at the very top pay at least the tax rate their own workers pay.”

The campaign against the proposition was financed by some of the most prominent figures in the tech, finance and investment industries—with Brin emerging as its largest individual financial backer.

Brin contributed approximately $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he established in January that became the main vehicle opposing the wealth tax. The contributions made Brin one of the most consequential financial players in California’s 2026 ballot-measure fight. He relocated to Nevada in December 2025—making his fortune, estimated at $231 billion by Bloomberg, potentially exempt from the tax.

Eric Schmidt, Google’s former CEO, was also a major contributor to the opposition effort. According to campaign finance filings, he contributed $40.2 million to the campaign.

Other prominent tech executives and investors also contributed millions, including DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe cofounder Patrick Collison, venture capitalist John Doerr, cryptocurrency entrepreneur Chris Larsen and former Sequoia Capital partner Michael Moritz.

The contributions were also not limited to Building a Better California’s fight against Prop 40. Through Oct. 20, Building a Better California spent more than $304 million supporting efforts to defeat Proposition 40 and advance Propositions 41 and 42—direct counters to the wealth tax. Of that amount, approximately $118.5 million went toward opposing Proposition 40, while the other $186 million supported Propositions 41 and 42, according to Capital & Main.

Proposition 41 would “require preelection audits for initiatives proposing special taxes and additional audits every four years. It also would prohibit new tax revenue from being exempted from state spending limits,” making it harder for the state to use funds raised by the billionaire tax. Proposition 42 would “prohibit taxes on personal savings, assets and retirement holdings”—outlawing retroactive taxation, directly countering Proposition 40. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, if either one gets more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, the wealth tax could be stopped even if it is approved.

And while the wealth tax didn’t get approved, a ballot measure meant to block it did. According to the AP, Proposition 41 did not pass by voters while Proposition 42 did—meaning Proposition 40 would have been shot down if it had passed regardless.

According to Politico, more than 70 current and former California billionaires had spent a record $612 million into the state elections this cycle. Of that money, at least 30 billionaires had contributed more than $293 million specifically to the wealth tax fight.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5431. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

#5430. How ‘Boring’ Businesses Can Turn Black Friday Into a Competitive Advantage

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. Here’s how small businesses can attract customers, boost sales and stand out without big budgets.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. It’s also an opportunity for the hardworking small businesses we see every day, from bakeries and hair salons to cleaning companies and accounting firms.

I affectionately call them “boring” businesses, but there’s nothing boring about the people behind them. They’re the familiar neighborhood businesses we rely on every day, run by hardworking people who often wear several hats to keep things going.

And these traditional industries continue to attract new entrepreneurs. According to internal Tailor Brands business formation data, cleaning and home service businesses saw growth ranging from 60% to more than 300% in 2026, depending on the subcategory. But whether you’re just starting out or have been serving your community for years, the challenge is the same: finding ways to attract customers and keep them coming back.

Black Friday gives small businesses an opportunity to do both. A record 202.9 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday in 2025, up from 197 million in 2024, as reported by inBeat. While much of the attention goes to major retailers, local businesses can use the shopping season to reconnect with existing customers and give new ones a reason to try their services.

Having worked with many small businesses, I’ve learned that successful Black Friday campaigns don’t always require big budgets or massive discounts. Sometimes, a personal gesture or a clever offer can make all the difference.

Here are a few practical strategies, including examples from my own experience, to help everyday businesses make the most of Black Friday.

Whether you run a hair salon, accounting firm or neighborhood bakery, Black Friday can be an opportunity to generate sales from customers who already know and trust your business. Instead of competing for attention with another promotional email, try sending a handwritten offer.

Handwrytten’s Consumer Survey found that only 11% of consumers had recently received a handwritten note from a brand, and just 4% found them annoying. That makes handwritten outreach an interesting way to stand out during a season dominated by digital promotions.

I’ve seen this work firsthand. I once worked with a client whose cake business was on the verge of bankruptcy. With bills and taxes piling up, we asked the owner’s 10-year-old daughter to handwrite thank-you letters to existing customers, offering them a special Black Friday deal: buy cake credits now and redeem them anytime over the next 12 months.

We sold credits for 271 cakes at an average of almost €60 each, generating nearly €16,000 in Black Friday sales. That cash injection gave the business much-needed breathing room. Customers also loved the letters, and the heartwarming gesture helped turn them into even more loyal supporters.

The same idea can work for almost any local business. Hair salons can sell prepaid appointments, cleaning companies can offer service credits, and accountants can create annual packages. The trick is to combine a personal touch with an offer that brings in revenue today while giving customers something valuable tomorrow.

For hotels, Black Friday is an opportunity to sell discounted spa weekends, romantic getaways and prepaid stays during the quieter winter months. But travelers need to discover these offers before they can book them.

AI-powered travel planning creates another opportunity to reach potential guests. According to Wanderboat, 56% of active U.S. travelers used AI for some aspect of their travel experience in the previous year.

Yet ranking highly on Google doesn’t guarantee visibility in AI-generated answers. Heroic Rankings reports that Google’s AI overlooks approximately 62% of pages ranking in the top 10 traditional search results.

To improve their chances of appearing in AI-generated recommendations, hotels should make their Black Friday offers as specific as possible. Instead of simply advertising “40% off winter stays,” imagine a small hotel offering a “Two-night spa getaway for two in Asheville for $299, including breakfast and spa access, valid December 12–14.”

I’d create a dedicated page for that offer, clearly listing the price, dates, amenities, cancellation policy and booking conditions. I’d also add guest reviews and answer questions travelers might ask, such as whether parking is included or if the spa requires advance booking. Make sure the details match what’s listed on booking platforms and add appropriate structured data to help search engines understand the package.

The easier it is for AI to find and understand your offer, the better your chances of reaching travelers looking for exactly that kind of getaway.

But optimizing your own website is only part of the equation. I’d also try to get my Black Friday offer featured in local media, relevant industry websites and articles rounding up the best Black Friday deals. In its GEO research, CSP analyzed more than 70,000 AI answers across three industries in 2026 and found that 85 earned-media placements generated 5,697 AI citations. This shows why getting your offer mentioned on relevant third-party websites can be just as important as making it easy to find on your own.

Video can make even the most ordinary services more appealing. In fact, 85% of consumers say they’ve been convinced to buy a product or service after watching a video, as reported by Flova. Even less flashy businesses like accounting firms, plumbers and cleaning companies can use humor to make their Black Friday campaigns stand out.

Last year, while managing a marketing campaign for a cleaning company, I wanted to create a funny video, but the employees weren’t comfortable on camera. We used AI animation instead, creating a humorous clip about the mess after a holiday party. The video converted particularly well in paid campaigns, driving plenty of sales while also generating strong organic engagement.

What makes this approach even more attractive today is how affordable it has become to experiment. As GPTProto reports, short AI video clips can cost between $0.04 and $0.50 per generation. That doesn’t mean producing an entire campaign costs a few cents, but it does mean small businesses can test different concepts, jokes and visual styles without spending heavily on every attempt.

I’ve since started incorporating AI video into the marketing services I offer clients. For a small business with someone comfortable using AI tools, the opportunity isn’t simply to produce cheaper videos. It’s to experiment with more ideas, discover what resonates with customers and put the strongest creative into a Black Friday campaign.

Small businesses can try the same approach. Show a relatable problem, add some humor, and finish with a clear Black Friday offer. You don’t need a big budget to make an ordinary service memorable.

Organic search traffic is declining across many industries, partly because Google’s AI Overviews now answer informational queries directly. According to Get Stuff Digital, organic traffic declined by 20% to 35% in its analysis following the introduction of AI-powered search features.

But I don’t see this as a reason to panic. Small businesses don’t necessarily need more informational traffic. They need visitors who are ready to book or buy. That’s why I’d focus Black Friday SEO efforts on high-intent searches rather than trying to recover every lost click.

For example, a cleaning company could create a dedicated page targeting searches like “Black Friday cleaning deals in Chicago” or “holiday deep cleaning discounts in Chicago,” with a specific package, price and clear booking option. I’d publish that page in September, or early October at the latest, to give Google time to discover and index it before Black Friday. I’d also add a few relevant internal links from existing service pages and blog posts to help search engines find it.

The goal isn’t to attract the most traffic. It’s to make sure that when someone searches for a Black Friday deal on a service you provide, your business is there with an offer they can act on.

Black Friday isn’t just about attracting new customers. It’s also a chance to bring back shoppers who never completed their purchases.

The average cart abandonment rate is 70.22%, as reported by Knowcrunch. These shoppers have already shown interest, making them a valuable audience for Black Friday offers.

For my clients, I already use automated emails year-round to remind customers about products they’ve left in their carts. During Black Friday, I take this a step further by targeting shoppers who abandoned their carts in the past 30 to 60 days and sending them personalized emails with a limited-time discount.

AI agents can make this process even easier by helping generate messages based on the products each customer considered. Scalably reports that sales professionals expect AI agents to reduce email-drafting time by 36% once fully implemented. In my experience, automating these repetitive follow-ups can save even more time, especially when you’re managing campaigns for multiple clients.

For example, a furniture store could automatically email someone who abandoned a sofa in their cart, remind them of the exact product and offer a Black Friday discount with a direct link to checkout. The system should also exclude customers who’ve already completed their purchases, so they don’t receive unnecessary reminders.

Instead of spending your entire Black Friday budget attracting new visitors, use automated emails and timely discounts to bring interested shoppers back and turn abandoned carts into sales.

One of the first rules of marketing is to be where your customers are. And sometimes, that’s behind the wheel. Munley Law highlights that Americans spend an average of 60.2 minutes driving each day. For local businesses, that creates an opportunity to reach customers during the busy Black Friday weekend.

Run short, frequent local radio ads with one clear offer and a promo code. Leave flyers with a time-limited deal on parked cars in busy shopping areas, where local rules allow.

Extend your opening hours over the holiday weekend and add them as special hours in your Google Business Profile. Drivers searching “near me” early in the morning or late in the evening may be looking for businesses they can visit immediately, so longer hours give you more opportunities to attract them. Add your offers to the profile too, and if your business allows it, offer curbside pickup.

Plan for parking, too. Reserve a few spots near the entrance for pickups. If you need more, offer to rent a few spaces from a neighbor just for the holiday weekend. Many will say no, but a small business only needs a handful of spots, and some neighbors will gladly take a few extra dollars for them. Then tell customers where to park in your emails and Google Business Profile.

On Cyber Monday, extend the deal online for anyone who heard the ad but didn’t make it in.

Giving away a small service can be a smart Black Friday strategy when it helps customers take the first step toward a much larger purchase. A limited-time offer gives them a reason to act now rather than keep postponing their decision.

Dental practices are a good example. According to Myra, 23% of adults have delayed dental treatment because of its cost. Offering a free initial consultation during Black Friday can remove that first financial barrier and encourage patients to explore treatments they might otherwise put off.

For example, a dental practice could invite patients considering implants, veneers or orthodontic treatment to book a complimentary examination and personalized treatment plan, with clinically appropriate imaging where needed. The dentist can explain the options, discuss installment payments if available and help patients understand the costs before committing.

And it’s not always just about money. Some patients feel anxious about visiting the dentist or discovering they need extensive treatment. A free, no-obligation first appointment can make that step feel less intimidating while giving the practice an opportunity to build trust.

The appointment can take place after Black Friday, as long as it’s booked during the promotion. For treatments involving a significant financial commitment, even a few new patients could make the offer worthwhile.

If there’s one thing I’ve learned from working with small businesses, it’s that a successful Black Friday campaign doesn’t have to be complicated or expensive. Sometimes, understanding your customers and coming up with a creative offer is enough to stand out.

My advice is to pick one or two strategies that make sense for your business, test them, and learn from the results. You might be surprised by what works.

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. It’s also an opportunity for the hardworking small businesses we see every day, from bakeries and hair salons to cleaning companies and accounting firms.

I affectionately call them “boring” businesses, but there’s nothing boring about the people behind them. They’re the familiar neighborhood businesses we rely on every day, run by hardworking people who often wear several hats to keep things going.

And these traditional industries continue to attract new entrepreneurs. According to internal Tailor Brands business formation data, cleaning and home service businesses saw growth ranging from 60% to more than 300% in 2026, depending on the subcategory. But whether you’re just starting out or have been serving your community for years, the challenge is the same: finding ways to attract customers and keep them coming back.

#5429. 60 million children got Trump Accounts. Fewer than 1% were claimed in the first week

Ashok Paudel (CPA, MBA) is a finance professional based in Munich, Germany.

Every finance team member has some experience with a suspense account, the place where money/transaction remains parked when nobody can match it to an owner. Controllers watch it closely, because a balance you can’t trace to a person isn’t really an asset yet. America has just opened tens of millions of children’s accounts that will need the same kind of matching.

On Oct. 1 the Treasury said it had finished automatically creating investment accounts for more than 60 million children; with those opened earlier, the total is about 70 million. Babies born from 2025 through 2028 qualify for a $1,000 federal deposit. Michael and Susan Dell say they have now put $250 into the accounts of almost 25 million children. Unlike the federal seed, which arrives only after a parent claims the account, the Dell money was deposited without any claim. The money sits in low-cost U.S. stock index funds. BNY runs the initial accounts as the Treasury’s financial agent, with Robinhood as broker and initial trustee.

A week later, according to Bloomberg Law, Helen Morrison, Treasury benefits tax counsel, speaking in her personal capacity at an American Bar Association tax meeting, said roughly 164,000 of the 60 million new accounts had been claimed. That’s less than 1%. It’s early. The program will succeed or fail at the claim, not the deposit.

Two failures are already built into the design. The first is an account a parent never claims. Under the Treasury’s rules, a parent has to claim the account in an app, verifying identity and relationship, before the $1,000 federal seed arrives or relatives and employers can contribute. Without that claim, the federal money never arrives. An unclaimed account that received Dell’s $250 holds that deposit; one that got neither the federal seed nor Dell money is an empty shell opened automatically. The second is an account that was funded but lost at 18, when a young adult has to find it and prove it’s theirs. Both depend on paperwork families often lose.

Britain’s Child Trust Fund shows how the second failure plays out. Children born between 2002 and early 2011 got a fund seeded with at least £250; the state opened one when parents didn’t. In September, HM Revenue & Customs said that of roughly 3.8 million accounts matured since 2020, around 827,000, more than one in five, were still unclaimed, averaging £2,310 each. That’s roughly £1.9 billion still waiting to be handed back. Britain has set up a government-and-industry taskforce to find the owners. In the U.S., the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators estimates that about one in seven Americans has property sitting unclaimed with a state.

The firms holding these accounts should care for two reasons. One is compounding. A $1,000 seed earning 7% a year would be worth about $3,400 at 18 if left invested. What happens to a Trump Account that loses touch with its owner is still an open question. These are federally created IRAs for minors, and state unclaimed-property clocks typically don’t start until an account is payable or distributable, often not before adulthood, so the money probably stays invested. Growth is worthless, though, to an owner who never receives it. If America does no better than Britain, where more than a fifth of matured accounts sit unclaimed, millions of young adults will start out without the stake they were given.

The other is commercial. A custodian holding millions of tiny, unclaimed accounts carries the servicing cost and regulatory risk without the client relationship. A reachable owner is a future customer. A lost one is a liability.

The money abroad was stranded by a design that left tracking to the people least able to do it. Families move and lose letters; phone numbers change. Every institution knew whose money it was on day one, and over the years that link broke.

On a software go-live across seven entities across three continents, my team agreed with each stakeholder on who owned which activity, and major issues still arose months later. A sign-off before launch did not give us an owner for each balance; only a monthly check did. For a program that runs across the Treasury, the IRS and the custodian, bodies that do not always talk to each other, that monthly check matters even more.

The same discipline applies here. Each account should stay tied to the Social Security number, and whoever holds the account should check contact details against official records every year, as brokers already screen customers for identity and sanctions.

The rule I would change is the one that makes core money wait on a form. Israel’s savings plan for every child, running since 2017, deposits a monthly sum for every child receiving child allowance and pays the management fees until age 21. For about a third of children born in 2023, the National Insurance Institute reported, parents never chose a fund, so the money was placed by default, and still arrived.

The handover at 18 deserves the care a brokerage gives a product launch, not a letter in the mail. Well before that birthday, the young owner should be able to see the account on a phone, with a plain statement of what it holds and what it has earned. Israel adds a grant of 582 shekels at 21 for savers who leave the money invested.

Done well, this could be a powerful investor-education tool. A statement showing $1,000 growing over 18 years teaches compounding better than any lecture. A forgotten account teaches nothing, and on a custodian’s books it is just another balance in suspense.
