#5428. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5427. This Billionaire Invested in OpenAI in 2019. Here’s What He’s Betting on Next.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This billionaire is betting that AI will revamp websites as we know them.

He made billions betting on what’s next. Now this 71-year-old investor’s latest move reflects his conviction that AI will change how the Internet works.

Vinod Khosla’s venture capital firm, Khosla Ventures, made early investments in OpenAI, DoorDash and Instacart. His latest investment, AI startup Coframe, targets another potential shift: how websites operate. Coframe wants to rewire the Internet so every visitor to a website sees a page custom-made for them.

“The world has changed because AI has enabled extreme customization,” Khosla said in an interview with Business Insider. Forbes reported earlier this year that Khosla’s net worth is around $10 billion.

Coframe announced this week that it raised $35 million in total funding, including a $25 million Series A led by Khosla Ventures and Hanabi Capital. Executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind also participated.

Coframe helps businesses improve their websites so more people buy something, sign up for something or take another desired action. The startup creates and tests different versions of a webpage, including text, images and design. It then tracks how visitors interact with the webpage to determine how to improve it.

For example, say an online store wants to sell more shoes. Coframe could help the company test different headlines, product images or page layouts and determine which versions lead to more purchases.

“For decades, the web has been frozen in place, showing every visitor essentially the same page,” Khosla said in the press release. “Coframe is building the living internet, where two people can visit the same website and have completely different experiences, personalized to who they are and what they need. These interfaces continuously learn and improve themselves. This is a huge leap beyond traditional A/B testing and the next iteration of the internet.”

Coframe claims that it can help businesses get more out of the visitors they already have and spend far less time figuring out how to capitalize on their audiences. The startup said in the press release that its AI-powered testing platform has helped customers generate more than $300 million in additional revenue, with conversion rates improving by more than 20% on average.

Coframe’s customers include Dropbox, BCG, Block, Backcountry and Sur La Table.

Speed is another part of the startup’s appeal. Coframe said it built and launched an experiment for Dropbox in 30 minutes that previously would have required four weeks of engineering, design and quality-assurance work. For an unnamed Fortune 500 customer, the company said it launched dozens of variations and increased conversions by 70% within 30 days of the contract being signed.

The idea is to let businesses try more approaches without adding weeks of production work each time. Faster testing can help teams identify promising changes and move past unsuccessful ones sooner.

Khosla sees AI as a way to deliver an experience built around each visitor to a website, like Coframe is doing.

“The alternative is to write code for every page that’s presented, but that’s too expensive and way too slow,” Khosla told Business Insider. “This idea of a customized page for every user is a really good idea.”

He made billions betting on what’s next. Now this 71-year-old investor’s latest move reflects his conviction that AI will change how the Internet works.

#5426. Verizon’s CEO turned down the job several times before leaving retirement on his ranch: ‘I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude’

Dan Schulman thought he had traded the corner office for cowboy boots for good. After nearly a decade running digital payments giant PayPal, he was enjoying retirement on a Montana ranch with his wife, Summerly, and roughly 900 head of cattle. He was happy, in love, and had no desire to return to the grueling CEO schedule.

So when his fellow Verizon board members came calling for him to step in as CEO, he said no. Several times.

But the telecommunications giant was losing market share, falling behind competitors, and struggling with a bureaucracy. Eventually, a sense of obligation—and some convincing from his wife—brought him out of retirement to take the top job in October 2025.

“I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude,” Schulman told Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell in the latest episode of Fortune 500: Titans and Disruptors of Industry. A year later, he said, he’s “absolutely loving it and pretty hopeful about our future.”

The reluctant hire is now one year into a three-year turnaround plan for Verizon, a Fortune 500 company with $138 billion in revenue last year. The early numbers are moving his way.

The former PayPal chief had stepped down in 2023 and retirement gave him plenty of time to embrace his inner cowboy. The New Jersey native had been wearing cowboy boots since eighth grade, long before he had a ranch—or cattle—to go with them.

“I really didn’t want to come back into the CEO job,” he said. “These jobs are all-consuming. You’re putting in 10 to 14 hours a day.”

Verizon, as it turns out, knows a thing or two about making repeat calls. Although Schulman may have been ready to hang up on corporate life, it wasn’t ready to part ways with him just yet.

He had sat on Verizon’s board since 2018 and had been its lead independent director since December 2024. He knew the management team, understood the business, and had watched the company struggle to compete. He was already the board’s backup plan.

“I was the hit-by-the-bus scenario,” he said. If anything had happened to then-CEO Hans Vestberg, “I would go in temporarily.”

Verizon had been losing market share for roughly five years, Schulman said. Once first in its industry by market capitalization, it had fallen to last, and its longtime reputation for having a superior wireless network was no longer enough to keep customers from looking elsewhere.

“We had the lowest P/E, which is what the Street thinks of our future growth potential,” he said.

Schulman acknowledged the board probably should have acted sooner. It had developed a plan to address the company’s struggles, but the strategy didn’t deliver. Quoting his father, he put it this way: “People plan, God laughs.”

“We had a plan. It didn’t work out, so we had to go to Plan B, which was me, not Plan A,” he said.

Despite his reservations, Schulman believed Verizon still had the assets to turn things around, including what he estimated at 150 million customer lines. The board kept asking. In the end, it was Summerly who convinced him, reminding her husband that he could still make a difference.

Once he accepted, Schulman wasn’t interested in easing into the job.

At his first all-employee meeting, he delivered a blunt assessment of the company’s problems without notes or slides. Verizon had become a “big, lumbering giant that had fallen behind,” he said, with a hierarchical culture, slow decision-making, and processes that required something like 35 signatures to move forward.

He also warned employees that layoffs were likely.

That warning became reality in November 2025, just weeks after he took over, when Verizon began cutting more than 13,000 jobs, the largest round of layoffs in its history. Verizon had cut 2,000 or 3,000 people, often through voluntary buyouts, every year, Schulman said. He wanted the cuts to free up money to reinvest in the business, and to show employees this turnaround was different.

“I needed to show this was different, that I was very serious about the change that was going to happen,” he said. “Playing to win is not just a slogan for me or a nice marketing thing.”

His strategy centers on replacing Verizon’s risk-averse culture with one willing to experiment, make decisions faster, and put customers ahead of internal processes. That means rethinking what Verizon has long put first.

The network is “foundational to everything we do,” Schulman said, but “it can’t be about the network. It has to be about the customer.”

The overhaul is beginning to show up in the numbers. In the third quarter of 2026, Verizon added a net 406,000 postpaid phone lines, up from 44,000 a year earlier. Its promotional costs to acquire customers fell 41%, and free cash flow rose 12% to $7.8 billion.

Part of the shift came from breaking an industry habit of luring customers with free phones and promotional offers.

“A free line is not really a net add from my perspective,” Schulman said.

Still, he knows the turnaround is far from over. He expects it to take three years, and the company has extended his contract through December 2028 to see it through.

The ranch will have to wait. Asked how he’ll judge his tenure when he eventually hands Verizon to a successor, Schulman pointed first to customer trust, then to pride inside a company many had written off as too big and too bureaucratic to change.

“We’re surprising a lot of people right now,” he said, “and it feels good when that happens.”

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

#5425. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:42 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

#5424. The Great Wealth Transfer Is About More Than Money. Here’s What’s Being Overlooked.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

We’re talking about the Great Wealth Transfer too narrowly. Here’s why millions of heirs are looking to value and sell inherited jewelry.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When economists and financial advisors talk about the Great Wealth Transfer, the conversation almost always centers on traditional financial assets: brokerage accounts, primary residences, retirement accounts and family businesses.

These numbers are massive, to be sure. Cerulli Associates estimates that $124 trillion will transfer through 2048, with $105 trillion passing directly to heirs. Nearly $100 trillion of that sum will originate with baby boomers and older generations.

Yet wealth does not sit exclusively on a balance sheet. It lives inside our homes, stored in safes, tucked into back drawers and resting quietly in velvet jewelry boxes.

It’s estimated that half of the gold ever mined in human history exists today as jewelry. Millions of families are about to inherit gold jewelry, luxury watches, diamonds, heirloom rings, coins and precious metals alongside standard investment portfolios.

We are not just approaching a Great Wealth Transfer. We are on the precipice of the Great Jewelry Transfer. Unlike a stock portfolio or checking account, heirloom pieces rarely arrive with a neat financial statement telling heirs what they own, leaving many unprepared when it’s time to evaluate, keep or sell inherited jewelry.

When people inherit jewelry, emotional value and real financial worth collide.

Most heirs can tell you the backstory without missing a beat:

What they rarely understand is the asset itself.

They’re left asking basic financial questions: Is this real? Is it worth $200 or $20,000? Does the value come from the gold, the quality of the stones, the brand or the item’s vintage status? And ultimately, what’s the right move: keep it, insure it, divide it among siblings or sell it?

Without clear answers on metal purity or stone quality, deciding whether to keep, divide or sell inherited jewelry becomes an educated guess made during an already stressful time.

Furthermore, younger generations often don’t want to inherit physical clutter. Modern estate research indicates that millennials and Gen Z heirs prefer a small, curated selection of meaningful possessions over taking custody of an entire household’s worth of heirlooms.

Inheriting an asset and understanding an asset are two completely different things.

This generational hand-off is occurring alongside a seismic shift in consumer behavior: the mainstream adoption of secondhand commerce.

Buying secondhand used to carry a subtle stigma; today it’s a mainstream consumer movement driven by younger consumers who actively prioritize circularity, sustainability and the unique appeal of vintage items. According to data from Deloitte, the broader U.S. resale market is projected to reach $73 billion by 2028, while the number of U.S. fashion brands hosting resale platforms on their own sites increased 325% between 2021 and 2025.

For the jewelry market, this shift changes everything.

A piece one generation no longer wants to wear doesn’t suddenly lose its intrinsic value. Its lifecycle can seamlessly evolve: Kept → Valued → Sold → Recycled → Worn by someone new.

This expands the concept of a circular economy beyond traditional “cash for gold” operations. The next generation doesn’t have to choose between keeping Grandma’s jewelry in a drawer forever or shipping it off to a refinery to be melted down.

When I founded Alloy, our initial premise was straightforward: The traditional process to sell gold jewelry, or any other high-value estate piece, was unnecessarily opaque and fundamentally built to favor the buyer over the consumer.

After working with thousands of consumers, one thing became clear quickly: Many customers acquired their pieces through inheritance, estate management or a major life transition. We quickly realized our main job wasn’t just facilitating a sale; it was helping people understand what they actually owned.

Solving that problem requires three foundational pillars:

That third pillar, optionality, is where the market’s future lies.

Historically, the secondary jewelry market has been deeply fragmented. A consumer sells a piece to a local business. That business flips it to another intermediary. Some pieces get resold; others are melted. Throughout the entire process, the original owner has zero insight into the asset’s true destination or value.

At The Alloy Market, we are building the infrastructure to connect these fragmented lifecycles.

By providing upfront valuation tools, real-time calculators and educational resources, we empower consumers to understand the exact value of their items before deciding. When an item is sold, our ecosystem evaluates whether to reintroduce it to the consumer market as a wearable piece, returning a portion of that resale upside to the original seller or whether to return its metals responsibly to the industrial supply chain.

We’re not merely building a better way to sell inherited jewelry; we’re building the underlying digital infrastructure that lets high-value physical assets transition smoothly from one generation to the next.

Leaving things behind isn’t new. But we’ve never seen a handoff like this, where trillions of dollars in physical items land with a generation that thinks very differently about what’s worth keeping, selling or passing along.

Some inherited jewelry will remain in families for another century. Some will be sold for financial liquidity. Some will be melted for reuse. And a growing percentage will find a second life with a new owner who appreciates its history.

The companies that win this transition won’t simply be those offering to buy these assets. They will be the trusted institutions that help heirs understand what they have and empower them to decide what happens next.

While standard wealth management focuses on paper assets and balance sheets, the Great Jewelry Transfer is about what happens to the physical history families leave behind. Trillions are at stake, but the real value is in the objects themselves.

When economists and financial advisors talk about the Great Wealth Transfer, the conversation almost always centers on traditional financial assets: brokerage accounts, primary residences, retirement accounts and family businesses.

These numbers are massive, to be sure. Cerulli Associates estimates that $124 trillion will transfer through 2048, with $105 trillion passing directly to heirs. Nearly $100 trillion of that sum will originate with baby boomers and older generations.

Yet wealth does not sit exclusively on a balance sheet. It lives inside our homes, stored in safes, tucked into back drawers and resting quietly in velvet jewelry boxes.

#5423. David Ellison’s Skydance replaces DC Studios bosses James Gunn and Peter Safran with a Marvel veteran

Skydance has removed James Gunn and Peter Safran as co-chairmen and co-CEOs of DC Studios, ending a four-year run that began with a hit Superman and was expected to survive the company’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.

Their replacement is Jeremy Latcham, a former Marvel Studios executive who helped launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Skydance Motion Picture Group announced the change on Nov. 9. Latcham starts Dec. 1 as president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, overseeing its film, television, and animation slate.

The move puts Batman, Superman, Wonder Woman, and the rest of the DC Comics roster under new creative control barely a month after Skydance closed its deal. It also resets a franchise strategy that Warner Bros. has now restarted twice in 13 years.

Paramount completed its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6 and renamed the combined company Skydance. Early reports said Gunn and Safran would keep their jobs, even as Warner Bros. film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy were expected to give way to Paramount’s Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein.

That assurance did not hold. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz visited Gunn and Safran’s office on Nov. 6 to deliver the news in person.

Gunn and Safran will still produce DC projects, and they are finishing post-production on Man of Tomorrow, the Superman sequel slated for July 2027. Latcham reports to Goldberg and Greenstein, now co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

“I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era,” Latcham said in a statement.

Gunn and Safran took over DC Studios on Nov. 1, 2022, hired to reboot the DC characters as a single connected universe. The deal came months after Discovery merged with WarnerMedia to form Warner Bros. Discovery.

Gunn arrived as a proven voice in the genre. He wrote and directed all three Guardians of the Galaxy films for Marvel, then made his DC debut with The Suicide Squad in 2021. Safran produced that film, other DC adaptations of the 2010s, and the Conjuring films for Warner Bros.’ New Line Cinema.

Their first release, Gunn’s Superman, opened to $217 million globally in July 2025 and finished with $618.7 million worldwide. It introduced David Corenswet as the Man of Steel and set up a wider universe of familiar DC characters.

The second did not soar. Supergirl cost a reported $170 million and became one of DC Studios’ worst opening-weekend flops this summer, grossing $126 million worldwide amid weak reviews.

The third paid off. Clayface, an R-rated body-horror film made for a reported $44 million, opened at No. 1 and had grossed $109 million worldwide as of Nov. 8. On television, the pair delivered a second season of Peacemaker, the animated Creature Commandos, and HBO’s Lanterns, a hit when it debuted in August.

Latcham was part of the founding team at Marvel Studios under Kevin Feige. He worked on Iron Man, The Avengers, and Tom Holland’s Spider-Man films, and he collaborated with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy.

He left Marvel in 2017 to found Latcham Pictures, whose films include Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves and Bad Times at the El Royale. DC is his return to superheroes.

The task he inherits has defeated Warner Bros. before. The studio’s first attempt at a Marvel-style connected universe, the DC Extended Universe, began with Zack Snyder’s Man of Steel in 2013 and ended with Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom in 2023, after Gunn and Safran had already been hired to start over.

In between came a decade of uneven results, from Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice and Wonder Woman to The Flash and Black Adam. Unlike Marvel’s tightly linked films, the DCEU fractured. Suicide Squad and The Suicide Squad are entirely separate movies released five years apart.

Troubled productions and turnover behind the camera made it worse. Fans campaigned for years after the 2017 theatrical Justice League until Warner Bros. released Snyder’s original vision as Zack Snyder’s Justice League in 2021.

Warner Bros. also kept DC stories outside the main universe. The CW’s Arrowverse, including Arrow, The Flash, Supergirl, and Black Lightning, built its own connected TV world. On the big screen, 2019’s Joker and 2022’s The Batman stood apart from the DCEU.

The split continued under Gunn and Safran. Joker: Folie à Deux arrived in 2024, while Matt Reeves’ Batman films and HBO’s The Penguin remain in their own world. John Cena’s Peacemaker, meanwhile, carried over from the old universe into the new one.

The near-term slate is set. Man of Tomorrow remains on the calendar, and Reeves’ The Batman: Part II is still in production, with Steven Soderbergh recently brought in to shoot the remaining scenes. The series The People v. Gorilla Grodd is also in the works.

Beyond that, little is settled. It is not yet clear whether Corenswet’s Superman continues after Man of Tomorrow, whether Lanterns gets a second season, or whether Latcham starts over from scratch and hands fans another round of whiplash. Whether the universe Gunn and Safran built survives is a Riddler-worthy mystery.

Latcham helped build Hollywood’s most successful franchise once. Nearly two decades after Iron Man, he will find out whether that origin story can be repeated, or whether the superhero universe no longer comes with a reliable playbook.

#5422. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

#5421. Anthropic Cut Its IPO Target by Hundreds of Billions — Here’s How Much Its Founders Will Now Likely Pocket

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A late AI selloff pushed big investors to demand a lower price. The payday will still be enormous.

Anthropic’s IPO is coming in cheaper than Wall Street once expected, but its founders aren’t exactly hurting. The Claude maker is now targeting a valuation of about $1.33 trillion, according to The Wall Street Journal. That’s lower than the roughly $2 trillion floated a few months ago, and it’s under the $1.5 trillion investors were expecting as recently as last week.

What changed? Last week’s AI selloff rattled major investors, and they pushed for a lower number.

The numbers are still eye-popping. Anthropic plans to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece, which would raise more than $61 billion at the midpoint. Investors, including Google and AMD, are adding another $26 billion on top of that. Shares are expected to hit the Nasdaq next Thursday under the ticker “ANT.”

Then there are the seven founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, President Daniela Amodei. Each one is selling about $250 million worth of stock and will still hold a stake worth around $18 billion. Together, they’ll own about 22% of the company, but an LLC they control locks in 50.1% of most shareholder votes.

#5420. Inside Dan Schulman’s war on the old Verizon

The former PayPal CEO left a Montana ranch to shake up one of America’s most profitable companies.

At his first companywide meeting after becoming Verizon’s CEO in October 2025, Dan Schulman dispensed with the usual corporate pleasantries. Speaking without notes or slides, he delivered a message that employees of the telecommunications giant weren’t used to hearing from the top: Verizon had surrendered market share to AT&T, -T-Mobile, and lower-cost providers, and its sprawling bureaucracy had become a problem. The company was losing badly. And, he warned, layoffs were coming.

It was a stark introduction to a new leader who, until recently, had been watching the deterioration unfold from a seat on Verizon’s board. Then 67, he had left an idyllic retirement in Montana to roll up his sleeves and fix it.

Schulman had at first been reluctant to take the top job, turning down the offer twice. But he also felt a sense of responsibility to its customers, shareholders, and employees. Should the board have acted sooner? “Yes, we probably should have,” he concedes. Ultimately, his wife persuaded him that he could make a difference. “I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude,” he says, but adds that now he’s “absolutely loving it.”

He also came in determined to dismantle the bureaucracy that had made even simple decisions needlessly complicated. The company, he says, had become “a big lumbering giant that had fallen behind.” In some cases, approving a decision required 35 signatures.

Verizon’s competitive troubles were mounting, too. In 2024, T-Mobile added a net 3.1 million postpaid phone lines and AT&T added 1.65 million; Verizon added less than 900,000. In the first three quarters of 2025, Verizon’s consumer business lost a net 414,000 postpaid phone lines, including 356,000 in the first quarter alone. Verizon remains the largest U.S. wireless carrier, generating billions in profits. But as its peers have narrowed the gap in network quality, the advantage that once let Verizon command a premium is becoming a baseline expectation for any major wireless carrier.

As if Verizon’s existing challenges weren’t daunting enough, Elon Musk’s company, SpaceX, purchased an $8 billion portfolio of low-band cellular spectrum licenses in October, a move that lays the groundwork to compete more directly with traditional wireless giants.

For years, Verizon summed up its pitch to American consumers in a familiar TV refrain: “Can you hear me now? Good.” The commercials featured a bespectacled Verizon employee, played by actor Paul Marcarelli, roaming the country and testing his service in remote locations. The catchphrase became a cultural touchstone, helping cement Verizon’s reputation for network reliability.

But over time, that advantage became harder to monetize as network coverage became less of a differentiator and consumers increasingly judged carriers on the overall customer experience, from their monthly bills to the deals available when they needed a new phone. “Customers don’t want to pay for a great network; that’s the expectation,” says Kevin Zavaglia, Verizon’s chief commercial officer for sales and service. (Adding insult to injury, Marcarelli resurfaced in 2016 as pitchman for rival Sprint, this time touting its network.)

Just over a year into Schulman’s tenure, Verizon is showing early signs of a turnaround. In the third quarter, it gained a net 406,000 phone lines, compared with just 44,000 a year earlier, its strongest third-quarter showing in five years. It also added 137,000 customer accounts, its best quarterly performance in more than a decade, even as the company slashed spending on promotional offers by 41%.

One tendency he encountered at Verizon was managers setting goals they were confident they could meet, then treating hitting those targets as success. Schulman recalls a manager proudly presenting a plan to raise a sales closing rate from 15% to 25%. “So, are you saying at the end of that, we are losing 75% of the time?” Schulman asked incredulously.

He’s pushing executives to set more ambitious goals, even if that means missing some targets, rather than consistently meeting easy ones. “Anytime the pace of change external is greater than the pace of change internal,” he says, “you’re falling behind.”

Tony Skiadas, Verizon’s chief financial officer, described how the company’s pricing strategy had become a costly cycle. Verizon had raised prices, contributing to customer defections, then spent heavily on promotions to win customers back. “We’ve seen that movie before over the years, and we know how it ends,” he says.

Roxanne Austin, a Verizon director, recalls watching the company finish third among the major wireless carriers for 20 consecutive quarters, losing customers and market share while management kept prioritizing network infrastructure over customers’ changing needs. “I’m like, ‘Guys, we’ve got to pay attention. Something’s happening,’ ” she remembers thinking. “Our playbook didn’t change for five years.” (Hans Vestberg, Verizon’s CEO from 2018 to 2025, declined to comment.)

Austin likens the scale and urgency of Schulman’s turnaround task to “turning an ocean liner at the speed of a race car.” And given the complexity of telecommunications, she adds, he must somehow “land that ocean liner on the moon, too.”

After stepping down as PayPal’s CEO in 2023 after nearly a decade at the helm, Schulman had settled happily into retirement on a Montana ranch. He rode horses daily, helped herd the couple’s roughly 900 head of cattle, and spent time with his children. Schulman, who was originally from New Jersey but had worn cowboy boots since eighth grade, finally had the lifestyle to match his footwear. “I did not miss the CEO job at all,” he says. Now, back on an executive’s grueling schedule, Schulman wants to make every hour count.

The mantra for the company’s new era under Schulman is familiar corporate gospel: Put customers first. But living up to it will require fundamental shifts at Verizon, including sacrificing some short-term revenue to rebuild customer trust. One of Schulman’s early decisions was to cancel a planned price increase. Verizon is also looking to compete more aggressively for customers with deals like the new Simplicity offering, which lowers the starting monthly price for a single line from $65 to as low as $30. And to reduce churn, it is offering incentives for customers to bundle cell phone service with home internet, including its Fios service.

Schulman made steep cost cuts, including the promised layoffs: A month after his appointment Verizon cut roughly 13,000 jobs, or about 13% of the workforce. Verizon had conducted smaller rounds of layoffs before, but Schulman wanted to send a stronger signal. “I really needed to show that this was different,” he says. “That I was very serious about the change that was going to happen.”

Schulman has set uncompromising expectations. He demands intensity, long hours, and a willingness to make difficult decisions. He expects managers to know their businesses inside out and answer questions on the spot. In meetings, when executives suggest taking a discussion offline, he challenges them: “Why would we take it offline? Like, we’re all here.”

Schulman readily describes himself as competitive and exacting of his employees, and he accepts that some may find his leadership style too demanding and leave. “And I’m okay with it, one way or another,” he says. As he puts it, “Heaven and hell are the same place. It’s just heaven for some and hell for others.”

The growing demand for infrastructure to support artificial intelligence offers new opportunities for Verizon, particularly in providing the high-capacity fiber networks connecting data centers. Verizon has signed agreements with Google, Amazon Web Services, and others worth billions, Schulman says.

AI is also helping improve systems within Verizon—for example, tools that help customer service employees quickly find information about plans, products, and policies. Zavaglia says AI has cut about six minutes from the in-store phone buying process.

As for Musk’s threat to challenge the incumbents in the mobile business, Schulman says he takes SpaceX’s ambitions “quite seriously.” But he estimates that building a network to rival Verizon’s would could take four to six years and cost some $300 billion. SpaceX also has other businesses competing for investment and attention, he points out. And even if Musk commits the resources, Schulman argues, he could end up with a network much like Verizon’s, without a significant cost advantage.

“Frankly, at that point, I welcome the opportunity to compete against them,” Schulman said during Verizon’s quarterly earnings call in October. “It’s very hard to throw a punch against something that doesn’t exist. But once they come into the market, we will be ferociously competitive.”

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

Ruth Umoh is the C-suite and Leadership editor at Fortune. She also authors Fortune’s Next to Lead newsletter.

#5419. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

#5418. Shake Shack Opened a Record 21 Stores in 3 Months — Here’s Their One Strict Rule for Growth That’s Paying Off

CEO Rob Lynch says new Shacks aren’t cannibalizing each other, and Wall Street likes what it’s hearing.

If a Shake Shack opens in your neighborhood, don’t expect another one nearby. Unlike some brands that flood the zone with locations (we’re talking to you, Starbucks), the burger chain doesn’t build a new store within 10 miles of an existing one, at least outside Manhattan, according to CEO Rob Lynch.

That doesn’t mean Shake Shack is growing. It opened a record 21 Shacks last quarter and 54 so far this year, with as many as 65 expected by year’s end. Lynch believes the U.S. has room for at least 1,500, Restaurant Business reports.

The biggest risk of opening stores this fast is cannibalization, where a new location steals sales from an existing one. That’s what the 10-mile rule is designed to prevent. Lynch says the only overlap comes from delivery, since a typical delivery radius is about 7 miles.

So far, the 10-mile strategy seems to be working. Same-store sales rose 2.5% in the third quarter, the fifth straight quarter of growth, even though new shacks open with lower sales than the chain’s $4 million average. Revenue climbed 15.2% to $423.3 million, and the stock jumped nearly 9% on Monday.

#5417. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5416. North Korea Hackers Launches Elon Musk Memecoins to Launder $6.4B Binance Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

North Korea backed hackers have created Elon Musk themed memecoins to launder stolen crypto in the $6.4 billion Binance hack. The hackers are using fake trading activity to disguise the movement of stolen funds.

One of the tokens featured Musk beneath an “Elon 2028 President” banner. Five others carried cartoon animals, crude jokes and familiar dog-coin branding. All six were created within three days and quickly abandoned.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic identified 117,000 NEAR tokens, worth $430,000, passing through the homemade coins between November 5 and November 7. The operation offers another look at how North Korea’s crypto laundering networks are adapting their techniques to move stolen assets.

Elliptic identified six newly created tokens on the NEAR blockchain: FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI and SINU. Each token was paired with NEAR in its own decentralized exchange liquidity pool. The hackers then used one group of wallets to purchase the tokens with stolen NEAR before another group sold them back.

North Korea’s launderers are creating their own meme coins to move funds stolen from Binance.Between November 5 and 7, they launched at least six tokens on NEAR, dressed up with meme-coin logos such as a monkey in a pink bow and a duck in front of a US flag. Stolen NEAR went…

This separated the buying and selling wallets, preventing the stolen funds from moving directly between them. The transactions consequently resembled ordinary crypto trading, with the receiving wallets appearing to collect proceeds from successful memecoin trades.

Blockchain investigators could still follow the money. Elliptic found that almost all trading activity came from wallets connected to the laundering operation. Outside buyers accounted for less than 1% of one token’s trading volume.

The operation was also remarkably inexpensive. Creating each token cost just as low as 25 NEAR, or worth around $90. Five of the six token creators received funding from wallets that had already participated in earlier token sales.

The tokens were effectively disposable. All six stopped trading by November 8, with the creators of four withdrawing remaining liquidity.

The technique does not erase the transaction trail. Instead, it introduces additional steps that slow investigators trying to connect stolen funds with their eventual destinations. The firm previously identified a similar approach following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. North Korean launderers moved at least $24 million through homemade tokens using the same basic mechanism.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The memecoin operation represents only a small fraction of the cryptocurrency stolen from Binance. The approximately $6.43 billion was taken from the exchange on October 29, making it the largest crypto theft ever recorded. Binance estimated its losses at $6.3 billion.

The FBI subsequently attributed the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Investigators have identified multiple laundering techniques since the breach, including cryptocurrency swaps, cross-chain transfers, and movements through decentralized finance platforms.

Approximately $2.85 billion has been frozen, representing around 44% of the stolen assets. This leaves billions requiring further tracing as investigators race to identify wallets and freeze assets wherever possible.

The use of North Korean hackers and memecoins adds another disposable layer to this operation. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional exchanges or direct wallet transfers, hackers can manufacture trading activity around virtually worthless tokens.

Bitcoin Hyper is among the projects pursuing this approach, combining a Solana Virtual Machine-based execution environment with Bitcoin settlement. Its proposed infrastructure targets near-instant transaction finality alongside decentralized applications and DeFi functionality.

#5415. A day after Anthropic’s office push, Databricks jumps in with AI agents that never sleep

The AI industry’s battle for the knowledge worker is heating up.

On Wednesday, San Francisco startup Databricks launched a new set of agentic AI tools that continuously analyze and organize the reams of data scattered throughout a business—a capability Databricks says will transform the way office workers do their jobs.

“The agents are running in the background all the time. So it’s always on,” Databricks CEO and cofounder Ali Ghodsi told Fortune ahead of the announcement. “I personally use it every day. Every hour of the day. It’s basically made me a 10x better CEO than I was a year ago,” Ghodsi said.

The product introduction comes a day after Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, released its own set of AI productivity tools aimed at corporate users. Those tools include a new AI-powered spreadsheet application that competes with Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, as well as a feature that lets Claude join video calls, allowing the AI to listen to the conversation and “start on the work while people are still talking.”

Databricks’ updated version of its Genie assistant, launched Wednesday, also operates in the background, shadowing an office worker throughout the day, proactively making suggestions and retrieving information based on whatever is happening. A separate “Ontology” feature essentially scans all the data within an organization—from management reporting lines to projects in various departments—so that an individual can quickly access information or run analyses.

“Lots of companies, both big and small, will use this,” said Ghodsi.

The AI industry is stepping up efforts to make inroads into corporations and to broaden the base of paying customers. While AI has transformed the way that software programmers do their jobs, becoming an indispensable tool in the profession, the technology is still in the experimental phase for other business functions where the return on investment is not as clear-cut.

With the advent of AI agents that autonomously perform tasks on a user’s behalf, as well as recent advances in AI model capabilities, some believe the technology may be ready to capture a broader swath of the market.

“We believe the work that knowledge workers perform represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025, and with frontier AI’s potential to make them meaningfully more productive, our near-term opportunity is to expand this value and accelerate economic growth,” Anthropic says in the prospectus for its initial public offering, expected next week.

The IPO, which could value Anthropic at $1.4 trillion, is being closely watched, with many in the industry hoping a strong debut on Wall Street will serve as a positive signal for the prospects of the broader AI industry. Databricks, which is still a privately held company, raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation in August.

The industry has also been shaken by the recent revelation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman that U.S. officials believe to be a spy for China. Given the importance of Nvidia’s chips, and its financing, across the AI industry, there are fears of a ripple effect if he is forced to step down.

Databricks’ Ghodsi brushed off the notion however. “I think that Jensen is an amazing CEO. He’s built that company for the last many decades. I think he should continue to be the CEO of that company,” he added.

“I think we will weather through this storm,” he added, noting that the AI revolution is too big to be impacted by the revelations of the Nvidia CEO’s affair.

Alexei Oreskovic is the Tech editor at Fortune.

#5414. He Started a Pizza Side Hustle in His San Diego Apartment After a Layoff. Now 3,500 People Battle for the 15 Pies He Makes a Week: ‘People Like What They Can’t Get’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Connecticut-native AJ Miller cooks New Haven-style “apizza” out of his San Diego apartment. Getting a pie is like winning the lottery.

After moving to San Diego in 2020, AJ Miller couldn’t find the East Coast-style pizza he grew up on, so he taught himself to make New Haven-style “apizza.” He sets his home oven to its 550-degree max, bakes on a heavy steel plate and finishes the pies under the broiler. “It took a couple years to really perfect my craft,” he told the California Post.

He didn’t realize how much this craft would pay off. This past summer, Miller was laid off from his marketing job and had to scramble to make ends meet. He started Echo Apizza out of his Ocean Beach apartment with a text list of about 75 customers. Word spread quickly and so did his list. More than 3,500 people now vie for the just 15 orders he makes a week. The 15-inch pies sell out in less than 30 seconds and cost $25 to $30 each.

The only obstacle Miller faces is keeping up with demand, but scarcity is sort of his secret sauce. “I think people do like what they can’t get,” he said.

He didn’t realize how much this craft would pay off. This past summer, Miller was laid off from his marketing job and had to scramble to make ends meet. He started Echo Apizza out of his Ocean Beach apartment with a text list of about 75 customers. Word spread quickly and so did his list. More than 3,500 people now vie for the just 15 orders he makes a week. The 15-inch pies sell out in less than 30 seconds and cost $25 to $30 each.

The only obstacle Miller faces is keeping up with demand, but scarcity is sort of his secret sauce. “I think people do like what they can’t get,” he said.

#5413. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5412. Report: Nvidia is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after admission to affair with alleged Chinese spy

Nvidia’s board of directors is preparing to remove Chief Executive Jensen Huang, an ouster that would follow his admission of having an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials deemed to be a Chinese spy. The decision by the chipmaking giant, reported by the Wall Street Journal, would deal a swift end to Huang’s 33-year reign as CEO and promises to send shockwaves throughout the technology industry and upend America’s race in artificial intelligence.

The Journal reported that Nvidia’s board could meet as soon as Wednesday to determine his fate. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang, 63 years old, had also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care. Powell could not immediately be reached for comment.

In after-hours trading, Nvidia’s shares were down more than 7%. According to LinkedIn, Powell has been with Nvidia for nearly two decades and previously spent 10 years in AI business development. Nvidia describes her as formerly leading the company’s higher education and research business, alongside Nvidia AI labs.

Huang’s long-term future with the company is not immediately clear. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia announced an investigation into the reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. At the time, the board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its inquiry would examine “all available information.”

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has been integral to the company’s success, particularly its magnificent run in recent years. For fiscal 2026, which ended in January, the company reported revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% over the prior year. Growth accelerated in the first half of fiscal 2027, with revenue of $96 billion, up 85% year over year. Nvidia previously guided third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, and chief financial officer Colette Kress said the company expected 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028.

Huang reigns supreme over the company. Since its founding, he has created a unique, flat structure in which he sits at the center of most decisions, with about 60 direct reports. Nvidia’s board operates without a chair, and the company has not set out a clear succession plan. It also does not have a chief operating officer. Huang is known to text and call small clients himself.

Nvidia’s succession challenge would not be whether its engineers can keep building chips without Huang, analysts say. It is whether anyone, or any leadership team, can inherit his authority to decide what gets built, secure the industry’s commitment to it, and keep customers confident in the next bet.

The factors behind Huang’s now-expected removal “hasten a transition the company is not prepared for,” Gil Luria, an analyst with D.A. Davidson & Co., told Fortune.

Nvidia’s board decision would be a forced hand. “There are rules about that; there are laws about that,” Jay Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners told Fortune, speaking about the untenability of Huang as CEO if there were internal policy violations. Nvidia won’t “go away. They’re sold out. It’s all contracted into next year, but it loses a lot of its luster. The chances of making a misstep are higher.”

If Huang is ousted, the most immediate question is who will succeed him, and what sort of new plan the company will put in place to fill the vacuum of power.

“Rarely has a board faced this much pressure. This is the board’s moment to shine or fade,” Michael Useem, a professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told Fortune. “If the board had been doing its job, it would already have a slate of possible successors: people identified as likely successors.”

Business and law experts have said Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, could be an option for interim CEO. Another option would be to have one of the company’s directors, such as lead independent director Stephen Neal, who is chairman emeritus and senior counsel at law firm Cooley LLP, take over as interim CEO if Huang is removed. Huang’s children and son-in-law also work at the company.

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies and Lester Crown Professor in Management Practice at Yale University’s School of Management, compared the Huang saga to what happened at McDonald’s with former CEO Steve Easterbrook, who was ousted in November 2019. The McDonald’s board investigated Easterbrook for a consensual relationship with an employee that involved the exchange of videos and romantic text messages, and then found that other undisclosed, improper relationships had occurred.

Easterbrook was later charged by the SEC with making false and misleading statements to investors about the circumstances that led to his termination. Easterbrook didn’t admit or deny the findings, but agreed to a five-year officer and director bar and paid a $400,000 civil penalty.

Huang’s ouster would create a massive hole for the AI industry. Huang has been central to the industry’s rapid growth. His success in creating world-leading graphics processing units, the chips that power AI by handling model training and regular user queries, has been instrumental in ushering in the AI boom and in the U.S.’s leading position.

Few executives in Silicon Valley and beyond exert the level of power and influence over one company and industry. Huang’s institutional knowledge and deep industry connections have been among the reasons tech analysts and other experts have said it would be impossible to replace him. Another reason has been President Trump, who has become a close friend of Huang and stood by the executive since Sunday’s revelations, saying Huang is an “amazing guy” and “honorable man.”

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.
